duchy-of-glogow.t: Silesian Piast duchy on the Oder whose dukes claimed Greater Poland, later a Bohemian fief held briefly by the future King Sigismund I of Poland.
duchy-of-glogow.o: Konrad I, a son of Henry II the Pious, received Głogów and the lands around it in a division of the Silesian inheritance around 1251. Głogów, a fortified town on the Oder, became the capital of a duchy covering much of northern Silesia.
duchy-of-glogow.r: Konrad's son Henry III of Głogów was one of the most powerful Silesian princes, holding Greater Poland for a time and claiming the Polish crown. After him the duchy was divided among branches, including Żagań and Oleśnica. Half of Głogów passed directly to the Bohemian crown in 1331, and the remaining dukes became vassals of the Kingdom of Bohemia. German settlement and town law transformed the region.
duchy-of-glogow.e: After the Piast lines died out and disputes followed, Głogów was granted to the Jagiellonian Sigismund, who ruled it from 1499 until 1506 before becoming King of Poland. It then returned to the Bohemian crown, passed to Prussia in 1742, and to Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-upper-bavaria.t: Wittelsbach duchy ruled from Munich, created in the first partition of Bavaria in 1255 and home of Emperor Louis IV the Bavarian.
duchy-of-upper-bavaria.o: In 1255 Duke Otto II's sons divided the Duchy of Bavaria, the first of many Wittelsbach partitions. Louis II the Strict received Upper Bavaria, with Munich as residence, together with the Rhenish Palatinate, while his brother Henry XIII took the Duchy of Lower Bavaria.
duchy-of-upper-bavaria.r: Louis II made Munich a ducal capital and acquired Hohenstaufen lands after Conradin's execution in 1268. His sons Rudolf I and Louis IV ruled jointly, then fought each other. Louis IV was elected King of the Romans in 1314, defeated Frederick the Fair at Mühldorf in 1322 and was crowned emperor in Rome in 1328. By the Treaty of Pavia in 1329 the Palatinate went to Rudolf's heirs.
duchy-of-upper-bavaria.e: When the Lower Bavarian line died out in 1340, Louis IV reunited Upper and Lower Bavaria. After his death in 1347 his sons divided the lands again, but Munich remained the Wittelsbach capital until 1918.

duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.t: The Dutch half of Limburg, made a duchy of the German Confederation in 1839 to compensate the Confederation for losing part of Luxembourg.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.o: The Treaty of London of 1839 divided Limburg between Belgium and the Netherlands. Because the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg lost its western half to Belgium, the Dutch part of Limburg was made a duchy and joined the German Confederation, held by the Dutch king, though Maastricht and Venlo were left outside the Confederation.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.r: The duchy was governed as a Dutch province while its estates sent representatives to the Confederation's diet in Frankfurt. In 1848 some Limburgers sought separation from the Netherlands to join Germany, and deputies sat in the Frankfurt Parliament. Mining and Maastricht's pottery and glass industries developed.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.e: The German Confederation dissolved after the war of 1866, and the Treaty of London of 1867 confirmed that Limburg was fully part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The title 'Duchy of Limburg' lingered in official use until 1906.

diauehi.t: A tribal union in the highlands of north-eastern Anatolia, known from Assyrian and Urartian war records and often linked with the later Georgian region of Tao.
diauehi.o: Known almost entirely from the inscriptions of its enemies. The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I names the lands of Daiaeni among the Nairi peoples he fought around 1112 BCE, and Shalmaneser III defeated its king Sien in 845 BCE. The union seems to have centred on the upper Euphrates and Chorokhi valleys.
diauehi.r: Its rulers commanded fortified settlements and a mixed economy of herding, farming and metalworking in rich ore country. Urartian annals record large tributes of gold, silver, copper and cattle, which suggests a wealthy, organised society, though nothing survives in its own words. Many scholars regard its people as early Kartvelian speakers.
diauehi.e: Diauehi was worn down by repeated campaigns of the Kingdom of Urartu under Menua and Argishti I, and its king Utupurshi was forced into tribute. By about 760 BCE it was absorbed, and its northern lands passed into the orbit of the rising Kingdom of Colchis.

dahae.t: A confederation of Iranian nomads east of the Caspian whose Parni tribe founded the Parthian dynasty that would rule Iran for nearly five centuries.
dahae.o: The Dahae appear in a daiva inscription of Xerxes I and in Greek accounts of the Achaemenid army, living on the steppes south-east of the Caspian Sea, in what is now Turkmenistan. They comprised three main tribes, the Parni, Xanthii and Pissuri, and are often counted among the Saka peoples.
dahae.r: They were horse-riding pastoralists famed as mounted archers, serving as cavalry for Darius III at Gaugamela and later for Alexander the Great and his successors. Their territory, later called Dahistan, bordered the farming lands of Hyrcania and Margiana, and they traded and raided along this edge.
dahae.e: Around 247 BCE Arsaces, leader of the Parni, seized the Seleucid province of Parthia, founding the Arsacid dynasty of the Parthian Empire. The remaining Dahae were absorbed into Parthian and later steppe populations, though the name Dahistan survived for the region into Islamic times.

duchy-of-aquitaine.t: The great duchy of south-western France, home of troubadour courts and Eleanor of Aquitaine, fought over by the kings of England and France for three centuries.
duchy-of-aquitaine.o: The Frankish kingdom of Aquitaine dissolved in the late 9th century, and in 893 William the Pious, count of Auvergne, took the ducal title; he founded the abbey of Cluny in 910. From the mid-10th century the counts of Poitou, the Ramnulfids, held the duchy and ruled from Poitiers.
duchy-of-aquitaine.r: The dukes ruled loosely over powerful vassals in Gascony, the Limousin and Auvergne. Their court was a centre of Occitan culture: Duke William IX is the earliest known troubadour. Bordeaux grew rich on wine exports to England. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought the duchy first to Louis VII of France and then, in 1152, to Henry II, joining it to the Angevin Empire.
duchy-of-aquitaine.e: English kings held the duchy as vassals of France, reduced after 1204 to Gascony, or Guyenne, and confirmed by the Treaty of Paris of 1259. Disputes over it helped spark the Hundred Years' War, which ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 and the annexation of Guyenne to the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-castro.t: A Farnese duchy in northern Lazio created by Pope Paul III for his son, whose capital was razed by a later pope in 1649.
duchy-of-castro.o: In 1537 Pope Paul III, born Alessandro Farnese, carved the Duchy of Castro out of the Papal States for his son Pier Luigi Farnese. It covered the old Farnese estates between Lake Bolsena and the Tyrrhenian coast.
duchy-of-castro.r: Castro was rebuilt as a small Renaissance capital, with buildings by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger. After 1545 its dukes were also dukes of the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza, and they ran Castro from afar, borrowing heavily against it. A quarrel over these debts and the Farnese's power led Pope Urban VIII to fight the First War of Castro in 1641–1644, which ended in a papal setback.
duchy-of-castro.e: In 1649, after the murder of the new bishop of Castro was blamed on the Farnese, Pope Innocent X's troops took the town and razed it to the ground. The duchy was absorbed into the Papal States.

duchy-of-westphalia.t: Ducal territory in the Sauerland held for six centuries by the archbishops of Cologne after the fall of Henry the Lion.
duchy-of-westphalia.o: When Henry the Lion was deposed, the Gelnhausen Charter of 1180 split his Duchy of Saxony. The western part, with the title Duke of Westphalia and Engern, went to Archbishop Philip of Heinsberg of Cologne. The archbishops turned this title into real rule over the Sauerland, buying the County of Arnsberg in 1368.
duchy-of-westphalia.r: Ruled by the Electorate of Cologne as a separate territory, the duchy had its own estates and diet meeting at Arnsberg, with an electoral governor there. The land was hilly and rural, known for iron working and forestry. Cologne's ambitions in the region were checked by its defeat at Worringen in 1288 and by the Soest Feud, in which Soest broke away to Cleves. The duchy stayed Catholic throughout.
duchy-of-westphalia.e: In 1803 the duchy was secularised and given to Hesse-Darmstadt. The Congress of Vienna transferred it to Prussia in 1816, and it became part of the Prussian Province of Westphalia; it now lies in North Rhine-Westphalia.

duchy-of-lotharingia.t: The duchy that held together the old middle kingdom of Lothair II, between France and Germany, before it was split into Upper and Lower Lorraine in 959.
duchy-of-lotharingia.o: Lotharingia was the kingdom created for Lothair II in 855, stretching from Frisia to the Vosges. After the Carolingian lines weakened, the East Frankish king Louis the Child appointed Gebhard as duke in 903. Local nobles, led by the Reginarids, repeatedly switched allegiance between East and West Francia.
duchy-of-lotharingia.r: The duchy held the old Carolingian heartland around Aachen, Trier, Metz and Liège, rich in bishoprics and royal abbeys. Duke Gilbert went over to the West Frankish king before Henry the Fowler recovered the region in 925; Gilbert drowned at Andernach in 939 while rebelling against Otto I. Otto's son-in-law Conrad the Red rebelled in 953.
duchy-of-lotharingia.e: Otto I then gave the duchy to his brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who divided it in 959 into the Duchy of Upper Lorraine and the Duchy of Lower Lorraine. Upper Lorraine became the later Duchy of Lorraine; the Low Countries principalities grew out of Lower Lorraine.
duchy-of-lotharingia.la: Old French and Old High German

duchy-of-brzeg.t: A Silesian Piast duchy on the Oder whose Lutheran dukes and Renaissance castle outlasted almost every other branch of the dynasty.
duchy-of-brzeg.o: In 1311 the sons of Duke Henry V of Legnica divided their inheritance, and Bolesław III the Generous took Brzeg (Brieg) on the Oder as his duchy, separating it from the Duchy of Legnica. In 1329 Bolesław did homage to King John of Bohemia, placing Brzeg under the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-brzeg.r: Brzeg was often held together with Legnica under one duke, and its rulers were among the leading Silesian princes. Duke Frederick II introduced the Lutheran Reformation in the 1520s and in 1537 made an inheritance treaty with Brandenburg. Under George II the castle was rebuilt in Renaissance style, with a gatehouse adorned with statues of the Piasts, and a gymnasium was founded in 1569.
duchy-of-brzeg.e: When George William, the last Silesian Piast, died in 1675, the Habsburgs as kings of Bohemia took the duchy, ignoring Brandenburg's claim. Frederick II of Prussia later used that claim to justify his invasion of Silesia, which Prussia won in 1742. Brzeg became part of Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-wroclaw.t: Lower Silesian Piast duchy centred on Wrocław, whose duke Henry IV Probus sought the Polish crown before the duchy passed to Bohemia.
duchy-of-wroclaw.o: In 1248 the sons of Henry II the Pious divided the Duchy of Silesia. Henry III the White received Wrocław, the richest city of the region, and its surrounding lands, while his brother Bolesław II took Legnica. Wrocław had been rebuilt after the Mongol attack of 1241 and refounded under German town law.
duchy-of-wroclaw.r: The dukes ruled a prosperous land of grain, cloth and trade, encouraging German settlers alongside the Polish population. Henry IV Probus, also remembered as a minnesinger, won Kraków and tried to unite Poland before his death in 1290. Henry V the Fat and Henry VI the Good lost lands to their relatives and had to balance Bohemia against Poland.
duchy-of-wroclaw.e: Henry VI the Good recognised the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1327. On his death in 1335 the duchy passed directly to the Bohemian crown. Wrocław remained Bohemian and Habsburg until Prussia took Silesia in 1742, and it has been Polish since 1945.

duchy-of-volhynia.t: The Lithuanian-ruled duchy of Volhynia, held by Lubart and later Svidrigaila from the great castle at Lutsk.
duchy-of-volhynia.o: When the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia collapsed after 1340, Lubart, a son of Gediminas who had married into the local dynasty, took control of Volhynia. For decades he fought Casimir III of Poland for the whole inheritance of Galicia-Volhynia, holding Volhynia while Poland kept Galicia.
duchy-of-volhynia.r: Lubart built the brick castle at Lutsk that still bears his name, and his rule mixed Lithuanian princes with Orthodox Ruthenian nobles and church. The duchy had its own court and was one of the most valuable lands of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Later Svidrigaila, a son of Algirdas, ruled it from the 1430s after losing the struggle for the grand ducal throne.
duchy-of-volhynia.e: After Svidrigaila died in 1452, Volhynia lost its status as a separate duchy and became a voivodeship of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. In 1569 the Union of Lublin transferred it to the Polish Crown.

duchy-of-the-archipelago.t: Latin duchy of the Cyclades centred on Naxos, founded by the Venetian Marco Sanudo, which outlived most crusader states in Greece by more than a century.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.o: Around 1207 Marco Sanudo, nephew of the doge Enrico Dandolo, led a private Venetian expedition that conquered Naxos and other Cycladic islands, sharing some with fellow adventurers. He took the title Duke of the Archipelago under the suzerainty of the Latin Empire and later of the Principality of Achaea.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.r: The dukes ruled from the Kastro of Naxos, granting fiefs to Latin lords on islands such as Andros, Paros and Milos. A Catholic minority lived alongside a Greek Orthodox majority, which kept its church. Revenues came from agriculture, emery and trade. In 1383 Francesco I Crispo seized the duchy and founded a new dynasty.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.e: Barbarossa's raids of 1537 made the duchy an Ottoman tributary. In 1566 the Ottomans deposed Giacomo IV Crispo and gave the duchy to the Jewish financier Joseph Nasi, who ruled through a deputy. After his death in 1579 it was annexed to the Ottoman Empire.

duchy-of-saxe-eisenach.t: Ernestine Saxon duchy around the Wartburg, birthplace of Johann Sebastian Bach, later merged with Weimar.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenach.o: After the 1662 division of Saxe-Weimar, Eisenach was briefly held by Adolf William, whose line ended in 1671. In 1672 John George I, previously lord of Marksuhl, received Eisenach as a separate Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach, founding the line that ruled it until 1741.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenach.r: The duchy took in parts of Saxe-Jena in 1690. It was Lutheran, with the Wartburg castle, where Luther had translated the New Testament, as its landmark. Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach in 1685, the son of a town musician, and Georg Philipp Telemann served as Kapellmeister at the Eisenach court. Johann Wilhelm ruled from 1698 to 1729.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenach.e: Duke William Henry died without heirs in 1741, and the duchy passed to Ernest Augustus I of Saxe-Weimar, creating the Duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, which lasted until 1918.

duchy-of-normandy.t: The Viking settlement on the lower Seine that became one of Europe's best-run principalities and launched the Norman conquest of England.
duchy-of-normandy.o: In 911, by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, King Charles the Simple granted lands around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in return for defending the Seine. Rollo's descendants expanded westwards to the Cotentin, adopted Christianity and the French language, and were styled dukes by the early 11th century.
duchy-of-normandy.r: The dukes built unusually firm control over their barons, castles and the Church. Monasteries such as Jumièges, Fécamp, Bec and Mont-Saint-Michel flourished, and Bec produced the scholars Lanfranc and Anselm. Normans also carved out lands in southern Italy and Sicily. In 1066 Duke William won the battle of Hastings and became king of England.
duchy-of-normandy.e: Normandy passed to the Plantagenets and formed a pillar of the Angevin Empire. Philip II of France took Château Gaillard and Rouen in 1204, annexing the duchy to the Kingdom of France. The Channel Islands remained with the English crown.

duchy-of-thuringia.t: A Frankish frontier duchy in central Germany, set up against the Slavs, whose dukes briefly ruled almost independently before Carolingian absorption.
duchy-of-thuringia.o: After the Franks destroyed the Kingdom of the Thuringians in 531, the area was ruled by Frankish officials. Around 631 King Dagobert I appointed Radulf duke to defend the eastern frontier against the Slavs of Samo's Empire, then raiding Thuringia. Radulf soon defeated Dagobert's son Sigebert III in 641 and ruled as a near-independent king.
duchy-of-thuringia.r: Later Thuringia was held by the Hedenid dukes, based at Würzburg on the Main. Duke Heden II supported the Anglo-Saxon missionary Willibrord, who received estates at Arnstadt in 704, and a church was founded on the Marienberg at Würzburg. The duchy guarded the border with the Saxons and the Sorbs.
duchy-of-thuringia.e: Heden II disappears around 717 to 719, perhaps after the Battle of Vincy, and Charles Martel brought Thuringia under direct Frankish control. Saint Boniface reorganised its church, founding the bishopric of Würzburg in 742. The region later formed part of the Duchy of Saxony and the Landgraviate of Thuringia.

duchy-of-montferrat.t: A Piedmontese duchy of the Gonzaga, whose fortress of Casale was one of the most contested strongholds in 17th-century Europe.
duchy-of-montferrat.o: The Gonzaga of the Duchy of Mantua had inherited the March of Montferrat in 1536. In 1574 Emperor Maximilian II raised it to a duchy for Duke Guglielmo Gonzaga, who governed it from Mantua through a council at Casale.
duchy-of-montferrat.r: Montferrat was a hilly wine-growing region split into two parts and surrounded by the Duchy of Savoy and the Duchy of Milan. Its local nobles resented Mantuan rule. Vincenzo I Gonzaga built the great citadel of Casale around 1590. When the main Gonzaga line died out in 1627, the War of the Mantuan Succession brought sieges of Casale by Spain and Savoy against France. The Peace of Cherasco in 1631 gave parts to Savoy and the rest to Charles I Gonzaga-Nevers.
duchy-of-montferrat.e: The last duke, Ferdinando Carlo, sided with France and was deposed in 1708. Montferrat was given to the Duchy of Savoy, a transfer confirmed by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

duchy-of-saxe-zeitz.t: Short-lived Albertine Saxon duchy based on the old bishopric of Naumburg-Zeitz, created by an elector's will.
duchy-of-saxe-zeitz.o: In his will, Elector John George I of Saxony created three secondary duchies for his younger sons. After his death in 1656, Maurice received Zeitz with the secularised bishopric of Naumburg and lands in the Vogtland and around Neustadt an der Orla, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Zeitz.
duchy-of-saxe-zeitz.r: Maurice built Moritzburg palace in Zeitz as his residence and kept a Lutheran court. The duchy remained under the Electorate of Saxony's sovereignty in foreign and military affairs. His son Maurice William converted to Catholicism in 1715, a shock to his Lutheran subjects, and his relative Christian August became a Catholic cardinal and archbishop of Esztergom.
duchy-of-saxe-zeitz.e: Maurice William died without surviving male heirs in 1718, and the duchy reverted to the Electorate of Saxony. Zeitz passed to Prussia in 1815 and lies today in Saxony-Anhalt.

duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia.t: Baltic duchy of the Kettler dynasty under Polish overlordship, famous for Duke Jacob's colonies in Africa and the Caribbean.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia.o: When the Livonian Order dissolved in 1561, its last master, Gotthard Kettler, secularised the Order's lands south of the Daugava and became hereditary Duke of Courland and Semigallia, a vassal of Poland-Lithuania. The duchy's capital was Mitau (Jelgava).
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia.r: The Lutheran Baltic German nobility dominated the duchy, holding Latvian peasants in serfdom, and the dukes often clashed with them. Duke Jacob Kettler (1642-1682) built ironworks, shipyards and a merchant fleet, and founded colonies at Courland Gambia and Courland Tobago. In the 18th century Russian influence grew; Ernst Johann von Biron, favourite of Empress Anna, became duke in 1737 and built Rundāle Palace.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia.e: Wars, especially the Great Northern War, ruined the duchy's prosperity. After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, the Courland nobility submitted to Catherine the Great, and the duchy was annexed by Russia, becoming the Governorate of Courland.

duchy-of-arenberg.t: Small Eifel territory of the Arenberg family, great nobles of the Habsburg Netherlands who held ducal rank in the Empire.
duchy-of-arenberg.o: The lordship of Arenberg, named after a castle in the Eifel, passed through heiresses to the Ligne family in the 16th century, which took the Arenberg name. It became a princely county in 1576, and in 1644 Emperor Ferdinand III raised it to a duchy under Philippe-Charles d'Arenberg.
duchy-of-arenberg.r: The Eifel territory was tiny; the dukes' wealth and influence lay in vast estates in the Spanish and later Austrian Netherlands, where they served as governors, generals and courtiers in Brussels. The family was Catholic. After losing the left-bank lands to France, the duke received the former Münster district of Meppen and the Cologne enclave of Recklinghausen in 1803.
duchy-of-arenberg.e: Arenberg joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806, but Napoleon annexed its northern lands to France in 1810. In 1815 Meppen came under the Kingdom of Hanover and Recklinghausen under Prussia, with the dukes as mediatised lords.

duchy-of-scinawa.t: Small Silesian Piast duchy on the Oder, split off from Głogów in the late 13th century and repeatedly passed between related princes.
duchy-of-scinawa.o: After the death of Konrad I of Głogów in 1274, his lands were divided among his sons, and Ścinawa on the Oder, with its surrounding district, became the seat of a small separate duchy. Its first rulers included Przemko of Ścinawa, who died fighting in 1289.
duchy-of-scinawa.r: Little is known of its internal history. The duchy was a modest territory of farmland and small towns between Głogów and Wrocław, ruled by Silesian Piasts who often held other lands as well, and it passed back and forth within the Głogów branch. Its dukes accepted Bohemian overlordship in the 1320s and 1330s.
duchy-of-scinawa.e: The duchy was absorbed back into the lands of the Głogów and Żagań Piasts in the mid 14th century, by 1365, and later followed them under the Bohemian crown. Ścinawa is now a small town in Poland.

duchy-of-saxe-weimar-eisenach.t: Thuringian duchy whose court at Weimar drew Goethe, Schiller, Herder and Wieland and became the heart of German classicism.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar-eisenach.o: Saxe-Weimar and Saxe-Eisenach were united in 1741 when Duke Ernest Augustus I of Saxe-Weimar inherited Eisenach on the extinction of its ducal line, creating Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar-eisenach.r: Duchess Anna Amalia, regent from 1758, invited Christoph Martin Wieland as tutor; her son Charles Augustus brought Goethe to Weimar in 1775, later followed by Herder and Schiller, while the University of Jena flourished. Raised to a grand duchy in 1815, it adopted one of the first German constitutions in 1816. Later grand dukes hosted Franz Liszt and founded the Weimar art school.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar-eisenach.e: The grand duchy joined the German Empire in 1871. Grand Duke William Ernest abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the territory joined the Free State of Thuringia, with Weimar as capital.

district-of-brankovic.t: Lordship of Vuk Branković in Kosovo and northern Macedonia, rich in silver mines, which later merged into the Serbian Despotate.
district-of-brankovic.o: Vuk Branković, son-in-law of Prince Lazar, built up lands in Kosovo after the collapse of the Serbian Empire. From about 1371 he held Priština, Peć and the mining districts, and later took Skopje, ruling as Lazar's ally.
district-of-brankovic.r: Vuk ruled from Priština and Vučitrn, drawing income from the silver mines of Trepča and Novo Brdo and protecting the Patriarchate of Peć. He fought at Kosovo in 1389 and survived; later legend unjustly made him the traitor of the battle. Afterwards he resisted Ottoman vassalage longer than other Serbian lords, seeking help from Hungary.
district-of-brankovic.e: The Ottomans captured Vuk and he died in captivity in 1397. His sons, including Đurađ Branković, held part of his lands as Ottoman vassals and in 1412 made peace with Stefan Lazarević; the district merged into the Serbian Despotate, which Đurađ inherited in 1427.

daorsi.t: Hellenised Illyrian people of the lower Neretva, whose walled hill town of Daorson near Stolac minted its own coins.
daorsi.o: The Daorsi emerged in the Neretva valley of Herzegovina, in contact with Greek traders at Narona and the island colonies of the Adriatic. By the 3rd century BCE they had a fortified centre at Daorson, on a hill near modern Stolac, enclosed by massive Cyclopean walls.
daorsi.r: Greek influence was strong: the Daorsi struck bronze coins with Greek legends, used Greek-style buildings and traded wine, oil and pottery through the Neretva. They broke with the Illyrian king Gentius and sided with Rome in 168 BCE, which rewarded them with exemption from tribute. Their wealthier neighbours, the Delmatae, repeatedly attacked them.
daorsi.e: Daorson was destroyed in the mid-1st century BCE, probably by the Delmatae. The Daorsi were absorbed into Roman Illyricum by the end of the 1st century BCE, and their region later belonged to the province of Dalmatia.

duchy-of-carniola.t: The Habsburg duchy at the heart of modern Slovenia, centred on Ljubljana, a borderland between the German, Slovene and Italian worlds.
duchy-of-carniola.o: Carniola appears as a march of the Empire around 1040, a frontier zone against Hungary. Over the next two centuries it was held by various families, including the Weimar-Orlamünde counts, the patriarchs of Aquileia and the Andechs. The Habsburgs acquired it in 1335 with Carinthia, and Rudolf IV called himself Duke of Carniola in 1364.
duchy-of-carniola.r: Carniola's population was mainly Slovene peasants under German-speaking nobility. Ljubljana (Laibach) was the capital. Ottoman raids struck repeatedly from the 15th century. Primož Trubar printed the first books in Slovene in 1550, and the polymath Johann Weikhard von Valvasor described the land in The Glory of the Duchy of Carniola in 1689.
duchy-of-carniola.e: Napoleon included Carniola in the Illyrian Provinces from 1809 to 1813, then it returned to Austria. It was a crown land of Austria-Hungary until 1918, when it joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and later Yugoslavia. Its core is part of modern Slovenia.

ditadura-nacional.t: The military dictatorship that ended Portugal's First Republic and brought António de Oliveira Salazar to power.
ditadura-nacional.o: On 28 May 1926 a military coup launched from Braga by General Manuel Gomes da Costa overthrew the First Portuguese Republic. Within weeks Gomes da Costa was pushed aside by General Óscar Carmona, who became president.
ditadura-nacional.r: The military regime dissolved parliament, introduced censorship and repressed several revolts. Unable to solve the financial crisis, it appointed the Coimbra economics professor António de Oliveira Salazar as finance minister in 1928, with control over all spending. He balanced the budget and steadily accumulated power, becoming prime minister in 1932.
ditadura-nacional.e: A new constitution, approved by plebiscite in 1933, transformed the military dictatorship into Salazar's civilian, corporatist Estado Novo (Portugal), with Carmona remaining president.

duchy-of-brunswick.t: North German duchy of the House of Welf, ruled by the 'Black Duke' and later the subject of a long succession dispute.
duchy-of-brunswick.o: Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel had been absorbed into the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807. Duke Frederick William, the Black Duke, who had fought Napoleon with his Black Brunswickers, recovered his lands in 1813, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna recognised them as the sovereign Duchy of Brunswick. He was killed at Quatre Bras that June.
duchy-of-brunswick.r: His son Charles II was driven out by a rising in 1830 and replaced by his brother William, who granted a constitution in 1832. The duchy was Lutheran and had industry around Brunswick, with sugar beet and canning. When William died in 1884, Prussia blocked the Hanoverian heir, and regents ruled until Ernest Augustus married the Kaiser's daughter Victoria Louise in 1913 and became duke.
duchy-of-brunswick.e: Ernest Augustus abdicated in November 1918, and the duchy became the Free State of Brunswick. In 1946 its territory was merged into the new state of Lower Saxony, though the city of Braunschweig keeps the ducal palace, rebuilt in 2007.

duchy-of-sandomierz.t: A Piast duchy of eastern Lesser Poland around the Vistula town of Sandomierz, usually joined to Krakow in the age of division.
duchy-of-sandomierz.o: Boleslaw III's testament of 1138 assigned Sandomierz and its land to his young son Henry, who took control in 1146. Henry went on crusade to the Holy Land in 1154 and was killed fighting the pagan Prussians in 1166, after which the duchy passed to his brother Casimir II the Just.
duchy-of-sandomierz.r: Sandomierz was a prosperous trading town on the Vistula, on the route between Krakow and Rus'. For most of the period it was ruled by the same dukes as Krakow, so the two duchies formed Lesser Poland. The Mongols sacked the town in 1241 and again in 1260, killing many of its inhabitants and the Dominican friars of Saint James.
duchy-of-sandomierz.e: Its rulers included Leszek the White, Boleslaw V the Chaste and Leszek the Black. Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high gained Sandomierz in the early 14th century, and in 1320 it became part of the reunited Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385).

duchy-of-saxe-meiningen.t: Ernestine duchy in the Werra valley whose 'theatre duke' George II made its court troupe the most influential in Europe.
duchy-of-saxe-meiningen.o: Bernhard I, third son of Ernest the Pious, received Meiningen in the 1680 partition of the Saxe-Gotha inheritance and made the small town his residence, building Elisabethenburg Palace. The duchy later gained parts of Saxe-Römhild and, in the 1826 redistribution, Hildburghausen and Saalfeld.
duchy-of-saxe-meiningen.r: The duchy was Lutheran and largely rural, with forestry and small industries. George II, who reigned from 1866, personally directed the court theatre; the Meininger company toured Europe from 1874 with historically accurate staging and disciplined ensemble acting, influencing Stanislavski. The court orchestra under Hans von Bülow and Fritz Steinbach was associated with Johannes Brahms.
duchy-of-saxe-meiningen.e: Saxe-Meiningen sided with Austria in 1866, forcing Duke Bernhard II to abdicate in favour of George II. It joined the German Empire in 1871. Bernhard III abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the Free State of Thuringia.

duchy-of-legnica.t: The longest-lived Silesian Piast duchy, ruled from Legnica until 1675 and home to the first Protestant university project in Europe.
duchy-of-legnica.o: In the 1248 partition of the Duchy of Silesia, Bolesław II the Bald, son of Henry II the Pious who died fighting the Mongols near Legnica in 1241, received the duchy around Legnica. His successors also gained Brzeg and at times Wrocław.
duchy-of-legnica.r: The Legnica Piasts accepted Bohemian overlordship in 1329 while keeping their ducal rule. The duchy prospered from agriculture, mining and cloth. Frederick II of Legnica introduced the Lutheran Reformation in the 1520s and founded a university in 1526, the first Protestant one, though it soon closed. The dukes later adopted the Reformed faith and maintained a cultivated court at Legnica and Brzeg.
duchy-of-legnica.e: The last Piast duke, George William, died in 1675, ending the dynasty that had ruled since the 10th century. The duchy passed to the Habsburgs and in 1742 to Prussia. Legnica has been part of Poland since 1945.
duchy-of-legnica.re: Catholicism, then Lutheranism and Reformed Protestantism

duchy-of-swidnica.t: Piast duchy below the Sudetes whose duke Bolko II was the last Silesian prince independent of Bohemia, until his lands passed to the Bohemian crown in 1392.
duchy-of-swidnica.o: Bolko I the Strict, already Duke of Jawor, acquired Świdnica around 1291 and built a strong duchy along the Bohemian border. On his death in 1301 his son Bernard received Świdnica, which became a separate duchy. Bernard married a daughter of the Polish king Władysław I the Elbow-high.
duchy-of-swidnica.r: Świdnica was a prosperous town of cloth, beer and trade on the routes to Bohemia. Bolko II the Small, Bernard's son, refused to accept Bohemian overlordship, ruling as an independent prince and uniting Świdnica with Jawor in 1346. Without sons, he arranged the marriage of his niece Anne to Charles IV, making the Bohemian crown his heir.
duchy-of-swidnica.e: After Bolko II died in 1368, his widow Agnes ruled until her death in 1392, when the duchy passed to the Bohemian crown. It later went to the Habsburgs and Prussia, and has been Polish since 1945; its Peace Church is a World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-siewierz.t: A small Silesian duchy owned for almost 350 years by the bishops of Krakow, who styled themselves dukes of Siewierz.
duchy-of-siewierz.o: Siewierz, on the border of Silesia and Lesser Poland, belonged to the Silesian duchies under Bohemian overlordship. In 1443 Bishop Zbigniew Olesnicki of Krakow bought it from Duke Wenceslaus I of Cieszyn, and from then on the bishops of Krakow ruled it as secular princes.
duchy-of-siewierz.r: The duchy was a small territory with its own laws, courts and officials, ruled from a castle at Siewierz. Its position between Poland and Silesia led to disputes about whether it belonged to the Polish Crown or the Kingdom of Bohemia. Its iron and lead workings brought income to the bishops, who added the ducal title to their own.
duchy-of-siewierz.e: In 1790 the Great Sejm incorporated Siewierz into the Polish Crown, ending the bishops' secular rule. After the Third Partition in 1795 it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia, and later to the Duchy of Warsaw and Congress Poland.

duchy-of-livonia.t: Polish-Lithuanian Livonia, created when the crusader state dissolved in 1561, and fought over by Sweden and Poland for six decades.
duchy-of-livonia.o: By the Treaty of Vilnius in 1561, the Livonian Order and the Archbishopric of Riga submitted to Sigismund II Augustus. The lands north of the Daugava became the Duchy of Livonia, with the last master, Gotthard Kettler, as administrator. After the Union of Lublin in 1569 it was held jointly by Poland and Lithuania.
duchy-of-livonia.r: The Livonian War and later conflicts devastated the country. Stephen Báthory drove out the Russians by 1582 and reorganised Livonia into districts, promoting the Counter-Reformation through the Jesuits at Riga and Dorpat, which offended the Lutheran German nobility and towns. Riga, a free city until 1581, was the chief port.
duchy-of-livonia.e: From 1600 Sweden and Poland-Lithuania fought over Livonia; the Polish victory at Kircholm in 1605 delayed Swedish conquest, but Gustav II Adolf took Riga in 1621. The Truce of Altmark in 1629 left most of the duchy as Swedish Livonia, while the south-east, Latgale, remained Polish as the Inflanty Voivodeship.

durotriges.t: Dorset confederation of hillfort dwellers whose resistance ended when Vespasian's legion stormed strongholds such as Maiden Castle and Hod Hill.
durotriges.o: The Durotriges took shape in the late Iron Age across Dorset and neighbouring parts of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, a landscape dominated by great multivallate hillforts. Their harbour at Hengistbury Head traded with Armorica in the 1st century BCE, bringing in Italian wine amphorae and Gaulish pottery in exchange for metals, grain and cattle.
durotriges.r: Power seems to have been spread among several centres rather than held by one king, and no ruler's name appears on their coins, which became crude cast and debased silver issues. Hillforts such as Maiden Castle were heavily refortified and stocked with sling stones. The Durotriges buried their dead in crouched inhumations, unlike the cremation rites of the south-east, and Kimmeridge shale was worked into bracelets.
durotriges.e: In 43 and 44 the future emperor Vespasian, leading the legio II Augusta, took more than twenty strongholds in the south-west according to Suetonius; a Roman fort was built inside Hod Hill. The territory became the civitas of the Durotriges with its centre at Durnovaria, modern Dorchester, within Roman Britain.

duchy-of-kuyavia.t: A Piast duchy on the lower Vistula whose ruler Casimir I fathered the dukes who later reunited Poland.
duchy-of-kuyavia.o: Kuyavia, the fertile land around Inowroclaw and Kruszwica west of the Vistula, belonged to the Duchy of Masovia under Konrad I. In 1233 Konrad gave it to his son Casimir, who made it a separate duchy and later added Leczyca and Sieradz to his lands.
duchy-of-kuyavia.r: Kuyavia was rich in farmland and salt, and Kruszwica and Wloclawek, seat of the bishops of Kuyavia, were important centres. Bordering the State of the Teutonic Order across the Vistula, the duchy faced frequent disputes over land and trade. Casimir I fought his neighbours for influence in central Poland.
duchy-of-kuyavia.e: When Casimir I died in 1267 his lands were divided among his sons: Leszek the Black received Sieradz, Ziemomysl took the Duchy of Inowroclaw, and Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high and Casimir II shared the Duchy of Brzesc Kujawski. Wladyslaw later reunited Poland.

duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346.t: Northern Estonia under the Danish crown, won by Valdemar II's crusade in 1219 and sold to the Teutonic Order after the great peasant revolt of 1343.
duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346.o: In 1219 Valdemar II of Denmark landed at Lindanise, defeated the Estonians and built a castle on Toompea, the start of Reval. Denmark competed with the Livonian Brothers of the Sword for northern Estonia, and the Treaty of Stensby in 1238 confirmed Danish rule over Rävala, Harjumaa and Virumaa.
duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346.r: The Danish king ruled through a captain at Reval, but real power on the land lay with German vassals who formed the Harrien-Wierland knighthood, holding estates recorded in the Liber Census Daniae. Reval received Lübeck law in 1248 and became a Hanseatic port. Cistercian monasteries and parish churches spread Christianity among the Estonian peasants.
duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346.e: In 1343 the Estonians of Harjumaa rose in the St George's Night Uprising, killing many Germans. The Livonian Order crushed the revolt, and in 1346 Valdemar IV sold the duchy to the Teutonic Order, which handed it to its Livonian branch. Northern Estonia became part of the Livonian Order's lands.

duchy-of-guastalla.t: A small Po valley state first ruled by the Torelli and then by a branch of the Gonzaga, before joining Parma in 1748.
duchy-of-guastalla.o: In 1406 Guido Torelli, a condottiere in the service of the Visconti, received Guastalla, a town on the Po between Mantua and Parma. The Torelli ruled it as counts under the overlordship of the Duchy of Milan.
duchy-of-guastalla.r: In 1539 Countess Ludovica Torelli sold Guastalla to Ferrante Gonzaga, general of Charles V and governor of Milan, whose branch of the Gonzaga ruled it from then on. Ferrante II was made duke in 1621. The duchy was a fortified town with its farmland, and its rulers were often drawn into the quarrels over the Duchy of Mantua.
duchy-of-guastalla.e: The Guastalla Gonzaga died out in 1746. By the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 the duchy was given to Philip of Bourbon and joined to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.

dilmacogullari.t: A minor Turkish dynasty that ruled Bitlis and Erzen in south-eastern Anatolia in the 12th century.
dilmacogullari.o: Known mainly from brief mentions in Arabic chronicles, the dynasty descended from a Turkish commander named Dilmac who received Bitlis and Erzen, south-west of Lake Van, after the Seljuk conquest of the region in the late 11th century.
dilmacogullari.r: Its best-documented ruler is Toghan Arslan, nicknamed the Hunchback, who held Bitlis and Erzen in the early 12th century, allied with the Artuqid Ilghazi against the Georgians and the Crusaders, and fought his neighbours over Mayyafariqin. The beylik controlled the pass between Lake Van and the Tigris basin and acted as a vassal of stronger neighbours.
dilmacogullari.e: The dynasty faded under the pressure of the Shah-Armens of Ahlat and later the Ayyubids; its lands were absorbed around the end of the 12th century.

duchy-of-brno.t: One of the Moravian appanage duchies held by junior Přemyslid princes, centred on Brno, until Moravia was reunited as a margraviate.
duchy-of-brno.o: Duke Bretislaus I of Bohemia arranged Moravia as a domain for junior members of the Přemyslid dynasty. After his death in 1055, his sons divided it; Conrad I received the Brno portion, centred on the castle of Brno (Brünn) in southern Moravia, while Olomouc and later Znojmo formed separate appanages.
duchy-of-brno.r: The princes of Brno owed allegiance to the senior duke in Prague but frequently joined in the dynasty's feuds; Conrad I himself briefly became Duke of Bohemia in 1092. Brno grew as a castle and market centre. Little is known in detail of its administration, which followed the Bohemian castle system.
duchy-of-brno.e: In the late 12th century the Moravian appanages were absorbed. Around 1182 Moravia was declared a margraviate directly subject to the emperor, and by about 1197 Vladislaus Henry united the Moravian lands under his rule. Brno later became the capital of the Margraviate of Moravia.

duchy-of-poland.t: The first Polish state, created by the Piast dukes around Gniezno, which adopted Christianity in 966 and became a kingdom in 1025.
duchy-of-poland.o: Around 960 Mieszko I of the Piast dynasty ruled the Polans of Greater Poland from strongholds at Gniezno and Poznan. He married the Bohemian princess Dubrawka and was baptised in 966, bringing his realm into Latin Christendom. By the 990s he had added Pomerania, Silesia and Lesser Poland.
duchy-of-poland.r: The Piast dukes ruled through a network of fortified centres and a mounted retinue, and supported themselves with tribute and the slave trade. Around 991 Mieszko placed his lands under papal protection in the document known as Dagome iudex. His son Boleslaw I welcomed Otto III at the Congress of Gniezno in 1000, which created an archbishopric at Gniezno.
duchy-of-poland.e: Boleslaw I fought the emperor Henry II for years, gaining Lusatia at the Peace of Bautzen in 1018, and the same year briefly took Kiev. Shortly before his death in 1025 he was crowned king, and the duchy became the Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385).

duchy-of-znojmo.t: The southern Moravian appanage of the Přemyslid dynasty, centred on Znojmo, whose Romanesque rotunda preserves rare paintings of the Bohemian dukes.
duchy-of-znojmo.o: Znojmo in southern Moravia was split off from the Brno appanage around 1092, when Conrad I of Brno became Duke of Bohemia and his son Litold received Znojmo. It was one of three Moravian appanages, alongside Olomouc and Brno, held by junior Přemyslid princes.
duchy-of-znojmo.r: The princes ruled from the castle of Znojmo on a crag above the Dyje (Thaya) river, close to the Austrian border. The castle's Romanesque rotunda of Saint Catherine contains wall paintings of 1134 showing the legendary and historical Přemyslid rulers, an important source for the dynasty's self-image. Conrad II of Znojmo was a strong contender for the Bohemian throne.
duchy-of-znojmo.e: The appanage system ended in the late 12th century as Moravia became a margraviate; around 1197 Vladislaus Henry united the Moravian lands. Znojmo became a royal town in the 13th century under Ottokar I.

duchy-of-krnov.t: A Silesian duchy, known in German as Jägerndorf, held successively by Přemyslids, Hohenzollerns and the princes of Liechtenstein.
duchy-of-krnov.o: Krnov (Jägerndorf) emerged from the Přemyslid lands of the Duchy of Opava. After Duke Nicholas II died in 1365 his sons divided his possessions, and by 1377 John I held Krnov together with Racibórz as his own duchy, a fief of the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-krnov.r: After several changes of ruler, Krnov was bought in 1523 by Margrave George of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who introduced Lutheranism and rebuilt the castle. His Hohenzollern heirs held it until 1621, when Johann Georg lost it for supporting the Bohemian revolt. Emperor Ferdinand II then granted it to Karl of Liechtenstein, whose family kept the ducal title thereafter.
duchy-of-krnov.e: Frederick II of Prussia cited the Hohenzollern claim to Krnov when he invaded Silesia, and in 1742 Prussia annexed the northern part, while the town stayed in Austrian Silesia. The Liechtensteins kept the title until 1918, when Krnov became part of Czechoslovakia.

duchy-of-saint-sava.t: Domain of the Kosača family whose ruler's title, herceg, gave the region of Herzegovina its name.
duchy-of-saint-sava.o: Stjepan Vukčić Kosača inherited the lands of Hum and the coast from his uncle Sandalj Hranić in 1435, becoming the mightiest noble of the Kingdom of Bosnia. In 1448 he styled himself Herceg of Saint Sava, after the relics of the Serbian saint kept at the monastery of Mileševa in his territory, asserting independence from the Bosnian king.
duchy-of-saint-sava.r: From his castle at Blagaj near Mostar, Stjepan controlled the caravan routes between the Adriatic and the interior, levying customs on trade with Ragusa and founding the port of Novi, today Herceg Novi. His lands mixed adherents of the Bosnian Church, Orthodox and Catholic Christians, and he quarrelled with Ragusa, Venice and his own son Vladislav.
duchy-of-saint-sava.e: The Ottomans conquered Bosnia in 1463 and most of Stjepan's lands by 1465; he died in 1466. His son Vlatko held a shrinking coastal remnant until Herceg Novi fell in 1482. Another son converted and became the Ottoman grand vizier Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha.

dobunni.t: Cotswold kingdom whose coins name a string of rulers, and whose Roman town at Cirencester became the second largest in Britain.
dobunni.o: The Dobunni held Gloucestershire, north Somerset, Worcestershire and parts of Oxfordshire and Wiltshire in the late Iron Age. By the 1st century BCE they were minting coins, and a large oppidum developed at Bagendon near Cirencester, with Roman imports reaching it before the conquest.
dobunni.r: Their gold and silver coins carry the names of rulers such as Corio, Bodvoc, Anted and Eisu, sometimes thought to mark a divided kingdom with northern and southern halves. The economy rested on sheep and cereal farming in the Cotswolds and on the salt springs of Droitwich. Cassius Dio records that part of the Bodunni, probably the Dobunni, had been subject to the Catuvellauni.
dobunni.e: In 43 part of the Dobunni surrendered to Aulus Plautius, and the region came under Roman control without major recorded conflict. A fort was built at Cirencester, and the town of Corinium Dobunnorum grew into the civitas capital and second largest town of Roman Britain.

duchy-of-the-franks.t: The great Robertian principality between the Seine and the Loire whose dukes overshadowed the last Carolingian kings and became the Capetian dynasty.
duchy-of-the-franks.o: The Robertian family had led the defence of Neustria against the Vikings since Robert the Strong in the 860s, and two of its members, Odo and Robert I, had briefly been kings. In 936 Hugh the Great helped restore the Carolingian Louis IV and was recognised as 'duke of the Franks', second only to the king.
duchy-of-the-franks.r: Hugh the Great held counties and lay abbacies around Paris, Orléans and Tours, including Saint-Martin of Tours and Saint-Denis, giving him more land and men than the king. He controlled royal successions and dealt as an equal with the dukes of Normandy and Burgundy. His son Hugh Capet inherited the title in 956.
duchy-of-the-franks.e: When the last Carolingian king, Louis V, died in 987, the magnates elected Hugh Capet king. The duchy's lands became the royal domain of the new Capetian Kingdom of France, which his descendants ruled for eight centuries.

danish-gold-coast.t: Denmark's forts on the coast of modern Ghana, centred on Christiansborg at Osu, a hub of the Danish slave trade until the colony was sold in 1850.
danish-gold-coast.o: Danish traders, led by Hendrik Carloff, arrived on the Gold Coast in 1658 and seized the Swedish forts. Denmark built Fort Frederiksborg near Cape Coast and in 1661 bought the site of Christiansborg at Osu, near modern Accra, from the king of Accra.
danish-gold-coast.r: The Danish West India and Guinea Company and later the crown ran a string of forts east of Accra, exchanging textiles, guns and alcohol for gold and enslaved Africans, who were shipped to the Danish West Indies. In 1792 Denmark became the first European state to ban the transatlantic slave trade, effective from 1803, after which the Danes tried plantation farming inland.
danish-gold-coast.e: Unprofitable after the end of the slave trade, the forts were sold to Britain in 1850 and joined the British Gold Coast colony. Christiansborg, also known as Osu Castle, later served as the seat of Ghana's government.
danish-gold-coast.re: Lutheran Christianity, Akan and Ga religion

duchy-of-lower-bavaria.t: Wittelsbach duchy ruled from Landshut after the 1255 partition of Bavaria, whose duke Otto III was briefly King of Hungary.
duchy-of-lower-bavaria.o: In the partition of the Duchy of Bavaria in 1255, Henry XIII received Lower Bavaria, the lands along the lower Isar, the Danube and the Inn, with Landshut as residence. His brother Louis II the Strict took the Duchy of Upper Bavaria. The two lines were often hostile.
duchy-of-lower-bavaria.r: The dukes ruled from Burg Trausnitz above Landshut, relying on the estates, whose charter of 1311, the Ottonian Handfeste, gave them taxation rights. Henry XIII's son Otto III was elected King of Hungary in 1305 but could not hold the throne. The duchy was repeatedly divided among co-rulers, and Louis IV of Upper Bavaria acted as guardian of its young dukes, defeating the Austrians at Gammelsdorf in 1313.
duchy-of-lower-bavaria.e: When the last Lower Bavarian duke, John I the Child, died in 1340, Emperor Louis IV inherited the duchy and reunited Bavaria. Lower Bavaria later re-emerged as Bavaria-Landshut and is now a district of Bavaria.

duchy-of-tuscia.t: Lombard duchy of Tuscany, centred on Lucca, whose duke Desiderius rose to become the last king of the Lombards.
duchy-of-tuscia.o: After the Lombards occupied most of Tuscany in the 570s, the region was organised under dukes, with Lucca as the chief seat. Smaller duchies existed at Chiusi and elsewhere, but Lucca, on the route to Rome later called the Via Francigena, emerged as the dominant centre.
duchy-of-tuscia.r: Little is known of the early dukes. Documents from Lucca, unusually rich for the 8th century, show a society of Lombard landowners, churches and notaries, and Duke Walpert appears in the early 8th century. The Lombard nobleman Desiderius held authority in Tuscia before becoming king in 756. Lucca minted gold coins and was the main town of Lombard Tuscany.
duchy-of-tuscia.e: After Charlemagne's conquest of 774, Tuscia passed to Frankish counts and dukes based at Lucca. By the 9th century these governors were styled margraves, and the region became the March of Tuscany.

dregovichs.t: An East Slavic tribe of the Pripyat marshes, whose lands around Turov later formed one of the principalities of Rus'.
dregovichs.o: The Dregovichs settled the wet, forested lands between the Pripyat and the Western Dvina in the 7th and 8th centuries. Their name is usually derived from a Slavic word for bog. Constantine VII mentions them as Dragovitai, paying tribute to the Rus', in the 10th century.
dregovichs.r: They lived in small villages and hill forts and farmed the drier ground, supplementing this with hunting, fishing and beekeeping. The river Pripyat linked them to the Dnieper and to Kiev, which made them early tributaries of the Kievan princes. The chronicle records that they had their own princely rule before Rus' control, but no names survive.
dregovichs.e: By the 10th century the Dregovichs had been absorbed into Kievan Rus'. Turov became the seat of a princely line, and the territory developed into the Principality of Turov and Pinsk. Their land is now southern Belarus.

duchy-of-lower-lorraine.t: The northern half of old Lotharingia, a duchy over the Low Countries whose title was carried by Godfrey of Bouillon and survived in Brabant.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.o: In 959 Archbishop Bruno of Cologne divided the Duchy of Lotharingia, creating a separate duchy for the lands of the lower Meuse, Scheldt and Rhine. The German kings appointed its dukes, including the Carolingian Charles, brother of the West Frankish king Lothair, from 977 to 991.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.r: Ducal power was always limited, since counts such as those of Louvain, Hainaut, Namur, Holland and Limburg and the prince-bishops of Liège and Utrecht built their own principalities. The emperors used the office to reward loyal families: Godfrey the Bearded's house held it, and Godfrey of Bouillon was duke before leading the First Crusade in 1096.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.e: From 1106 the title was disputed between the counts of Louvain and Limburg. At the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 Emperor Henry VI limited the duke's authority to his own lands, and the Louvain dukes thereafter ruled as dukes of Brabant, keeping the title duke of Lothier.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.t: A junior Mecklenburg duchy around Neubrandenburg and Stargard that lasted just over a century before reuniting with the main line.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.o: In 1352 the brothers Albert II and John I, raised to dukes of Mecklenburg in 1348, divided their lands. John received the Lordship of Stargard in the east, with Neubrandenburg and Strelitz, which Mecklenburg had acquired from Brandenburg in the 13th century.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.r: The duchy was an agrarian land of knightly estates and small towns such as Neubrandenburg, with its brick Gothic gates, Friedland and Woldegk. Its dukes remained junior partners of their cousins in the Duchy of Mecklenburg and joined in their wars with Brandenburg and Pomerania. Few details of its administration survive.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.e: When Duke Ulrich II died without sons in 1471, Stargard reverted to the main Mecklenburg line. The region re-emerged in 1701 as the core of the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

duchy-of-croatia.t: Early medieval Croatian duchy on the Dalmatian coast, ruled by the Trpimirović line, which became the Kingdom of Croatia under Tomislav.
duchy-of-croatia.o: Croats settled the Dalmatian hinterland in the 7th century. Around 800 a duchy emerged under Frankish overlordship, confirmed by the Peace of Aachen of 812 between the Franks and Byzantium. Duke Borna is the first well-attested ruler.
duchy-of-croatia.r: Dukes ruled from seats at Nin, Klis and Bijaći, with a Latin-influenced Christian elite and Byzantine Dalmatian towns such as Zadar and Split nearby. Trpimir I issued a charter in 852 calling himself duke of the Croats. In 879 Branimir won papal recognition, and Croatia turned firmly to Rome. Stone churches with interlace decoration and Latin inscriptions survive.
duchy-of-croatia.e: Around 925 Tomislav united it with the Duchy of Pannonian Croatia and is recognised as the first king, creating the Kingdom of Croatia (925-1102).

duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.t: The small Kuyavian duchy of Wladyslaw the Elbow-high, the starting point of the duke who reunited Poland in 1320.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.o: When Casimir I of Kuyavia died in 1267, his sons divided the Duchy of Kuyavia, and the southern part around Brzesc Kujawski went to the young Wladyslaw and his brother Casimir. Wladyslaw, nicknamed the Elbow-high for his small stature, was born nearby around 1260.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.r: Brzesc was a modest farming land on the Vistula plain, bordered by the State of the Teutonic Order. From this small base Wladyslaw I gathered further duchies, including Sieradz and Leczyca, and after long struggles with Bohemian and Silesian rivals he was crowned King of Poland in 1320.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.e: After 1320 the duchy merged into the reunited Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385). In 1332 the Teutonic Knights occupied Kuyavia during their war with Poland, and it was returned to the Polish Crown by the Treaty of Kalisz in 1343.

despotate-of-dobruja.t: Bulgarian principality on the Black Sea coast ruled from Kaliakra, a naval power that fought Byzantium and Genoa before falling to the Ottomans.
despotate-of-dobruja.o: In the breakup of the Second Bulgarian Empire's authority, a local realm emerged in the coastal region of Karvuna, later called Dobruja. Its first known ruler, Balik, appears in 1346 sending troops to aid the Byzantine empress Anna of Savoy in the civil war.
despotate-of-dobruja.r: Balik's brother Dobrotitsa (c. 1347–1386), styled despot by Byzantium, ruled from Kaliakra and Varna. He built a fleet that fought Genoese traders and backed claimants to the Empire of Trebizond. The despotate controlled Black Sea ports and the grain trade, and remained Orthodox and broadly Bulgarian, while also dealing with the Tsardom of Vidin and Wallachia.
despotate-of-dobruja.e: Dobrotitsa's son Ivanko made peace with the Ottomans and Genoa, but the Ottomans conquered the despotate around 1388. Mircea the Elder of Wallachia held part of Dobruja briefly before it passed fully to the Ottomans.

duchy-of-zator.t: A tiny Silesian Piast duchy on the upper Vistula, sold to the Polish king in 1494.
duchy-of-zator.o: Zator, east of Oswiecim, was created in 1445 when the Duchy of Oswiecim was divided among the sons of Duke Casimir I, and Wenceslaus I took the Zator lands. Like Oswiecim, it was formally a fief of the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-zator.r: The duchy was a small agricultural land in the Vistula valley, known for its fish ponds, where the breeding of carp later became a local speciality. Its dukes were minor Piasts with limited resources, and the duchy was further divided among Wenceslaus's sons.
duchy-of-zator.e: In 1494 Duke Jan V sold Zator to King John I Albert of Poland. It was incorporated, together with Oswiecim, into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569) in 1564.

duchy-of-jawor.t: Lower Silesian Piast duchy at the foot of the Sudetes, later joined with Świdnica, which kept its independence from Bohemia longer than any other.
duchy-of-jawor.o: In 1274 the Duchy of Legnica was divided among the sons of Bolesław II the Bald, and Bolko I the Strict received Jawor with its lands. He soon added Świdnica and built a strong duchy on the Bohemian border, protected by castles such as Bolków and Grodziec.
duchy-of-jawor.r: Bolko I founded Krzeszów Abbey and fortified the mountain passes. After his death the lands were divided, with Henry I ruling Jawor until 1346. They were then reunited under Bolko II the Small, who resisted Bohemian overlordship, ruling as an independent Piast prince while other Silesian dukes became Bohemian vassals. German settlers and town law shaped the economy of farming and cloth.
duchy-of-jawor.e: Bolko II married his niece Anne to Charles IV, so on the death of his widow Agnes in 1392 the duchy passed to the Bohemian crown. Jawor later passed to the Habsburgs and Prussia, and has been Polish since 1945; its Lutheran Peace Church is a World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-athens.t: Crusader state of Athens and Thebes ruled in turn by Burgundian, Catalan and Florentine lords for two and a half centuries.
duchy-of-athens.o: In 1205 Boniface of Montferrat granted Athens and Thebes to the Burgundian knight Otho de la Roche, who took the title Lord of Athens. His nephew Guy I was styled Duke of Athens by the mid-13th century. The duchy covered Attica, Boeotia and parts of Locris, and was nominally subject to the Principality of Achaea.
duchy-of-athens.r: Under the de la Roche family the duchy prospered, with its court at Thebes, a silk industry and a Latin church that turned the Parthenon into a Catholic cathedral of Our Lady. Greek peasants remained Orthodox. In 1311 the Catalan Company killed Duke Walter of Brienne at Halmyros and ruled the duchy for the Crown of Aragon and Sicily.
duchy-of-athens.e: Nerio I Acciaioli, a Florentine banker's son, took Athens in 1388 and founded a new ducal line. The Ottomans, who already exacted tribute, captured Athens in 1456 and the Acropolis in 1458, annexing the duchy.
duchy-of-athens.la: Old French, Catalan, Italian, Medieval Greek

duchy-of-krakow.t: The senior duchy of fragmented Poland, whose throne at Krakow carried overlordship of the other Piast dukes.
duchy-of-krakow.o: In his testament of 1138 Boleslaw III Wrymouth divided Poland among his sons, creating a senior province around Krakow to be held by the eldest Piast with authority over the others. The first senior duke, Wladyslaw II the Exile, tried to rule alone and was driven out by his brothers in 1146.
duchy-of-krakow.r: Krakow passed in turn to Boleslaw IV, Mieszko III and Casimir II the Just, and the seniority principle broke down as rival dukes fought for the city. Lesser Poland's nobles and bishops gained great influence. The Mongols devastated the duchy in 1241, but under Boleslaw V the Chaste Krakow received town rights in 1257 and the salt mines of Wieliczka and Bochnia brought wealth.
duchy-of-krakow.e: After the Silesian Henry IV Probus and the Bohemian king Wenceslaus II, who ruled from 1291, Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high took Krakow in 1306. He was crowned there in 1320, and the duchy became the core of the reunited Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385).

dal-riata.t: A Gaelic kingdom spanning north-east Ireland and Argyll whose kings, settling Scotland's west coast, helped make Gaelic the language of medieval Scotland.
dal-riata.o: Dal Riata originated in County Antrim, and by about 500 its rulers held lands across the North Channel in Argyll. Tradition credits Fergus Mor mac Eirc with moving the dynasty to Britain, though the story was shaped by later writers. The Scottish part grew into a federation of kindreds centred on the hillfort of Dunadd.
dal-riata.r: Power was shared among kindreds such as Cenel nGabrain, Cenel Loairn and Cenel nOengusa, recorded in the Senchus fer nAlban, a census of houses and naval levies. Columba's monastery on Iona, founded in 563 with royal favour, made the kingdom a centre of Irish Christianity, scholarship and missionary work reaching Northumbria.
dal-riata.e: Defeat at Mag Rath in 637 cost Dal Riata its Irish lands. In the 8th century it fell under the Picts, and Viking raids from the 790s shattered its sea power. By the mid 9th century its territory and Gaelic culture merged with Pictland into the kingdom later known as Alba, the Kingdom of Scotland.

duchy-of-florence.t: The first Medici duchy, created by Charles V in 1532, under which Cosimo I conquered Siena and turned Florence into a princely state.
duchy-of-florence.o: After the siege of 1529–1530 ended the last Republic of Florence, Emperor Charles V made Alessandro de' Medici hereditary duke in 1532. Alessandro ruled with the support of imperial troops and built the Fortezza da Basso to control the city.
duchy-of-florence.r: Alessandro was murdered by his cousin Lorenzino in 1537, and the 17-year-old Cosimo I de' Medici was chosen to succeed him. Cosimo crushed the republican exiles at Montemurlo that year and built an efficient absolutist state. He founded the Uffizi offices, designed by Giorgio Vasari from 1560, created a navy and the Order of Saint Stephen, and conquered the Republic of Siena in 1555.
duchy-of-florence.e: In 1569 Pope Pius V raised Cosimo to Grand Duke of Tuscany, and the duchy became the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

duchy-of-pomerania.t: A Baltic duchy ruled by the native Griffin dynasty for five centuries, from its Christianisation in the 1120s to its partition after the Thirty Years' War.
duchy-of-pomerania.o: Wartislaw I united Slavic tribes around the lower Oder and Szczecin in the early 12th century under Polish overlordship. In 1124 and 1128 Bishop Otto of Bamberg converted the Pomeranians to Christianity. In 1181 Bogislaw I became a vassal of Frederick Barbarossa, making Pomerania part of the Empire.
duchy-of-pomerania.r: The Griffin dukes encouraged German settlement and founded towns, many of which joined the Hanseatic League, including Stralsund, Greifswald and Szczecin. The duchy was frequently divided into Pomerania-Wolgast and Pomerania-Stettin. Bogislaw X reunited it in 1478, and Johannes Bugenhagen introduced the Reformation in 1534. Brandenburg long claimed overlordship.
duchy-of-pomerania.e: The last duke, Bogislaw XIV, died in 1637 during the Thirty Years' War, with Sweden occupying the land. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 split the duchy: Sweden took western Pomerania and Brandenburg the east. Most of the region became Polish in 1945.

domain-of-soissons.t: Last Roman-ruled territory in northern Gaul, held by the generals Aegidius and Syagrius until Clovis conquered it in 486.
domain-of-soissons.o: Around 457 the emperor Majorian appointed Aegidius as commander of the Roman army in Gaul. When Majorian was murdered in 461, Aegidius refused to recognise his successors and kept control of the region between the Somme and the Loire, cut off from Italy.
domain-of-soissons.r: Aegidius ruled as a Roman general rather than a king, allying with the Franks and fighting the Visigoths at Orléans in 463. After his death in 464 his son Syagrius held the region from Soissons; Gregory of Tours calls him king of the Romans, though he probably never used the title.
domain-of-soissons.e: In 486 Clovis of the Salian Franks defeated Syagrius near Soissons. Syagrius fled to the Visigothic Kingdom, but Alaric II handed him over, and Clovis had him killed. The domain became the core of the Kingdom of the Franks.

duchy-of-savoy.t: The Alpine duchy of the house of Savoy that straddled France and Italy and grew into the Kingdom of Sardinia, the core of united Italy.
duchy-of-savoy.o: In 1416 Emperor Sigismund raised Count Amadeus VIII of the County of Savoy to the rank of duke. Amadeus later retired and was elected antipope Felix V in 1439. The duchy then included Savoy, Piedmont, Nice, Bresse and the Vaud.
duchy-of-savoy.r: The dukes ruled an Alpine state of pass tolls, farming and soldiers. French occupation from 1536 ended when Emmanuel Philibert recovered his lands at Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 and moved the capital from Chambéry to Turin in 1563. Savoy lost Geneva and the Vaud but built a centralised military state. Victor Amadeus II gained Sicily in 1713, exchanged for Sardinia in 1720.
duchy-of-savoy.e: From 1720 the dukes were kings of Sardinia. France annexed Savoy in 1792–1815. In 1847 the 'perfect fusion' merged the mainland states with Sardinia, ending the duchy as a separate state; Savoy itself passed to France in 1860.

demetae.t: People of south-west Wales whose name survives in Dyfed, and who accepted Roman rule with little recorded fighting.
demetae.o: The Demetae lived in what is now Pembrokeshire and western Carmarthenshire, a region of small defended farmsteads, known as raths, and coastal promontory forts. Ptolemy recorded them in the 2nd century, but no earlier writer describes them, and they were probably a grouping of local communities with long roots in the Iron Age.
demetae.r: Unlike their neighbours the Silures and Ordovices, the Demetae are not recorded as resisting Rome, and their territory needed few garrisons. Farming and cattle-rearing sustained a dispersed population, and the region looked west across the Irish Sea. The Romans mined gold at Dolaucothi on the eastern edge of their land.
demetae.e: After the conquest of Wales in the 70s the Demetae formed a civitas centred on Moridunum, modern Carmarthen, one of the westernmost towns of Roman Britain. The name passed to the post-Roman Kingdom of Dyfed, ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, and survives in the modern county of Dyfed.

danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The Viking kingdom founded by Guthrum in East Anglia after his defeat by Alfred, the first Danish state in England to accept Christianity.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: After Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878, the Danish leader accepted baptism with the name Aethelstan. In 879 his army settled East Anglia, the former Kingdom of East Anglia, and a treaty with Alfred around 886 fixed the boundary along the Lea, the Ouse and Watling Street.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Guthrum ruled as a Christian king and minted coins under his baptismal name. Danish settlers took land across Norfolk and Suffolk, and soon after his death coins honouring the martyred King Edmund were issued, showing rapid integration. Later rulers, such as Eohric, are poorly documented.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: The kingdom joined attacks on English territory, but Edward the Elder conquered it in 917 to 918, and the East Anglian Danes submitted. It became part of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons and later an earldom of England.

duchy-of-podolia.t: A frontier duchy won from the Tatars by Lithuania, ruled by the Koriatovich princes from the cliff-top fortress of Kamianets.
duchy-of-podolia.o: Podolia, the steppe and forest land between the Southern Bug and the Dniester, was under the Golden Horde until Algirdas of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania defeated three Tatar princes at the Blue Waters around 1362. He gave the land to his nephews, the sons of Koriat, who made Kamianets their capital.
duchy-of-podolia.r: The Koriatovich brothers fortified Kamianets and other towns, invited settlers and granted town rights under German law. They issued their own coins and ruled a mixed Ruthenian, Armenian and Polish population in an exposed land on the edge of the steppe. They looked both to Lithuania and to Poland for support.
duchy-of-podolia.e: Around 1393 Vytautas expelled Fyodor Koriatovich and divided the duchy, with the western part passing to Poland. After long rivalry over the region, western Podolia became the Podolian Voivodeship of the Polish Crown in 1434, while the east remained with Lithuania.

darini.t: People of north-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, sometimes linked with the Dáirine of early Irish genealogies.
darini.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 lists the Darini in north-east Ireland, inland or on the coast between the Robogdii and the Voluntii, in what is now County Antrim or north Down. Like his other Irish names, this information came from earlier seafarers' reports and is hard to locate precisely.
darini.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society from classical sources. Some scholars connect the name with the Dáirine, descendants of a legendary ancestor Dáire, a grouping that in Irish tradition includes the ruling families of the Érainn and of Dal Fiatach in Ulster, though the link is uncertain.
darini.e: The Darini disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their region later lay within the territories of the Kingdom of Ulaid and the Dal nAraidi.

duchy-of-franconia.t: The short-lived stem duchy of the Franks in central Germany whose duke Conrad I became king of East Francia in 911.
duchy-of-franconia.o: In the early 10th century the Conradine family won a bloody feud with the Babenbergs for dominance in Franconia, the Frankish heartland along the Main and the middle Rhine. After Adalbert of Babenberg was executed in 906, Conrad the Younger became the leading magnate, recognised as duke of the Franks.
duchy-of-franconia.r: In 911 Conrad was elected king of East Francia as Conrad I, the first non-Carolingian ruler, while his brother Eberhard governed Franconia. Conrad struggled against the Saxon, Bavarian and Swabian dukes and the Magyars. Dying in 918, he reportedly sent the royal insignia to Henry the Fowler of Saxony, his former enemy.
duchy-of-franconia.e: Eberhard accepted Henry I's kingship but rebelled against Otto I and was killed at the Battle of Andernach in 939. Otto did not appoint a new duke; Franconia passed directly to the crown and fragmented into bishoprics such as Würzburg and Bamberg and later secular lordships.

duchy-of-teck.t: Swabian duchy of a Zähringen branch named after Teck castle near Kirchheim, a ducal title without a duchy that later passed to the British royal family's ancestors.
duchy-of-teck.o: Adalbert, a younger son of Duke Conrad of Zähringen, inherited lands around the castle of Teck on the edge of the Swabian Jura and called himself Duke of Teck from 1187. The ducal title came from his family's rank rather than any ancient duchy, and the lands were modest, centred on Kirchheim and Owen.
duchy-of-teck.r: The dukes ruled a small cluster of castles, towns and farmland and often served greater lords, including the Habsburgs. The family split into lines and, under financial pressure, sold its holdings piece by piece. Most of the territory, including Kirchheim, was sold to the Counts of Württemberg in 1381 to 1386.
duchy-of-teck.e: The last duke, Ludwig, Patriarch of Aquileia, died in 1439. Württemberg later took the ducal title, and in 1871 it was revived for Francis of Teck, father of Queen Mary of Great Britain. Teck castle survives in part.

district-of-pilten.t: Small Baltic territory around Piltene, the remnant of the Bishopric of Courland, governed by its own nobles under the Polish crown until 1795.
district-of-pilten.o: After Magnus of Holstein died in 1583, Denmark sold its rights to the former Bishopric of Courland to Poland-Lithuania in 1585. The district, scattered around Pilten (Piltene) and Hasenpoth in western Latvia, was not merged into the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia but held directly by the Polish crown.
district-of-pilten.r: The local German nobility governed through their own diet and kept wide privileges, with a Lutheran church. The dukes of Courland repeatedly claimed the district and controlled it for periods, while the nobles resisted, preferring the distant Polish king. Latvian peasants worked the estates as serfs.
district-of-pilten.e: With the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, Pilten was annexed by Russia together with Courland and absorbed into the Governorate of Courland. Its separate status disappeared, though its nobility kept privileges as part of the Courland knighthood.

domain-of-matthew-csak.t: Vast private domain of the magnate Matthew Csák in north-western Hungary, ruled like an independent state during the struggle for the crown.
domain-of-matthew-csak.o: Matthew III Csák, of a leading baronial clan, built up power in the Váh valley in the 1290s as royal authority collapsed. After the death of Andrew III in 1301 ended the Árpád line, he backed rival claimants and seized castles across north-western Hungary, centred on Trencsén (Trenčín).
domain-of-matthew-csak.r: At its height he controlled some fourteen counties in modern Slovakia and northern Hungary, with around 50 castles. He kept his own court, palatine and household officials, granted lands, made treaties with Bohemia and ran justice and taxation like a king. He refused to submit to Charles I, and the pope excommunicated him in 1311.
domain-of-matthew-csak.e: Charles I defeated his allies at Rozgony in 1312 but could not take his heartland. After Matthew died in 1321, royal armies quickly took his castles, and the domain returned to the Kingdom of Hungary (1301-1526).
