duchy-of-naples.t: Byzantine duchy that became an independent city-state, resisting Lombards and Arabs for nearly five centuries until the Normans took it in 1137.
duchy-of-naples.o: Naples remained in Byzantine hands after the Lombard conquest. In 661 Emperor Constans II appointed Basil as its first duke, subject to the strategos of Sicily. Over the next century the dukes came from local families, and Duke Stephen II, who also became bishop, ruled with little reference to Constantinople.
duchy-of-naples.r: Naples was a Greek-Latin city of merchants and landowners, governed by dukes who also controlled Cumae, Sorrento and Amalfi for a time. Sergius I founded a hereditary dynasty in 840. The duchy fought the Lombards of Benevento, but sometimes allied with Arab raiders, earning papal condemnation. Greek liturgy and learning survived alongside Latin, and Naples kept a strong civic identity.
duchy-of-naples.e: The Normans conquered the surrounding lands in the 11th and 12th centuries. After resisting a siege in 1135–36, Duke Sergius VII submitted to Roger II and was killed in battle in 1137, and Naples joined the Kingdom of Sicily. It later became capital of the Kingdom of Naples.

duchy-of-bavaria.t: One of Germany's oldest territories, a duchy for more than a thousand years under the Agilolfings, Welfs and Wittelsbachs, and the core of modern Bavaria.
duchy-of-bavaria.o: The Bavarians (Baiuvarii) appear in the mid 6th century between the Danube, the Lech and the Alps, a people formed from Germanic groups and the Romanised population. Around 555 the Frankish kings recognised Garibald I of the Agilolfing family as duke. Bavaria later became a stem duchy of East Francia and the Holy Roman Empire.
duchy-of-bavaria.r: The Agilolfing dukes ruled almost as kings, with their own law code, the Lex Baiuvariorum, and bishoprics organised by Saint Boniface in 739 at Salzburg, Regensburg, Freising and Passau. Regensburg was the early capital. From 1180 the Wittelsbach family held the duchy, ruling from Munich, Landshut and Ingolstadt during long periods of division.
duchy-of-bavaria.e: Charlemagne deposed Duke Tassilo III in 788, but the duchy was revived. Albert IV reunited Bavaria in 1505 and imposed primogeniture. In 1623 Maximilian I received the electoral dignity during the Thirty Years' War, and the duchy became the Electorate of Bavaria, later the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806.

duchy-of-cleves.t: A lower Rhine duchy, home of Anne of Cleves, whose union with Jülich and Berg and later inheritance by Brandenburg brought Prussia to the Rhine.
duchy-of-cleves.o: The counts of Cleves appear around 1092, with a castle on a hill above the lower Rhine at Kleve. Their county lay on both banks of the river near the modern Dutch border. In 1368 it passed to the counts of the Mark, and Adolf I was raised to duke by Emperor Sigismund in 1417.
duchy-of-cleves.r: Cleves was a wealthy trading land on the Rhine, with towns such as Wesel, Emmerich and Kalkar. In 1521 Duke John III united Cleves with Jülich and Berg, forming the United Duchies. His daughter Anne of Cleves married Henry VIII of England in 1540. The dukes favoured the humanist middle way of Erasmus.
duchy-of-cleves.e: After the Jülich succession crisis, the Treaty of Xanten in 1614 gave Cleves to Brandenburg, giving the Hohenzollerns their first foothold in the west. France took the left bank in 1795, and after 1815 the region returned to Prussia; it is now part of North Rhine-Westphalia.
duchy-of-cleves.re: Catholic Christianity, later mixed Catholic and Protestant

duchy-of-sorrento.t: Minor Byzantine-era duchy on the Sorrento peninsula, independent of Naples from the 9th century until the Normans took it in 1137.
duchy-of-sorrento.o: Sorrento, an old Roman town on the peninsula south of the Bay of Naples, was part of the Byzantine Duchy of Naples. In the 9th century, amid the conflicts with Lombard Benevento and Arab raiders, it gained self-government under its own dukes, like neighbouring Amalfi.
duchy-of-sorrento.r: Little is known of the duchy, which was small and overshadowed by Naples and Amalfi. It ruled the western part of the peninsula and nearby islands, and its economy rested on fishing, farming and coastal trade. In 1035 Guaimar IV of Salerno seized it and gave it to his brother Guy, and it later passed among Lombard and Norman lords.
duchy-of-sorrento.e: Sorrento submitted to Roger II and was absorbed into the Norman Kingdom of Sicily by 1137, after which it was ruled as part of the kingdom's mainland territories.

duchy-of-bukovina.t: Habsburg crown land carved from northern Moldavia, a mosaic of Romanians, Ukrainians, Jews and Germans centred on Czernowitz.
duchy-of-bukovina.o: In 1774 Austrian troops occupied the north-western corner of Moldavia, linking newly acquired Galicia with Transylvania, and the Ottomans ceded it in 1775. Named Bukovina, the beech land, it was ruled by the military until 1786, then attached to Galicia. In 1849 it became a separate crown land with the title of duchy.
duchy-of-bukovina.r: Bukovina had its own diet from 1861 and a governor at Czernowitz, which grew into a German-speaking university town after 1875. Romanians, Ukrainians, Jews, Germans and Poles lived side by side, and in 1910 the diet adopted a compromise sharing seats among national groups. The Orthodox metropolitan resided in Czernowitz, and the painted monasteries of Suceava were preserved.
duchy-of-bukovina.e: As Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918, a congress in Czernowitz voted for union with Romania. In 1940 the Soviet Union annexed northern Bukovina, which is now part of Ukraine, while southern Bukovina remains in Romania. Its Jewish community was largely destroyed in the Holocaust.
duchy-of-bukovina.re: Eastern Orthodox Christianity, Judaism, Catholic Christianity

duchy-of-bavaria-ingolstadt.t: A short-lived Bavarian duchy ruled from Ingolstadt, best known for its brilliant and quarrelsome duke Louis the Bearded.
duchy-of-bavaria-ingolstadt.o: In the Bavarian partition of 1392 Stephen III received the lands around Ingolstadt, scattered across Upper Bavaria. His daughter Isabeau married King Charles VI of France, giving the house close ties with the French court.
duchy-of-bavaria-ingolstadt.r: Stephen's son Louis VII the Bearded spent years at the French court and returned with great wealth, building the New Castle and the Church of Our Lady in Ingolstadt. He was constantly at war with his cousins in Landshut and Munich and was placed under the imperial ban. In 1443 he was captured in a conflict that involved his own son, Louis the Hunchback.
duchy-of-bavaria-ingolstadt.e: Louis the Hunchback died in 1445 and his father in 1447 as a prisoner at Burghausen, ending the line. The duchy passed to Henry XVI of the Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut. Ingolstadt later became the seat of Bavaria's first university, founded in 1472.

duchy-of-magdeburg.t: The secularised Archbishopric of Magdeburg as a Brandenburg-Prussian duchy, rebuilt after the Thirty Years' War's worst massacre.
duchy-of-magdeburg.o: The Archbishopric of Magdeburg was devastated in the Thirty Years' War, when Tilly's army sacked the city in 1631. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 promised it to Brandenburg on the death of its administrator, Augustus of Saxe-Weissenfels; when he died in 1680, it became the Duchy of Magdeburg.
duchy-of-magdeburg.r: Prussia made Magdeburg one of its strongest fortresses and an administrative centre. The duchy was a rich grain region of the Magdeburg Börde, and Huguenot and Palatine refugees settled in the city. The University of Halle, founded in 1694 in the duchy, became a centre of Pietism and the early Enlightenment under August Hermann Francke and Christian Thomasius.
duchy-of-magdeburg.e: Prussia lost the duchy to the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807. In 1815 it returned to Prussia and formed the core of the Province of Saxony, with Magdeburg as provincial capital, a role it now holds in Saxony-Anhalt.

duchy-of-limburg.t: A small duchy in the hills east of the Meuse whose succession war ended at the battle of Worringen in 1288, binding it to Brabant for five centuries.
duchy-of-limburg.o: The castle of Limbourg on the Vesdre was built in the early 11th century, and around 1065 Walram Udo of the house of Arlon became count of Limburg. His son Henry I claimed the duchy of Lower Lorraine, and later rulers kept the ducal title for their own lands.
duchy-of-limburg.r: Limburg was a land of pasture, woods and later cloth and lead mining around Verviers and the Vesdre valley. Its dukes, among them Waleran III, intermarried with Luxembourg and the Rhineland nobility. When the line ended in 1283, John I of Brabant fought for the inheritance and won at Worringen in 1288.
duchy-of-limburg.e: Limburg was then ruled with the Duchy of Brabant, passing to the Burgundian State, the Habsburg Netherlands and the Spanish Netherlands. In 1661 the Overmaas lands were divided with the Dutch Republic. France annexed the rest in 1795.

dutch-republic.t: The federal republic born of the revolt against Spain, which became the world's leading trading power and a centre of art, science and toleration.
dutch-republic.o: The northern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands rose against Philip II from 1568 under William the Silent. They allied in the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and renounced Philip by the Act of Abjuration in 1581. After failing to find a new sovereign, the provinces governed themselves as a republic, recognised by Spain in the Peace of Münster in 1648.
dutch-republic.r: Each province was sovereign, sending delegates to the States General at The Hague, while Holland's Grand Pensionary and the Orange-Nassau stadtholders competed for leadership. Founded in 1602, the Dutch East India Company built an Asian trading empire. Amsterdam became Europe's financial centre, and Rembrandt, Vermeer, Spinoza and Huygens worked in relative freedom, though the Reformed church was official.
dutch-republic.e: After the disaster year of 1672, William III led resistance to France and became king of England in 1689. The 18th century brought decline and clashes between Orangists and Patriots. In 1795 French armies and Dutch revolutionaries founded the Batavian Republic.

dilmun.t: The island trading power of Bahrain that linked Mesopotamia with Magan and the Indus, remembered in Sumerian myth as a pure land.
dilmun.o: Dilmun appears in Sumerian texts by the late 3rd millennium BCE as a trading partner of Ur. From around 2200 BCE the settlement at Qal'at al-Bahrain grew into a walled town, and the Barbar culture built temples at Barbar and Saar and tens of thousands of burial mounds across northern Bahrain, with influence reaching Failaka in Kuwait and the coast of eastern Arabia.
dilmun.r: Dilmun was a merchant state, handling copper from Magan, carnelian and ivory from the Indus and grain and textiles from Mesopotamia, and it set its own weight standard and stamp seals. Its gods Inzak and Enki were worshipped at freshwater springs. Around 1500 BCE Kassite Babylonia ruled the island through governors at Qal'at al-Bahrain, and its date trade flourished.
dilmun.e: Later kings of Dilmun paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire: Uperi sent gifts to Sargon II in 709 BCE. Dilmun passed under Neo-Babylonian control and vanishes as a political entity in the 6th century BCE, the island later reappearing as Tylos in Greek sources. Its burial mounds are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

dauphine-of-viennois.t: The Alpine principality around Grenoble whose last ruler sold it to France on condition that the heir to the throne bear the title Dauphin.
dauphine-of-viennois.o: Around 1029 Guigues the Old, count of Albon, began gathering lands in the Viennois and the Grésivaudan as royal power in the Kingdom of Arles weakened. His descendants made Grenoble their centre, and Guigues IV, nicknamed 'Dauphin', gave the family its distinctive title in the 12th century.
dauphine-of-viennois.r: The dauphins governed a mountain land of pastures, mines and passes towards Italy, and later added the Briançonnais and Gapençais. In 1339 Humbert II founded a university at Grenoble. The principality had its own council and courts, and its lords balanced between Savoy, Provence and the French crown.
dauphine-of-viennois.e: Humbert II, childless and deep in debt, sold the Dauphiné to Philip VI under the Treaty of Romans, completed in 1349. It went to the king's grandson Charles, and from then on the eldest son of the French king held the title Dauphin, while the province joined the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-alamannia.t: The Frankish duchy that ruled the Alemanni of south-west Germany and Switzerland for two centuries, until the Carolingians abolished it at Cannstatt.
duchy-of-alamannia.o: After Clovis' victories over the Alemanni around 496 and 506, the southern Alemanni stayed under Ostrogothic protection until 536, when the Ostrogoth king Witigis ceded them to the Franks. The Merovingian kings then placed the Alemanni under dukes, a region covering modern Baden-Württemberg, Alsace, eastern Switzerland and Bavarian Swabia.
duchy-of-alamannia.r: The dukes governed under Frankish overlordship but often acted independently, especially as Merovingian power weakened. Law was codified in the Pactus and the Lex Alamannorum of the early 8th century. Christianity spread through bishoprics at Constance and Basel and monasteries such as St Gall, founded on the hermitage of Gallus, and Reichenau, founded in 724.
duchy-of-alamannia.e: Duke Lantfrid and his successor Theudebald resisted the rising Carolingian mayors of the palace. In 746 Carloman summoned the Alemannic nobility to Cannstatt and executed many of them, ending the ducal office. Alamannia was then ruled by Frankish counts until the Duchy of Swabia emerged in the early 10th century.

duchy-of-inowroclaw.t: A Kuyavian Piast duchy on the Teutonic border, ruled by Ziemomysl and his sons until Casimir the Great absorbed it.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.o: In the division of the Duchy of Kuyavia after Casimir I's death in 1267, the northern lands around Inowroclaw went to his son Ziemomysl. He relied on support from the Teutonic Order and the dukes of Pomerelia, which caused revolts among his own nobles.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.r: Inowroclaw was a salt-producing land near the Vistula, and its towns grew under German law. After Ziemomysl died in 1287 his sons Leszek, Przemysl and Casimir shared and exchanged its parts, including Gniewkowo. The duchy was devastated during the war between Poland and the Teutonic Knights in the 1320s and 1330s.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.e: Casimir III the Great gradually bought out the local dukes. The last claimant, Wladyslaw the White of Gniewkowo, gave up his rights and became a monk in the 1360s, and around 1364 Inowroclaw was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385).

duchy-of-wurttemberg.t: The south-west German duchy, raised in 1495, that combined strong estates, a model Lutheran church and a constitution dating from 1514.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.o: The County of Württemberg, reunited by Count Eberhard im Bart in 1482, was raised to a duchy at the Diet of Worms in 1495; Eberhard had founded the University of Tübingen in 1477. His successor Ulrich proved a violent ruler, and the peasant revolt of the Poor Conrad in 1514 forced him to accept the Treaty of Tübingen, guaranteeing the estates' rights.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.r: Expelled by the Swabian League in 1519, Ulrich lost the duchy to the Habsburgs until 1534, when he returned and introduced Lutheranism. Duke Christoph built a model Lutheran church order and school system. The Landtag, dominated by town notables because the nobility had left the duchy, controlled taxation. Stuttgart was the capital, and Ludwigsburg was built as a Baroque residence from 1704.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.e: Duke Frederick II gained the rank of elector in 1803 and, allied with Napoleon, became king in 1806, doubling his lands; the duchy became the Electorate of Württemberg and then the Kingdom of Württemberg. Its territory is now part of Baden-Württemberg.

duchy-of-split.t: Short-lived Dalmatian duchy granted to the Bosnian magnate Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić, uniting Split and the central Dalmatian islands under one lord.
duchy-of-split.o: In the struggle for the Hungarian crown between Sigismund of Luxembourg and Ladislaus of Naples, the powerful Bosnian noble Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić backed Ladislaus. In 1403 Ladislaus rewarded him with the title of Duke of Split, together with the islands of Brač, Hvar and Korčula, carving a duchy out of royal Dalmatia.
duchy-of-split.r: Hrvoje ruled from Split while remaining Grand Duke of Bosnia, so the duchy linked the inland Bosnian lands with the Adriatic trade of the city. Split kept its communal statutes and council. Hrvoje's court produced the richly illuminated Glagolitic Missal of Hrvoje, made in Split around 1404, one of the finest Croatian medieval manuscripts.
duchy-of-split.e: Hrvoje later reconciled with Sigismund, but fell from favour and was declared a traitor in 1413; Split threw off his rule and returned to the Hungarian crown. Hrvoje died in 1416, and in 1420 Split passed to Venice, which held it for nearly four centuries.

drevlians.t: Forest-dwelling East Slavs west of Kiev who killed Prince Igor in 945 and suffered the ferocious revenge of his widow Olga.
drevlians.o: The Drevlians, the people of the trees, lived in the forests between the Pripyat and the middle Dnieper, west of the Polans. They appear in the Primary Chronicle as an old tribe with their own princes and their chief town at Iskorosten, modern Korosten in Ukraine.
drevlians.r: They were farmers, hunters and beekeepers, and the Kievan chronicler, hostile to them, describes them as living in a bestial way. After Oleg subdued them in the early 10th century they paid tribute to Kiev. In 945 Prince Igor tried to collect a second tribute, and the Drevlians under their prince Mal killed him.
drevlians.e: Igor's widow Olga took vengeance in 946, burying and burning Drevlian envoys and setting Iskorosten alight with birds carrying burning tinder. The Drevlian land was then ruled directly from Kiev, and in 970 Sviatoslav I gave it to his son Oleg. The tribe merged into the population of Kievan Rus'.

decapolis-levant.t: The Decapolis, a group of Greek cities east of the Jordan freed by Pompey, famous for the colonnaded streets of Gerasa.
decapolis-levant.o: The Decapolis cities, among them Gerasa, Gadara, Pella, Philadelphia, Scythopolis and Hippos, had grown as Greek-style towns under the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire. The Hasmonean Kingdom conquered many of them, and in 63 BCE Pompey freed them and attached them to Roman Syria.
decapolis-levant.r: Each city governed itself, minted coins and dated years from Pompey's liberation. They were less a formal league than a regional group with shared Greek culture, temples to Zeus and Artemis, and trade with the Nabataean Kingdom. The Gospels mention the Decapolis as the setting of Jesus' ministry.
decapolis-levant.e: In 106 CE Trajan created the province of Arabia, dividing the cities between it and Syria. Gerasa, modern Jerash, preserves one of the best-preserved Roman cityscapes.

duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.t: Twin Ernestine duchy whose dynasty placed rulers on the thrones of Belgium, Britain, Portugal and Bulgaria.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.o: In the Ernestine redistribution of 1826, Duke Ernest I of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld gave up Saalfeld and received Gotha, forming Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. The two duchies remained legally separate, joined only in the person of the duke, with separate parliaments.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.r: Ernest I's brother Leopold became King of the Belgians in 1831, and his son Albert married Queen Victoria in 1840. Ernest II was a liberal patron of the German national movement and of music. Gotha was a centre of cartography with the Justus Perthes firm and of insurance, while Coburg was a court town. Victoria's son Alfred and grandson Charles Edward later succeeded as dukes.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.e: Charles Edward abdicated in November 1918. The Free State of Coburg voted to join Bavaria in 1920, while Gotha joined the Free State of Thuringia.

duchy-of-leczyca.t: A small Piast duchy of central Poland that changed hands among the Kuyavian and Masovian dukes before rejoining the Crown.
duchy-of-leczyca.o: Leczyca, an old stronghold where Polish church synods were held in the 12th century, became a separate duchy in the age of division. In 1229 Konrad I of Masovia took control of it, and in the 1230s it passed to his son Casimir I of Kuyavia, whose descendants ruled it in various combinations with Sieradz and Kuyavia.
duchy-of-leczyca.r: Leczyca was a farming land in the middle of Poland with a fortified castle and a collegiate church at Tum, one of the finest Romanesque churches in the country. Its dukes were minor Piasts, among them Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high, who held it in the 1290s while building his base for reuniting Poland. The duchy suffered raids by the Lithuanians and the Teutonic Order.
duchy-of-leczyca.e: After Poland was reunited in 1320, Leczyca continued as a duchy under Wladyslaw of Dobrzyn, a nephew of the king. When he died in 1352 it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385) as a province, later the Leczyca Voivodeship.

duchy-of-swabia.t: The stem duchy of south-west Germany, home of the Hohenstaufen emperors, which collapsed with the execution of the last Staufer in 1268.
duchy-of-swabia.o: After the death of the Alemannic dukes in 746, Alamannia was governed by counts. In 915 Count Erchanger defeated King Conrad I's forces at Wahlwies and was proclaimed duke; Conrad executed him in 917, but Burchard II established the duchy, recognised by Henry the Fowler in 919. Swabia covered south-west Germany, Alsace and eastern Switzerland.
duchy-of-swabia.r: Dukes were often royal relatives, and from 1079 the office went to the Staufer family, who became emperors with Conrad III and Frederick Barbarossa. Swabia was rich in monasteries, imperial cities such as Ulm and Augsburg, and lesser nobles. Its knightly culture produced Minnesang poets.
duchy-of-swabia.e: After the fall of the Staufer, the last duke, Conradin, was beheaded at Naples in 1268. The duchy dissolved into many territories, including the County of Württemberg, the Margraviate of Baden, Habsburg lands and free imperial cities, which later formed the Swabian League and the Swabian Circle.

duchy-of-austria.t: The Babenberg and Habsburg duchy on the Danube, created by the Privilegium Minus in 1156, which became the core of the Habsburg monarchy.
duchy-of-austria.o: In 1156 Frederick Barbarossa issued the Privilegium Minus, raising the Margraviate of Austria to a duchy for Henry II Jasomirgott, in compensation for giving up Bavaria. The new duchy received special privileges, including inheritance through female lines. Vienna became the ducal capital.
duchy-of-austria.r: The Babenbergs acquired Styria in 1192 and made Vienna a centre of Minnesang. After the line died out in 1246, Ottokar II of Bohemia took Austria, but in 1278 Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated him at the Marchfeld. Rudolf IV founded the University of Vienna in 1365 and forged the Privilegium Maius to claim higher rank.
duchy-of-austria.e: In 1453 Emperor Frederick III, himself a Habsburg, confirmed the Privilegium Maius, raising Austria to an archduchy. The Archduchy of Austria became the core of the Habsburg monarchy, the Austrian Empire and, ultimately, the modern Republic of Austria.

duchy-of-sieradz.t: A Piast duchy in central Poland, a stepping stone for Leszek the Black and Wladyslaw the Elbow-high on their way to Krakow.
duchy-of-sieradz.o: Sieradz, on the Warta, was part of the lands of Casimir I of Kuyavia. In the early 1260s his eldest son Leszek the Black received it as his own duchy, which he kept after his father's death in 1267.
duchy-of-sieradz.r: It was a farming land on the borders of Greater Poland and Silesia. Leszek the Black used it as a base to become duke of Krakow in 1279, and later his half-brother Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high held Sieradz as he fought for the reunification of Poland. Its towns were developed under German law in the 13th century.
duchy-of-sieradz.e: After 1320 Sieradz remained a duchy within the reunited kingdom, held by Przemysl, a nephew of the king. When he died in 1339 it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385) and later became the Sieradz Voivodeship.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.t: North German duchy that briefly passed to Wallenstein during the Thirty Years' War, ruled from a fine Renaissance palace at Güstrow.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.o: Mecklenburg had already been divided before, but the partition of 1621 between the brothers Adolf Frederick I and John Albert II created a lasting Mecklenburg-Güstrow in the east of the country, with Mecklenburg-Schwerin in the west. Rostock and the estates remained shared between the two duchies.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.r: Both dukes were deposed in 1628 by Emperor Ferdinand II, who gave Mecklenburg to his general Albrecht von Wallenstein; Wallenstein governed from Güstrow until Swedish troops restored the dukes in 1631. Government was weakened by powerful noble estates, and the countryside suffered heavily from war and depopulation. The duchy was Lutheran.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.e: Gustav Adolph, the last duke, died without male heirs in 1695. A long succession dispute followed until the Treaty of Hamburg in 1701 divided Mecklenburg into the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.t: Tiny Ernestine duchy in eastern Thuringia whose single duke built a celebrated baroque palace chapel.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.o: In the 1680 division of the inheritance of Ernest the Pious, his fifth son Christian received Eisenberg and its district, between Gera and Jena, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Eisenberg.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.r: Christian rebuilt Christiansburg Palace in Eisenberg and added a richly decorated baroque chapel, still one of the finest in Thuringia. He was interested in alchemy and kept a small Lutheran court. The duchy was largely rural, with no independent policy of note.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.e: Christian died in 1707 without a male heir. After a dispute among his relatives, Saxe-Eisenberg passed to Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg; in 1826 it went with Altenburg to the new Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg.

duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.t: A Wittelsbach inheritance that joined a Lower Bavarian duchy with the rich Low Country counties of Holland, Zeeland and Hainaut.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.o: After the death of Emperor Louis the Bavarian his sons divided their lands, and in 1353 a further partition created Bavaria-Straubing for William I and Albert I, together with the counties of Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland inherited through their mother Margaret. Albert governed the whole inheritance from 1358, after his brother became insane.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.r: The dukes lived mostly in The Hague and governed Straubing through deputies, while in the County of Holland they were drawn into the Hook and Cod factional wars. In Bavaria they built the ducal castle at Straubing from 1356. The Danube plain of the Gäuboden around the town was among the most fertile farmland in Bavaria.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.e: After William VI died in 1417 his daughter Jacqueline of Hainaut fought her uncle John III for the inheritance. John died in 1425, the Low Countries passed to Philip the Good of Burgundy, and in 1429 the Straubing lands were divided among the Duchy of Bavaria-Munich, the Duchy of Bavaria-Ingolstadt and the Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut.

duchy-of-ziebice.t: A Lower Silesian duchy, known in German as Münsterberg, that passed from the Piasts to the Poděbrady and Auersperg families before being sold to Prussia.
duchy-of-ziebice.o: In 1322 the sons of Duke Bolko I of Świdnica divided his lands, and Bolko II received Ziębice (Münsterberg), south of Wrocław, as a separate duchy split from the Duchy of Świdnica. Bolko II resisted Bohemian overlordship longer than most Silesian dukes but did homage to King John of Bohemia in 1336.
duchy-of-ziebice.r: The duchy was a modest agrarian territory of small towns and villages. The Piast line ended in 1428, and in 1456 the duchy passed to George of Poděbrady, later king of Bohemia, whose sons held it as dukes of Münsterberg and introduced the Reformation. In 1654 the emperor granted it to the Auersperg family, who seldom lived there.
duchy-of-ziebice.e: Silesia came under Prussia in 1742, though the Auerspergs kept the ducal title and estates. In 1791 they sold their remaining Silesian holdings to the Prussian crown, ending the duchy. The town, now Ziębice, became part of Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-cantabria.t: A Visigothic frontier duchy in northern Spain whose last duke, Peter, was father of King Alfonso I of Asturias.
duchy-of-cantabria.o: The Visigothic king Leovigild conquered Cantabria in 574, taking its stronghold of Amaya. A frontier duchy was then set up to watch the mountain peoples and the Basques, though its extent and organisation are poorly documented.
duchy-of-cantabria.r: The duchy was ruled by a dux appointed by the Visigothic kings, with its centre probably at Amaya in the north of modern Burgos. Its population lived from herding and farming in the valleys of the Cantabrian range, and Visigothic control seems to have been loose.
duchy-of-cantabria.e: After the Muslim conquest of 711, Duke Peter of Cantabria kept his independence. His son Alfonso married the daughter of Pelagius and became Alfonso I of Asturias in 739, uniting the duchy with the Kingdom of Asturias.

duchy-of-nysa.t: Silesian duchy ruled by the bishops of Wrocław from Nysa, the Silesian Rome, a Catholic stronghold for over five centuries.
duchy-of-nysa.o: The bishops of Wrocław held the castellany of Nysa and Otmuchów from the 12th century. In 1290 Duke Henry IV Probus granted Bishop Thomas II full princely rights there, making the territory an episcopal duchy. Its bishops took the title Prince of Nysa and in 1342 accepted the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-nysa.r: The bishop-dukes ruled from Nysa and Otmuchów through officials and the estates. Nysa became a wealthy town of churches and convents, called the Silesian Rome. After the Reformation spread in Silesia, the bishops led the Counter-Reformation, and Archduke Charles of Austria, bishop from 1608, founded the Jesuit college Carolinum. The population was largely German-speaking.
duchy-of-nysa.e: In 1742 most of the duchy passed to Prussia, which secularised it in 1810, while the southern part around Jeseník remained Austrian under the bishops until 1850. Nysa has been Polish since 1945.

dal-fiatach.t: Ruling dynasty of east County Down, centred on Downpatrick, which claimed to be the true Ulaid and held the Ulster kingship until 1177.
dal-fiatach.o: The Dál Fiatach were a dynasty of the Ulaid in what is now east County Down. They claimed descent from the ancient Ulaid royal line, and after the Ulaid were pushed east of the River Bann they became one of the two main powers in the Kingdom of Ulaid, with their stronghold at Dún Lethglaise, Downpatrick, associated with St Patrick's burial.
dal-fiatach.r: Dál Fiatach kings alternated the over-kingship of the Ulaid with the Dal nAraidi. Báetán mac Cairill, who died in 581, is said to have claimed authority as far as the Isle of Man and Scotland. Fiachnae mac Demmáin fought for the kingship in the early 7th century. Their wealth lay in the fertile lands of Lecale and the Ards, and the monasteries of Bangor and Movilla lay nearby.
dal-fiatach.e: From the 11th century their kings were the Mac Duinn Sléibe, MacDunleavy. In 1177 the Anglo-Norman John de Courcy seized Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, founding the Earldom of Ulster and ending Dál Fiatach rule.

duchy-of-brittany.t: The Celtic-speaking peninsula of western France, an independent-minded duchy for six centuries until its heiress Anne married two French kings.
duchy-of-brittany.o: After Viking occupation in the early 10th century, Alan Twisted Beard returned from exile in England and drove the Norse out, completing the reconquest with the victory at Trans in 939. He took the title of duke and made Nantes his base. The duchy's frontier with Anjou and Normandy remained contested for generations.
duchy-of-brittany.r: Brittany kept its own customs, coinage, Estates and courts, with Breton spoken in the west and Gallo and French in the east. The Montfort and Blois families fought the War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364), won by John IV at Auray. Under the Montfort dukes the duchy prospered from salt, linen and shipping and was nearly sovereign.
duchy-of-brittany.e: Francis II's defeat at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier in 1488 sealed French dominance. His daughter Anne of Brittany married Charles VIII and then Louis XII, and the Edict of Union of 1532 joined the duchy to the Kingdom of France. When the Dauphin, its last duke, became Henry II in 1547, the title merged with the crown.

duchy-of-saxe-gotha.t: Ernestine Saxon duchy in Thuringia whose founder, Ernest the Pious, made it a model of Lutheran school reform and orderly government.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.o: Saxe-Gotha was created in 1640 when the Ernestine lands of Saxe-Weimar were divided among the brothers of the ducal house, and Ernest I received Gotha. He built Friedenstein Palace as his residence. In 1672 he inherited Saxe-Altenburg, and the state became known as Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.r: Ernest the Pious introduced compulsory schooling, a famous school method and detailed church and state ordinances, rebuilding a land ruined by the Thirty Years' War. On his death in 1675 his lands were divided among seven sons, creating the duchies of Coburg, Meiningen, Römhild, Eisenberg, Hildburghausen and Saalfeld. Ernest II, in the 18th century, was an Enlightenment patron of astronomy who founded the Seeberg observatory.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.e: The line died out with Duke Frederick IV in 1825. In the redistribution of 1826 Gotha went to the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, forming the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, while Altenburg became the Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg.

duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.t: A small north German duchy on the lower Elbe that kept the Saxon ducal title for centuries but lost the electoral vote to its Wittenberg cousins.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.o: When the Ascanian dukes of Saxony divided their lands, the younger line received the scattered northern territories around Lauenburg on the Elbe and Ratzeburg, formally separated from the Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg in 1296. The Golden Bull of 1356 gave the Saxon electoral vote to Wittenberg rather than Lauenburg, leaving Lauenburg a minor duchy.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.r: The dukes were often in debt and pledged lands, including the Vierlande and Bergedorf, to Lübeck and Hamburg. The estates of the duchy held real power, and the old salt road from Lüneburg to Lübeck crossed its territory. The duchy turned Lutheran in the 16th century. When the Ascanian line died out in 1689, the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg seized it.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.e: Lauenburg passed with the Electorate of Hanover and in 1815 to Denmark. After the war of 1864 it went to Prussia, whose king ruled it in personal union until it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Prussia in 1876. Bismarck later received the honorary title Duke of Lauenburg in 1890.

daunians.t: Iapygian people of northern Apulia, known for their carved stone stelae and painted pottery, who allied with Rome against the Samnites.
daunians.o: The Daunians were the northernmost of the Iapygian peoples of Apulia, settled in the Tavoliere plain and the Gargano from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek legend made the hero Diomedes, returning from Troy, the founder of Arpi and other towns, a story the Daunians themselves seem to have adopted.
daunians.r: Daunian society was organised in large settlements such as Arpi, Canusium, Salapia and Sipontum, with chieftains whose wealth appears in their tombs. Between the 7th and 6th centuries BCE they set up hundreds of anthropomorphic stone stelae near Sipontum, carved with weapons, ornaments and scenes of daily life. Their matt-painted pottery is distinctive. They farmed the plain, raised horses and traded across the Adriatic.
daunians.e: During the Samnite Wars the Daunian towns sided with Rome; Livy records alliances in 318 BCE, and Rome founded Luceria in 314 BCE. Arpi went over to Hannibal after Cannae in 216 BCE and was punished when retaken. The towns became Roman municipia after the Social War, and Daunian identity faded into Roman Apulia.

duchy-of-kozle.t: A minor Upper Silesian Piast duchy around the Oder town of Koźle, carved from the lands of the dukes of Bytom in the early 14th century.
duchy-of-kozle.o: Koźle belonged to the Upper Silesian lands of the Duchy of Bytom, ruled by a branch of the Silesian Piasts. Around 1303 it was set apart for a junior member of the dynasty, beginning a short history as a separate duchy, though for much of the period it was held together with Bytom itself.
duchy-of-kozle.r: Like other small Silesian duchies, Koźle was a fortified market town on the Oder with surrounding villages, settled partly by German colonists under German town law. In 1327 its duke did homage to King John of Bohemia, making the duchy a fief of the Kingdom of Bohemia. Little else is recorded of its government.
duchy-of-kozle.e: The Bytom-Koźle line ended in 1355, and after a dispute Koźle passed to the dukes of the Duchy of Oleśnica, who held it until the late 15th century. It later reverted to the Bohemian crown, followed Silesia to Prussia in 1742 and became part of Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-lucca.t: A small Tuscan duchy created in 1815 for the former queen of Etruria, Maria Luisa of Bourbon, and absorbed by Tuscany in 1847.
duchy-of-lucca.o: The Congress of Vienna gave Lucca to Maria Luisa of Spain, former regent of the Kingdom of Etruria, as compensation for losing Parma, which went to Napoleon's widow Marie Louise. Maria Luisa took possession in 1817 and ruled until her death in 1824.
duchy-of-lucca.r: Maria Luisa revived court life, built roads and the aqueduct of Lucca and encouraged the arts. Her son Charles Louis, Duke Charles I, ruled from 1824, an extravagant and unpredictable prince who spent much time abroad and left government to ministers. The duchy was small, conservative and dependent on Austria.
duchy-of-lucca.e: Under the Vienna settlement, the Bourbons were to return to Parma when Marie Louise died. In October 1847, shortly before her death, Charles Louis handed Lucca to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and later became Duke of Parma.

duchy-of-saxony.t: The stem duchy of northern Germany whose dukes became kings and emperors, later the power base of Henry the Lion before its break-up in 1180.
duchy-of-saxony.o: After Charlemagne's conquest, Saxony was ruled by Frankish counts. In the mid 9th century the Liudolfing family, descended from Count Liudolf, emerged as dukes; Liudolf founded Gandersheim Abbey in 852. His grandson Henry the Fowler was elected king of East Francia in 919, and Otto I passed the duchy to the Billung family.
duchy-of-saxony.r: The duchy covered Westphalia, Engern and Eastphalia between the Rhine and the Elbe, with Slavic marches to the east. Henry the Lion of the Welf family, duke from 1142, made it a near-royal power, founding Lübeck and Munich and ruling from Brunswick, where he built Dankwarderode Castle and set up the bronze lion.
duchy-of-saxony.e: In 1180 Frederick Barbarossa deposed Henry the Lion. The western part became the Duchy of Westphalia under the Electorate of Cologne, and the name Saxony passed with a smaller duchy to the Ascanian Bernhard. In 1296 this split into Saxe-Lauenburg and Saxe-Wittenberg, whose electoral title later moved the name Saxony up the Elbe.

duklja.t: Medieval Serbian principality and kingdom on the Montenegrin coast, the first South Slav state whose ruler received a crown from the pope.
duklja.o: Duklja, named after the Roman town of Doclea, emerged among Serbs of the southern Adriatic hinterland. It appears in the 10th century under Byzantine overlordship; Prince Jovan Vladimir ruled it until his murder in 1016, and is venerated as a saint.
duklja.r: Around 1040 Stefan Vojislav threw off Byzantine control and defeated a Byzantine army near Bar in 1042. His son Mihailo I extended rule over Raška, Travunia and Zachlumia and received a royal crown from Pope Gregory VII in 1077, and Bar became an archbishopric. Constantine Bodin briefly ruled a wide realm. The state lay on the Catholic-Orthodox divide, with Latin coastal towns such as Kotor and Bar.
duklja.e: Dynastic strife after Bodin's death around 1101 let Byzantium and Raška intervene. Stefan Nemanja of the Grand Principality of Serbia annexed it around 1186, and the region, later called Zeta, became a Nemanjić appanage.

dyme.t: Westernmost city of Achaea and one of the four cities that refounded the Achaean League in 280 BCE.
dyme.o: Dyme lay on the coastal plain of western Achaea, near Cape Araxos, facing the Ionian Sea. It was one of the twelve cities of Achaea, formed in the early Iron Age from local villages.
dyme.r: Little is known of its government before the Hellenistic age. In 280 BCE Dyme, Patrae, Tritaea and Pharae revived the Achaean League, which grew into a major power. Exposed to the west, Dyme was sacked in 208 BCE by a Roman force during the First Macedonian War, its people enslaved and later ransomed by Philip V of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia.
dyme.e: Dyme passed under Roman control in 146 BCE. In 67 BCE Pompey resettled defeated Cilician pirates there, and it later became a Roman colony under Augustus before declining in favour of Patrae.

duchy-of-trakai.t: The western half of medieval Lithuania, ruled by Kestutis and Vytautas from the island castle of Trakai.
duchy-of-trakai.o: Trakai, west of Vilnius among lakes, became the seat of Kestutis, son of Gediminas, in the late 1330s. After 1345 Lithuania was effectively shared between Algirdas in Vilnius and Kestutis in Trakai, who governed the western lands including Samogitia and led the defence against the Teutonic Order.
duchy-of-trakai.r: The duchy bore the brunt of the crusaders' raids from Prussia, and Kestutis fought them for almost fifty years. Trakai's castles became seats of power and residence. Vytautas brought Karaite and Tatar settlers to the town, whose Karaite community still lives there. The duchy had its own court and nobility, closely tied to the grand duke.
duchy-of-trakai.e: After Algirdas died, his son Jogaila fought Kestutis, who was killed in captivity at Kreva in 1382. Kestutis's son Vytautas regained Trakai and later became grand duke. In 1413 the Union of Horodlo turned the duchy into the Trakai Voivodeship of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

despotate-of-the-morea.t: Late Byzantine principality based at Mistras in the Peloponnese, a last flowering of Byzantine culture and the home of the philosopher Plethon.
despotate-of-the-morea.o: Byzantium regained Mistras, Monemvasia and the Mani in 1262 from the Principality of Achaea and slowly expanded from there. In 1349 John VI Kantakouzenos made his son Manuel Kantakouzenos despot of the province, giving it a permanent ruler. From 1383 it passed to members of the Palaiologos family, beginning with Theodore I.
despotate-of-the-morea.r: Despots, usually younger sons of the emperor, ruled from Mistras, whose churches with their frescoes survive. They gradually conquered the Frankish principality, completing it in 1432. Greek, Albanian and Slavic farmers formed the population. The philosopher Gemistos Plethon proposed radical reforms there. The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus was rebuilt in 1415 against the Ottomans.
despotate-of-the-morea.e: After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, the despots Thomas and Demetrios Palaiologos quarrelled and faced Albanian revolts. Mehmed II conquered the Morea in 1460, the last Greek fortresses falling in 1461.

despotate-of-melnik.t: Rhodope principality of Alexius Slav, a relative of the Asen tsars, who ruled from Melnik as an ally of the Latin crusaders.
despotate-of-melnik.o: After the death of Tsar Kaloyan in 1207, his relative Alexius Slav refused to recognise the new tsar Boril and seized the Rhodope region. He made Melnik, in the Struma valley, his capital and held Tsepina and other fortresses.
despotate-of-melnik.r: Alexius Slav allied with the Latin Empire of Constantinople, marrying a daughter of Emperor Henry of Flanders, and received the Byzantine title of despot. He built churches and a residence at Melnik, whose monastery of the Mother of God Spileotissa has a charter from him, and he fought Boril and the Epirotes.
despotate-of-melnik.e: After 1228 he disappears from the record. The Bulgarian tsar Ivan Asen II absorbed his lands around 1230, after defeating Epirus at Klokotnitsa, into the Second Bulgarian Empire.

duchy-of-neopatras.t: Catalan duchy in southern Thessaly, created on the ruins of the Greek Principality of Thessaly and ruled with Athens by the kings of Sicily and Aragon.
duchy-of-neopatras.o: After the Catalan Company conquered the Duchy of Athens in 1311, it pushed north into Thessaly. When John II Doukas of the Principality of Thessaly died without heirs in 1318, the Catalans occupied the south of the region with its capital Neopatras (modern Ypati) and organised it as a duchy in 1319.
duchy-of-neopatras.r: Neopatras was held together with Athens by the Aragonese kings of Sicily, who appointed vicars-general such as Alfonso Fadrique to govern it. A small Catalan military class ruled over Greeks and Vlachs, following the customs of Barcelona. In 1379-1380 the duchies passed to Peter IV of Aragon, who called the Acropolis the most beautiful jewel in the world.
duchy-of-neopatras.e: Attacks by the Navarrese Company, the Florentine Nerio Acciaioli and the Ottomans broke the Catalan hold. Neopatras fell around 1390, and the Ottomans took Thessaly in the 1390s.

duchy-of-niemodlin.t: A small Upper Silesian Piast duchy around the castle of Niemodlin, split from the Duchy of Opole in 1313 and reabsorbed in 1382.
duchy-of-niemodlin.o: On the death of Duke Bolko I of Opole in 1313, his lands were divided among his sons. Bolesław the Elder received Niemodlin (Falkenberg), a castle town west of Opole, as his own duchy. He was close to the Bohemian court and in 1327 did homage to King John of Bohemia.
duchy-of-niemodlin.r: The duchy consisted of Niemodlin and its surrounding villages, settled partly under German law, with the castle as the ducal residence. Its dukes depended on Bohemian patronage and on their cousins in the Duchy of Opole. Little is recorded of its internal government.
duchy-of-niemodlin.e: The Niemodlin line died out with Duke Henry in 1382, and the duchy returned to the Duchy of Opole. Niemodlin later passed through various Silesian lords, went to Prussia in 1742 and became part of Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-ahtum.t: Realm in the Banat ruled from Morisena by Ahtum (Ajtony), a powerful Orthodox lord defeated by Stephen I of Hungary.
duchy-of-ahtum.o: Ahtum is known from the Legend of Saint Gerard. Around 1000 he held the land between the Mureș, the Tisza and the Danube, ruling from Morisena (Cenad). He had been baptised by the Orthodox rite at Vidin, and the Gesta Hungarorum makes him a descendant of Glad of the Duchy of Glad.
duchy-of-ahtum.r: Ahtum was rich in horses and cattle and taxed the salt carried down the Mureș to the king of Hungary, which provoked conflict. He founded a Greek monastery at Morisena, staffed by Byzantine monks, and recognised Byzantine authority.
duchy-of-ahtum.e: Stephen I sent his commander Csanád, who defeated and killed Ahtum. Most historians date this to around 1028. Csanád became count of the region, renamed Csanád, and Gerard founded a Latin bishopric there, part of the Kingdom of Hungary (1000-1301).

diocese-of-hispania.t: The late Roman administrative unit that grouped the provinces of Iberia and north-west Africa under a single vicar based at Mérida.
diocese-of-hispania.o: The diocese was created in Diocletian's reforms around 297 to 314, grouping the provinces of Baetica, Lusitania, Carthaginiensis, Gallaecia and Tarraconensis with Mauretania Tingitana across the Strait. The Balearica province was added around 369. It formed part of the Praetorian Prefecture of the Gauls.
diocese-of-hispania.r: A vicarius at Emerita Augusta oversaw the provincial governors, mainly in justice and taxation, while separate officers commanded the army. Hispania was largely peaceful in the 4th century, a land of rich villas and cities. Christianity grew strong, as the Council of Elvira shows, and the emperor Theodosius I came from Cauca in the north.
diocese-of-hispania.e: In 409 Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Pyrenees during the usurpation of Constantine III and his general Gerontius. Rome partly restored control with Visigothic help, but the diocese effectively broke up as barbarian kingdoms took over.

duchy-of-sabbioneta.t: The small Lombard duchy of Vespasiano Gonzaga, who built Sabbioneta from scratch as an ideal Renaissance city.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.o: Vespasiano Gonzaga, a soldier and courtier of Philip II of Spain from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga, inherited Sabbioneta and the surrounding lands between Mantua and Parma. From the 1550s he rebuilt the village as a fortified ideal city, and Emperor Rudolf II made it a duchy in 1577.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.r: Sabbioneta was laid out on a regular plan with star-shaped walls, a ducal palace, a long gallery for Vespasiano's art and antiquities, and the Teatro all'Antica by Vincenzo Scamozzi, completed around 1590, one of the first purpose-built theatres in modern Europe. The duke ran a small, tightly controlled court and drew craftsmen and Jewish printers to the town.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.e: Vespasiano died in 1591 without a surviving son, and the duchy passed through his daughter to the Carafa and then other heirs, losing its importance. It was absorbed into Austrian-ruled Lombardy when the Gonzaga lands were seized in 1708.

duchy-of-glad.t: Duchy in the Banat described in the Gesta Hungarorum as resisting the conquering Hungarians around 900; its existence is debated.
duchy-of-glad.o: The main source is the Gesta Hungarorum, written by an anonymous notary around 1200. It says Glad, who came from Vidin, ruled the land between the Mureș, the Tisza and the Danube, with Cumans, Bulgarians and Vlachs, from the fortress of Keve (Kovin).
duchy-of-glad.r: Nothing is known of its government beyond the Gesta, which claims Glad fought the Hungarians with Cuman, Bulgarian and Vlach forces before being defeated and submitting. Historians disagree on whether he was a real ruler, perhaps a Bulgarian governor, or a figure invented from later place-names.
duchy-of-glad.e: The Gesta says the Hungarians took his lands, which then passed to the Principality of Hungary. The same source makes Ahtum, of the Duchy of Ahtum, his descendant.

duchy-of-slutsk.t: A Ruthenian duchy in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, ruled by the Olelkovich princes and famous for resisting Tatar raids.
duchy-of-slutsk.o: In 1395 Vytautas removed Volodymyr Olgerdovich from the Principality of Kiev and gave him Slutsk and Kapyl in compensation. Volodymyr's descendants, the Olelkovich princes, held Slutsk as a hereditary duchy within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania for two centuries.
duchy-of-slutsk.r: The Olelkovich princes were among the greatest Orthodox magnates of the grand duchy, with their own court, troops and towns. In 1506 the regent Anastasia of Slutsk defended the town against a Tatar siege. The princes built churches and monasteries, and Slutsk became a centre of Orthodox learning and crafts.
duchy-of-slutsk.e: The male line ended with the death of Yury Yurievich in 1592. Through the marriage of the heiress Sophia Olelkovich to Janusz Radziwill, the duchy passed to the Radziwill family, who held it as a private estate. Slutsk later became famous for its woven silk sashes.

dal-naraidi.t: Leading kingdom of the Cruthin in south Antrim, whose king Congal Cáech fought for the high kingship and fell at Mag Rath in 637.
dal-naraidi.o: The Dál nAraidi were the leading dynasty of the Cruthin, a people of east Ulster distinguished in early Irish sources from the Ulaid proper. By the 6th century they held south and central County Antrim, with their royal centre in Mag Line near the town of Antrim, and they competed with the Dal Fiatach for the kingship of the Kingdom of Ulaid.
dal-naraidi.r: Fiachnae mac Báetáin, who died in 626, became king of the Ulaid and is said to have campaigned in Britain. Congal Cáech, king of the Ulaid and briefly claimant to the kingship of Tara, allied with Dál Riata but was defeated and killed by Domnall mac Áedo at Mag Rath in 637. St Comgall, founder of the monastery of Bangor, belonged to this people.
dal-naraidi.e: After Mag Rath their power declined, though their kings still held the Ulaid kingship at times until the 10th century. Pressure from Viking raiders, the Uí Néill and the Dal Fiatach reduced them, and by the 12th century their lands passed under Anglo-Norman and Ua Néill rule.

danish-greenland.t: Greenland as a Danish colony, from the missionary Hans Egede's arrival in 1721 to its integration into the Danish realm in 1953.
danish-greenland.o: Hoping to find the lost Norse colonists, the Norwegian priest Hans Egede sailed to Greenland in 1721 with the support of Denmark-Norway and founded a mission and trading post, moving it to Godthåb (Nuuk) in 1728. Danish trading stations then spread along the west coast.
danish-greenland.r: From 1776 the Royal Greenland Trade Department held a monopoly on trade, keeping the island closed to outsiders. The Inuit population lived by seal hunting, while the Danes bought skins, blubber and later cod. Lutheran missions, including Moravians, converted most Greenlanders. When Norway was ceded to Sweden in 1814, Greenland stayed Danish, and in 1933 the Permanent Court of International Justice rejected Norway's claim to East Greenland.
danish-greenland.e: During the German occupation of Denmark the United States protected Greenland and built bases there. In 1953 a new Danish constitution ended colonial status and made Greenland an integral part of the Kingdom of Denmark. Home rule followed in 1979 and self-government in 2009.

delos.t: The sacred island of Apollo, independent from 314 to 167 BCE, when its sanctuary became a meeting place of kings and a hub of Aegean commerce.
delos.o: Delos, birthplace of Apollo and Artemis in Greek myth, had long been under Athenian control. In 314 BCE, with Antigonus I extending his power into the Aegean, the Athenians were ousted and the Delians governed their island as an independent city, also hosting the Nesiotic League.
delos.r: Independent Delos was run by an archon, council and assembly, while elected hieropoioi managed the sanctuary's lands, loans and treasures; their yearly inscribed accounts are among the richest economic records from antiquity. Kings of Macedon, Egypt and Pergamon built porticoes and dedications. Banking and trade grew, drawing merchants from Italy and the East.
delos.e: In 167 BCE Rome handed Delos to Athens and made it a free port to damage Rhodes; the Delians were expelled to Achaea. Delos then boomed as a slave and grain market until sacked in 88 BCE by the forces of Mithridates VI and again by pirates in 69 BCE. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-gelou.t: Transylvanian duchy of Gelou, called a Vlach by the Gesta Hungarorum, whose defeat opened Transylvania to the Hungarians; its existence is debated.
duchy-of-gelou.o: The Gesta Hungarorum, written around 1200, is the only source. It describes Gelou as a Vlach ruling Vlachs and Slavs in the Someș valley of Transylvania at the time of the Hungarian conquest, with his centre usually placed at Dăbâca.
duchy-of-gelou.r: Nothing is known of the duchy beyond the chronicle, which praises the land for its salt and gold-bearing rivers and says its people were poorly armed and suffered Cuman and Pecheneg raids. An early medieval fortification at Dăbâca has been excavated, but its dating is disputed.
duchy-of-gelou.e: The Gesta says Tuhutum, a Hungarian chief, defeated and killed Gelou at the river Almaș, and the inhabitants accepted him as lord; his descendants are linked to the Realm of the Gyulas. The episode is central to debates over the early history of Romanians in Transylvania.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.t: The larger Mecklenburg state on the Baltic, ruled by one of Europe's oldest dynasties and known for its archaic feudal constitution.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.o: After the extinction of the Güstrow line in 1695, a succession dispute in the House of Mecklenburg was settled by the Treaty of Hamburg in 1701. Frederick William received the larger western share as the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, with Schwerin, Rostock and Wismar's hinterland, while a smaller share became Mecklenburg-Strelitz.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.r: The dynasty descended from the Obotrite prince Niklot of the 12th century. Under the 1755 settlement with the estates, power was shared with the knighthood, preserving large noble estates and serfdom until 1820. The economy rested on grain and cattle. Frederick Francis I joined the Confederation of the Rhine and became grand duke in 1815. No modern constitution was adopted before 1918.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.e: Mecklenburg-Schwerin joined the North German Confederation and in 1871 the German Empire. Grand Duke Frederick Francis IV abdicated in November 1918, and the state continued as the Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin.

duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.t: Northern Estonia under the Swedish crown, Sweden's first Baltic conquest, held from 1561 until Peter the Great took it in the Great Northern War.
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.o: As Terra Mariana collapsed under Russian attack, the city of Reval and the knighthoods of Harrien, Wierland and Jerwen submitted to Eric XIV of Sweden in 1561. Sweden held on through the long Livonian War, and the Treaty of Teusina in 1595 confirmed its possession of northern Estonia.
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.r: The duchy was ruled by a Swedish governor at Reval, but the Baltic German nobility kept wide self-government, their Lutheran church and control of their serfs. Swedish rule founded schools and printed the first Estonian books; Charles XI's reduction of noble estates in the 1680s angered the nobles. Reval and Narva were key ports for Baltic trade.
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.e: In the Great Northern War Russian forces took Reval in 1710, and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 confirmed the loss. The region became the Governorate of Estonia within the Russian Empire, its nobles' privileges guaranteed by Peter the Great.

duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.t: The marble-quarrying state of the Malaspina and Cybo families on the Tuscan coast, whose white stone supplied Michelangelo and Europe's sculptors.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.o: The Malaspina, a feudal family of Lunigiana, ruled Massa, and in 1473 Jacopo Malaspina bought Carrara with its marble quarries. Through the marriage of Ricciarda Malaspina, the state passed to the Cybo family, and Alberico I Cybo-Malaspina was made prince in 1568; it became a duchy in 1664.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.r: The rulers governed a narrow strip between the Apuan Alps and the sea. Carrara's marble, quarried since Roman times, was the state's wealth; Michelangelo chose blocks there. Alberico I laid out a new town centre at Massa. The state survived as an imperial fief protected by Spain and its neighbours.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.e: The heiress Maria Beatrice Cybo d'Este married Ferdinand of Austria-Este. After Napoleonic rule under Elisa Bonaparte, she was restored in 1814, and on her death in 1829 the duchy passed to her son Francis IV, joining the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.t: Duchy created in 1235 for Otto the Child, grandson of Henry the Lion, which reconciled the Guelphs with the Hohenstaufen and founded the house of Brunswick.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.o: After Henry the Lion's fall in 1180, his family kept their allodial lands around Brunswick and Lüneburg. At the Diet of Mainz in 1235 his grandson Otto the Child surrendered these lands to Emperor Frederick II and received them back as a new imperial duchy, ending the long feud between the Guelphs and the Hohenstaufen.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.r: Otto ruled from Brunswick, where Henry the Lion's castle of Dankwarderode and the bronze lion stood, and from Lüneburg, whose salt works were the duchy's main source of wealth. The duchy lay between the Weser and the Elbe and included Hanover, Celle and Göttingen. After Otto's death in 1252 his sons Albert I the Tall and John ruled jointly.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.e: In 1269 Albert and John divided the duchy, creating the Principality of Wolfenbüttel and the Principality of Lüneburg. The ducal title stayed common to all Guelph lines, from which the Electorate of Hanover and the British royal house of Hanover later descended.

despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.t: Albanian principality in Aetolia under the Shpata family, holding Angelokastron and the port of Lepanto after the Serbian conquest of Epirus.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.o: After Nikephoros II Orsini of Epirus was killed by Albanian clans in 1359, Albanian leaders divided southern Epirus. Gjin Bua Shpata took Angelokastron and Lepanto (Naupaktos) in Aetolia, while Peter Losha held the Despotate of Arta. Both received the title of despot from the Serbian ruler Simeon Uroš.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.r: The Shpata ruled Albanian clans who had migrated south as herders and soldiers, alongside a Greek population. They fought the Angevins, the Tocco of Kefalonia, the Navarrese Company and the Ottomans. In 1374 Gjin Bua Shpata also took Arta, joining the two Albanian despotates.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.e: After Gjin's death in 1399 his family held on briefly: Lepanto was sold to Venice in 1407, and Angelokastron fell to Carlo I Tocco around 1408.

duchy-of-burgundy.t: The wine-rich duchy around Dijon, home of Cluny and Cîteaux, that under its Valois dukes became the seed of a great European power.
duchy-of-burgundy.o: Richard the Justiciar, count of Autun, gathered the counties of western Burgundy and was recognised as duke by around 918. After a century of disputes the duchy went in 1032 to Robert, younger brother of King Henry I, founding a Capetian line that ruled from Dijon for over 300 years.
duchy-of-burgundy.r: The dukes were great vassals of France, governing through their council and the Estates of Burgundy. The duchy was a heartland of monastic reform: Cluny lay on its borders, and Cîteaux, founded in 1098, launched the Cistercian order. Its vineyards in the Côte d'Or were already famous in the Middle Ages.
duchy-of-burgundy.e: When Philip of Rouvres died in 1361, John II of France took the duchy and in 1363 gave it to his son Philip the Bold, founding the Burgundian State. After Charles the Bold fell at Nancy in 1477, Louis XI annexed the duchy to the Kingdom of France.

decapole.t: A league of ten imperial cities of Alsace, founded in 1354 for mutual defence, which survived until Louis XIV absorbed it.
decapole.o: In 1354 Emperor Charles IV joined ten free imperial cities of Alsace in an alliance: Haguenau, Colmar, Wissembourg, Turckheim, Obernai, Kaysersberg, Rosheim, Munster, Sélestat and Mulhouse. They were placed under the imperial bailiff at Haguenau to defend their rights against local lords.
decapole.r: The cities governed themselves but pledged mutual aid, shared costs and met in diets. Mulhouse left in 1515 to ally with the Swiss and Landau joined in 1521. Members were wine and market towns, and some, like Colmar, adopted Lutheranism while others stayed Catholic. The league had no army or capital of its own.
decapole.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 transferred imperial rights in Alsace to France ambiguously, and Louis XIV occupied the cities in 1673. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French control, ending the league.

duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.t: Ernestine duchy in eastern Thuringia, home of the card game Skat and of the dukes who exchanged Hildburghausen for Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.o: When Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg died out in 1825, the Ernestine lands were rearranged in 1826. Duke Frederick of Saxe-Hildburghausen gave up his old duchy and received Altenburg, founding the new Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.r: The duchy was Lutheran and agriculturally rich, with prosperous peasant farms and later lignite mining. The card game Skat was developed in Altenburg around 1810-1820, and the town remains its centre, with a Skat court. A constitution was granted in 1831, and in 1848 unrest forced Duke Joseph to abdicate. Ernest I ruled from 1853 to 1908.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.e: Saxe-Altenburg joined the North German Confederation and the German Empire. Duke Ernest II abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the Free State of Thuringia. Altenburg Castle now houses a museum of playing cards.

duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.t: Small Ernestine duchy in southern Thuringia whose princess's 1810 wedding in Munich gave rise to the Oktoberfest.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.o: Ernest, the sixth son of Ernest the Pious, received Hildburghausen in the 1680 partition of the Saxe-Gotha inheritance. He made the small town his residence and was given full ducal sovereignty, later adding Eisfeld and Königsberg in Franconia.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.r: The dukes built a palace and attracted Huguenot refugees to a new town quarter. Extravagance led to bankruptcy, and in 1769 an imperial debt commission took over the finances. Duke Frederick's daughter Therese married Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria in Munich in October 1810, and the horse race held in her honour became the Oktoberfest; the Theresienwiese still bears her name.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.e: After Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg died out, the Ernestine lands were redistributed in 1826. Duke Frederick exchanged Hildburghausen for Altenburg, becoming Duke of Saxe-Altenburg, and Hildburghausen went to Saxe-Meiningen.

duchy-of-masovia.t: The long-lived duchy of central Poland whose duke invited the Teutonic Knights and whose town of Warsaw became Poland's capital.
duchy-of-masovia.o: Masovia, on the middle Vistula with its centre at Plock, was given to Boleslaw IV the Curly under the testament of Boleslaw III in 1138. From 1199 it was held by Konrad I and his descendants, a branch of the Piasts that ruled it for over three centuries.
duchy-of-masovia.r: Exposed to raids by the pagan Prussians and Lithuanians, Konrad I invited the Teutonic Order in 1226 and gave it the land of Chelmno, a decision with lasting consequences. Masovia was a poor, heavily forested land with a large petty nobility. Its dukes often divided it into smaller duchies such as Plock and Rawa, and from 1351 they were vassals of the Polish king.
duchy-of-masovia.e: Janusz I made Warsaw his main seat in the early 15th century. When the last dukes, Stanislaw and Janusz III, died young in 1524 and 1526, Masovia was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569), and Warsaw became the royal capital in 1596.

duchy-of-mantua.t: The Gonzaga state of Mantua, whose court commissioned Mantegna, Giulio Romano and Monteverdi before war and plague ruined it.
duchy-of-mantua.o: In 1328 Luigi Gonzaga overthrew the Bonacolsi lords of Mantua and became captain of the people. The Gonzaga ruled as imperial vicars, became marquises in 1433 under Gianfrancesco Gonzaga and dukes in 1530 under Federico II, who also acquired the Duchy of Montferrat.
duchy-of-mantua.r: Mantua's court was among the most brilliant in Italy. Andrea Mantegna painted the Camera degli Sposi for Ludovico III; Isabella d'Este collected art; Giulio Romano built the Palazzo Te for Federico II. Under Vincenzo I, Monteverdi's Orfeo was staged in 1607. The duchy lived from farming, textiles and the condottiere service of its lords.
duchy-of-mantua.e: The main line died out in 1627, and the War of the Mantuan Succession brought an imperial sack in 1630. The Gonzaga-Nevers line ruled until Ferdinando Carlo sided with France and was deposed in 1708, when Austria annexed Mantua.

duchy-of-opava.t: Duchy carved out of northern Moravia for a son of King Ottokar II, later ruled by the Liechtensteins and capital of Austrian Silesia until 1918.
duchy-of-opava.o: Around 1269 King Ottokar II of Bohemia gave the Opava region of northern Moravia to his illegitimate son Nicholas I. Nicholas's descendants ruled it as a separate duchy, and it gradually came to be counted among the Silesian duchies rather than Moravia, under the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-opava.r: The Opava Přemyslids ruled until the 15th century, after which the duchy passed to the Poděbrady family, the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus and the Habsburgs. In 1614 it was granted to Karl I of Liechtenstein, whose family kept the ducal title. Opava was a town of German and Czech speakers, cloth and trade, and the Counter-Reformation restored Catholicism after 1620.
duchy-of-opava.e: In 1742 Prussia took the northern part; the rest became the core of Austrian Silesia, with Opava as capital, and hosted the Congress of Troppau in 1820. In 1918 it joined Czechoslovakia and is now in the Czech Republic.

deisi-muman.t: Kingdom of the Déisi in Waterford and south Tipperary, whose legendary migrations reached Wales and whose name survives in the Decies.
deisi-muman.o: The Déisi were a population group whose name means 'vassals'. The early Irish tale The Expulsion of the Déisi tells how they were driven from Brega near Tara and wandered south, some settling in Munster and others crossing to Dyfed in Wales, where the Kingdom of Dyfed's kings later claimed Déisi descent. In Munster they settled in what is now County Waterford and south Tipperary.
deisi-muman.r: The Déisi Muman were a subject kingdom within the Kingdom of Munster, paying tribute to the Eóganachta of Cashel. The monastery of Lismore, founded by St Mochuda in the 7th century, was one of the great schools of early Ireland and lay in their territory. A northern branch, the Déis Tuaiscirt, later grew into the Dál Cais, the dynasty of Brian Bóruma.
deisi-muman.e: The Ua Fáeláin, O'Phelan, kings ruled the Déisi in the 11th and 12th centuries. After the Anglo-Normans took Waterford in 1170 their lands were granted to settlers, and the kingdom faded around 1200. The name survives in the baronies of Decies in Waterford.

damnonii.t: People of the Clyde valley recorded by Ptolemy, whose territory was crossed by the Antonine Wall and later formed the heart of Strathclyde.
damnonii.o: The Damnonii appear in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography in the region of the Clyde, Ayrshire and parts of Stirlingshire, with places such as Vanduara and Alauna listed among their settlements. They derived from the Iron Age communities of west central Scotland, who lived in hillforts, crannogs and enclosed farms.
damnonii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Their land lay on the line of the Antonine Wall, built across the Forth and Clyde isthmus from 142, and was occupied by Roman forts during the periods of Roman advance into Scotland. Their society was otherwise rural and cattle-based, much like their neighbours.
damnonii.e: After the Roman withdrawal to Hadrian's Wall the Damnonii lived beyond the frontier. They are generally regarded as ancestors of the British people of the Clyde, whose Kingdom of Strathclyde was centred on Alt Clut, Dumbarton Rock.

duchy-of-oldenburg.t: North German duchy, later grand duchy, created by a Danish-Russian exchange and ruled by a branch of the house that also held the Russian throne.
duchy-of-oldenburg.o: The County of Oldenburg had been ruled by the Danish kings since 1667. In the Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo of 1773, Denmark exchanged it with Russia for the Gottorp share of Holstein, and Grand Duke Paul passed it to his relative Frederick Augustus, prince-bishop of Lübeck. In 1774 the emperor raised Oldenburg to a duchy.
duchy-of-oldenburg.r: The dukes of the Holstein-Gottorp line governed a Lutheran land of marshes, moors and cattle farming, with the secularised Principality of Lübeck at Eutin and, from 1817, the Principality of Birkenfeld. Peter Frederick Louis was a careful administrator. Napoleon annexed Oldenburg to France in 1811, but it was restored in 1813 and became a grand duchy, adopting a constitution in 1849.
duchy-of-oldenburg.e: Oldenburg joined the North German Confederation and the German Empire. Grand Duke Frederick Augustus II abdicated in November 1918, and the state became the Free State of Oldenburg.

duchy-of-finland.t: Short-lived Finnish duchy granted to the future John III of Sweden, whose independent policy led his brother Eric XIV to crush it in 1563.
duchy-of-finland.o: In 1556 Gustav Vasa granted his second son John the Duchy of Finland, covering south-western Finland, as an appanage. John set up his court at Turku Castle, which he enlarged in Renaissance style, and governed with considerable independence.
duchy-of-finland.r: Duke John ran his own administration, collected taxes and pursued a foreign policy of his own, which brought him into conflict with his half-brother, King Eric XIV. In 1562 he married Catherine Jagiellon, sister of King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, and lent money to Poland while Sweden and Poland competed for Livonia.
duchy-of-finland.e: Eric XIV regarded this as treason. In 1563 his army besieged and took Turku Castle, and John and Catherine were imprisoned at Gripsholm. The duchy was abolished, and Finland returned to direct rule by the Kingdom of Sweden. John deposed Eric in 1568 and reigned as John III.

duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.t: The southern Pomeranian duchy created in 1295, centred on the Oder port of Stettin and long contested with Brandenburg.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.o: The partition of the Duchy of Pomerania in 1295 gave Otto I the lands around Stettin (Szczecin) on the lower Oder, while his brother Bogislaw IV took Pomerania-Wolgast. Otto's descendants spent much of the 14th and 15th centuries resisting the Margraviate of Brandenburg's claims to overlordship and to the succession.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.r: Stettin was a Hanseatic port exporting grain, timber and herring, and its burghers often acted independently of the dukes. Bogislaw X, who reunited all Pomerania in 1478, reformed its administration and finances. The Treaty of Grimnitz in 1529 freed the dukes from Brandenburg's feudal claims in exchange for a promise of succession, and Pomerania adopted Lutheranism in 1534.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.e: After a new division in 1532, Stettin was ruled by a series of dukes who died without heirs. Bogislaw XIV united both duchies in 1625, but Sweden occupied Pomerania in 1630. On his death in 1637 the Griffin line ended, and in 1648 the lands were divided between Swedish Pomerania and Brandenburg.

duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.t: The small part of Silesia that Austria kept after Frederick the Great's conquest, an industrial crown land of the Habsburgs.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.o: Prussia seized most of Silesia in the War of the Austrian Succession, and under the Treaty of Breslau and the Peace of Berlin in 1742 Austria kept only a southern strip, including the duchies of Troppau, Teschen and part of Jägerndorf. This remnant was governed as the Duchy of Upper and Lower Silesia, usually called Austrian Silesia.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.r: Austrian Silesia was administered from Troppau (Opava), at first jointly with Moravia and from 1849 as a separate crown land with its own diet. Its population was German, Czech and Polish, Catholic with Lutheran minorities in Teschen. Coal mining in the Ostrava-Karviná basin and the Vítkovice ironworks made it one of the most industrialised parts of the monarchy.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.e: With the collapse of Austria-Hungary in 1918, the territory was claimed by Czechoslovakia and Poland. After a brief war over Teschen in 1919, it was divided in 1920, with most going to Czechoslovakia.
