duchy-of-julich.t: A Rhineland county turned duchy between Aachen and Cologne, whose union with Cleves and Berg created a powerful state and a famous succession crisis.
duchy-of-julich.o: A count named Gerhard appears in the Jülichgau around 1003, and his family built a county around the old Roman town of Jülich west of the Rhine. The counts fought the archbishops of Cologne for supremacy in the lower Rhineland, sharing the victory at Worringen in 1288 with Berg and Brabant.
duchy-of-julich.r: Count William V was made margrave in 1336 and duke in 1356. In 1423 Jülich united with the Duchy of Berg, and in 1521 with the Duchy of Cleves and the County of the Mark, forming the United Duchies. Duke William the Rich built Jülich into an Italian Renaissance fortress town with a citadel.
duchy-of-julich.e: When the last duke, John William, died in 1609, the Jülich succession crisis between Brandenburg and Palatinate-Neuburg nearly sparked a European war. The Treaty of Xanten in 1614 gave Jülich and Berg to Palatinate-Neuburg. French revolutionary armies took Jülich in 1794, and in 1815 it became Prussian.

duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.t: The Este duchy that became the family's main state after the loss of Ferrara, lasting until Italian unification in 1859.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.o: In 1452 Emperor Frederick III made Borso d'Este duke of Modena and Reggio, imperial fiefs held alongside the papal Duchy of Ferrara. When Ferrara passed to the papacy in 1598, Cesare d'Este moved his court to Modena, which became the capital.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.r: The Este rebuilt Modena as a capital, with a ducal palace and the Biblioteca Estense, where the scholar Ludovico Antonio Muratori worked as librarian. The duchy added Mirandola, Correggio and Novellara. After French occupation from 1796, when it joined the Cispadane Republic, the restored duchy passed in 1814 to Francis IV of Austria-Este, who ruled harshly and executed the revolutionary Ciro Menotti in 1831.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.e: Francis V fled after the Austrian defeat in 1859. The duchy joined the United Provinces of Central Italy and was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

domnonee.t: Breton kingdom of northern Brittany, named after Dumnonia in Britain, whose king Judicael treated with Dagobert I as an equal.
domnonee.o: Migrants from Dumnonia in south-west Britain, the land of modern Devon and Cornwall, settled the northern coast of Armorica in the 5th and 6th centuries and gave it the name of their homeland. Its early rulers are known mainly from saints' lives, which may preserve legend.
domnonee.r: The kingdom stretched along the Channel coast from the Rance to the Morlaix area. Its life centred on monastic foundations such as Saint-Malo, Dol and Saint-Pol-de-Léon, linked to saints from Wales and Cornwall. The chronicle of Fredegar records that King Judicael met Dagobert I at Clichy in 636 and made peace with the Franks.
domnonee.e: In the 9th century Domnonée was absorbed into the Kingdom of Brittany created by Nominoe and Erispoe. The bishopric of Dol and the later counties of Penthièvre and Léon preserved parts of its territory.

duchy-of-greater-poland.t: The duchy of the Piast heartland around Poznan and Gniezno, which produced Poland's first crowned king after two centuries of division.
duchy-of-greater-poland.o: Under the testament of Boleslaw III in 1138, his son Mieszko III the Old received Greater Poland, with Poznan and Gniezno, the cradle of the Piast state. For much of the next century the duchy was contested between Mieszko's descendants and was at times divided between Poznan and Kalisz.
duchy-of-greater-poland.r: Greater Poland was a farming region, settled in the 13th century by German colonists and towns founded under Magdeburg law, such as Poznan in 1253. Its dukes, especially Wladyslaw Odonic and his sons, built up their power with the support of the church of Gniezno. Duke Przemysl II gained Pomerelia in 1294 and was crowned King of Poland in Gniezno in 1295.
duchy-of-greater-poland.e: Przemysl II was murdered in 1296, and the duchy passed to Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high, Wenceslaus II of Bohemia and Henry of Glogow. Wladyslaw I took it back in 1314, and in 1320 it became part of the reunited Kingdom of Poland (1025-1385).

duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.t: Two secularised prince-bishoprics between Elbe and Weser that passed from Sweden to Hanover, controlling the approaches to Bremen and Hamburg.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.o: The Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen and the Prince-Bishopric of Verden had been occupied by Sweden during the Thirty Years' War. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 they were secularised and granted to the Swedish crown as the duchies of Bremen and Verden, with the government seated at Stade.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.r: The duchies kept their estates and Lutheran church while Sweden used them as a strategic base. The city of Bremen resisted Swedish claims and remained an imperial free city. Denmark occupied the duchies in 1712 during the Great Northern War and sold them to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715, a transfer recognised by Sweden in 1719. Farming in the marshlands and moors was the mainstay.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.e: After Napoleonic occupation the lands returned to the Kingdom of Hanover in 1813. In 1823 they were merged into the Stade administrative region, ending the duchies as distinct units; the area passed to Prussia in 1866.

duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.t: The Norman duchy of Robert Guiscard, which drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy and laid the groundwork for the Kingdom of Sicily.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.o: Norman mercenaries in Byzantine Apulia elected William Iron Arm as their count at Melfi around 1042–1043. His half-brother Robert Guiscard took over, and in 1059 Pope Nicholas II invested him at Melfi as duke of Apulia, Calabria and, in prospect, Sicily, making the papacy the duchy's overlord.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.r: Guiscard captured Bari in 1071, ending Byzantine rule in Italy, and Salerno in 1077, which became his capital. The duchy ruled Greek-speaking Calabria and Lombard and Latin Apulia, keeping Byzantine officials and Greek monasteries alongside Latin bishops. Its army also invaded the Byzantine Empire across the Adriatic in 1081, and in 1084 sacked Rome while rescuing Pope Gregory VII.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.e: After Guiscard's death in 1085, his son Roger Borsa and grandson William II struggled to control rebellious barons. When William died childless in 1127, his cousin Roger II of the County of Sicily claimed the duchy, and in 1130 merged it into the new Kingdom of Sicily.

despotate-of-arta.t: Albanian despotate in southern Epirus, ruled by the Losha and Shpata clans from Arta until Carlo Tocco took the city in 1416.
despotate-of-arta.o: In 1358–1359 Albanian clans defeated Nikephoros II Orsini, the last Orsini despot, and divided southern Epirus. Peter Losha took Arta and was recognised as despot by Simeon Uroš, the Serbian ruler of Thessaly; Gjin Bua Shpata held the Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto to the south.
despotate-of-arta.r: The despots relied on Albanian clans who had moved into Epirus, ruling a Greek town population around Arta. They fought the Serbian rulers of Ioannina, notably Thomas Preljubović, and later Esau de' Buondelmonti. After Losha's death in 1374 Gjin Bua Shpata ruled both despotates until 1399, followed by Muriq Shpata and Yaqub Shpata, who allied with the Ottomans.
despotate-of-arta.e: Yaqub Shpata was killed in 1416, and Carlo I Tocco, ruler of Ioannina, captured Arta. The city was taken by the Ottomans in 1449.

duchy-of-lorraine.t: The duchy between France and the Empire, ruled for seven centuries by one dynasty from Nancy before passing to France in 1766.
duchy-of-lorraine.o: Lorraine grew from the Duchy of Upper Lorraine, created in 959 when the Duchy of Lotharingia was divided. In 1048 Emperor Henry III gave it to Gerard of Alsace, whose descendants ruled until 1737. The dukes settled on Nancy as their capital and held their lands as vassals of the Holy Roman Empire.
duchy-of-lorraine.r: The duchy was bilingual, French in the west and German in the east, and surrounded by the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun. René II defeated and killed Charles the Bold before Nancy in 1477. The Guise branch led the Catholic League in France, and Nancy's Renaissance and baroque palaces reflected a brilliant court.
duchy-of-lorraine.e: France occupied Lorraine repeatedly in the 17th century; Duke Leopold recovered it in 1697. In 1737 Francis Stephen exchanged it for Tuscany, and the deposed Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński ruled it for life. On his death in 1766 it was annexed to the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-brabant.t: The duchy of Brussels, Leuven and Antwerp, famous for its charter of liberties, the Joyous Entry, and the economic heart of the Low Countries.
duchy-of-brabant.o: The counts of Louvain had held the title of duke of Lower Lorraine since 1106. Around 1183 Henry I began styling himself duke of Brabant, and after the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 the County of Louvain and its neighbouring lands formed the Duchy of Brabant.
duchy-of-brabant.r: Brabant's dukes ruled with powerful towns: Brussels, Leuven, Antwerp and 's-Hertogenbosch. John I won Limburg at Worringen in 1288. The Joyous Entry of 1356 bound Duchess Joanna to respect the estates' rights, a charter sworn by every later ruler. Cloth, then Antwerp's world trade in the 16th century, made Brabant the richest part of the Low Countries.
duchy-of-brabant.e: Brabant passed to Philip the Good in 1430 and joined the Burgundian State, then the Habsburg Netherlands. The Dutch Revolt split it: the north went to the Dutch Republic in 1648, the south stayed in the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands, rose in the Brabant Revolution of 1789, and was annexed by France in 1795.

duchy-of-rome.t: Byzantine district around Rome in which the popes gradually took over government, the seed of the Papal States.
duchy-of-rome.o: After the Lombard invasion, the territory around Rome remained in Byzantine hands, cut off from Ravenna by Lombard Spoleto. A duke (dux) commanded its garrison under the exarch of Ravenna. From the pontificate of Gregory the Great (590–604), who organised Rome's food supply and defence, the popes became the area's real leaders.
duchy-of-rome.r: The duke led the local militia while the pope administered the vast Church estates, fed the city and negotiated with the Lombards. A local military aristocracy grew powerful. Disputes with Constantinople over doctrine and taxation, especially Iconoclasm under Leo III, loosened ties to the empire. King Liutprand's gift of Sutri to the pope in 728 was its first territorial grant.
duchy-of-rome.e: When the Lombards took Ravenna in 751 and threatened Rome, Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps and gained the protection of Pepin the Short in 754. Pepin's donation of 756 created the Papal States, into which the duchy was absorbed.

duchy-of-bohemia.t: The Czech duchy of the Přemyslid dynasty, home of Saint Wenceslas, which grew from Prague into a strong state and a kingdom of the Empire.
duchy-of-bohemia.o: Bořivoj I, the first historically attested Přemyslid, was baptised around 870, probably by Methodius, while under Great Moravian overlordship. After Great Moravia fell, the Přemyslids of Prague unified the Bohemian tribes. In 895 they sought East Frankish protection, and Bohemia became tied to the German kingdom.
duchy-of-bohemia.r: Dukes ruled from Prague Castle through a network of castle districts. Wenceslas, murdered by his brother Boleslaus I in 935, became the country's patron saint. Boleslaus II founded the bishopric of Prague in 973. Dukes were vassals of the German kings, while slave trade, silver and later colonisation shaped the economy.
duchy-of-bohemia.e: Vratislaus II received a personal royal title in 1085 and Vladislaus II in 1158. In 1198 Ottokar I secured a hereditary royal crown, confirmed by the Golden Bull of Sicily in 1212, and the duchy became the Kingdom of Bohemia, a leading state of the Empire.

duchy-of-trent.t: Lombard frontier duchy in the Adige valley guarding the Brenner route into Italy against Franks and Bavarians.
duchy-of-trent.o: Soon after the Lombard invasion of 568, a duchy was set up at Tridentum (Trento) to control the Adige valley, the main route from the Brenner Pass into the Po plain. Paul the Deacon names Euin as its first duke, who repelled Frankish invasions in the 570s and 580s and married a Bavarian princess.
duchy-of-trent.r: The dukes of Trent were military lords on a sensitive frontier, dealing by war and marriage with the Franks and the Bavarians to the north. Their territory covered much of modern Trentino and the upper Adige. Duke Alahis rebelled against King Cunipert, seized Pavia and was killed at the battle of Coronate around 689. Otherwise little is recorded of their government.
duchy-of-trent.e: After Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard Kingdom in 774, Trent was placed under Frankish counts as part of the Carolingian Kingdom of Italy. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II gave the county to the bishops of Trent, founding the prince-bishopric.

duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.t: Albertine Saxon secondary duchy on the Saale, created by an elector's will and absorbed back into the Electorate after eighty years.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.o: Elector John George I of Saxony divided parts of his lands in his will among his younger sons. After his death in 1656, Christian I received Merseburg, the secularised bishopric and its district, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Merseburg, which also held parts of Lusatia.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.r: The dukes held their lands as secundogenitures under the sovereignty of the Electorate of Saxony, with limited independence in foreign affairs. They rebuilt Merseburg Castle and maintained a court with music and a library. The duchy was Lutheran and agrarian. Its later dukes were known more for extravagance than for policy; Maurice William was nicknamed the Fiddle Duke.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.e: Heinrich, the last duke, died without heirs in 1738, and the territory reverted to the Electorate of Saxony. Merseburg passed to Prussia in 1815 and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

duchy-of-plock.t: The northern Masovian duchy around the old Piast city of Plock, a Polish vassal until its incorporation in 1495.
duchy-of-plock.o: In 1275 the Duchy of Masovia was split, and the part centred on Plock, an early Piast capital and bishopric on the Vistula, went to Boleslaw II of Masovia. For two centuries Plock was sometimes reunited with the rest of Masovia and sometimes ruled as a separate duchy.
duchy-of-plock.r: Plock was an old episcopal city with a Romanesque cathedral containing Piast tombs. Its dukes balanced between Poland, Bohemia and the Teutonic Order: Wenceslaus of Plock did homage to John of Bohemia in 1329. From 1351 the Masovian dukes were vassals of the Polish Crown.
duchy-of-plock.e: The last duke of Plock, Janusz II, died in 1495, and King John I Albert incorporated the duchy into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569). The rest of Masovia followed in 1526.

duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.t: German client state proclaimed by Courland's Baltic German nobles in 1918, which offered its ducal crown to Kaiser Wilhelm II.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.o: Under German occupation, the Courland Landesrat, a council dominated by Baltic German nobles, proclaimed on 8 March 1918 the restoration of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia, covering the former Governorate of Courland. It offered the ducal crown to Wilhelm II, and Germany recognised the duchy on 15 March.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.r: The duchy had no real government of its own and depended on the German military administration that had replaced Ober Ost. Its leaders planned German settlement and close union with the German Empire. Latvians, the great majority of the population, were excluded from its councils and rejected it.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.e: In autumn 1918 the duchy was to join the United Baltic Duchy, but Germany's defeat in November ended the scheme. The Republic of Latvia, proclaimed on 18 November 1918, took over its territory after the War of Independence.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.t: The smaller of the two Mecklenburg states, a quiet grand duchy whose princesses became queens of Britain and Prussia.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.o: The Treaty of Hamburg in 1701 ended a succession dispute by creating Mecklenburg-Strelitz for Adolf Frederick II from the eastern Stargard lands and the detached Principality of Ratzeburg. After Strelitz palace burned in 1712, Adolf Frederick III founded the planned town of Neustrelitz in 1733 as the new residence.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.r: The duchy shared Mecklenburg's estates and its feudal constitution of 1755, so the knights retained great power and no modern constitution was adopted. It was rural, poor and Lutheran. Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz married George III of Great Britain in 1761, and her niece Louise became Queen of Prussia and a national heroine. The state became a grand duchy in 1815.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz.e: Mecklenburg-Strelitz joined the German Empire in 1871. Grand Duke Adolf Frederick VI died by suicide in February 1918, leaving no clear successor, and after the November revolution it became the Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

don-cossack-host.t: The self-governing Cossack community of the Don, frontier warriors and rebels who became the elite cavalry of the Russian Empire.
don-cossack-host.o: Free men and runaways from Muscovy and Ukraine settled along the lower Don in the 16th century, living by fishing, hunting and raiding the Tatars and Turks. The Host traditionally dates its foundation to 1570, when Ivan IV sent a charter to the Don Cossacks. Their capital was Cherkassk, on an island in the Don.
don-cossack-host.r: The Host was run by a general assembly, the krug, which elected the ataman, and it kept its own laws in return for military service to Moscow. In 1637 the Cossacks took Azov from the Ottomans and held it for five years. The Don also bred great rebellions, led by Stepan Razin in 1670 and Kondraty Bulavin in 1707, which Moscow crushed.
don-cossack-host.e: Over the 18th century the Host lost its self-government and became a privileged military estate of the Russian Empire, with its capital moved to Novocherkassk in 1805. Ataman Matvei Platov led Don Cossacks against Napoleon. After 1917 they formed the anti-Bolshevik Don Republic, and Soviet rule dissolved the Host.

duchy-of-spoleto.t: Powerful Lombard duchy of central Italy whose later dukes, Guy and Lambert, became kings of Italy and emperors in the 9th century.
duchy-of-spoleto.o: Lombard warriors under Faroald I took Spoleto in the Umbrian Apennines around 570, cutting the Byzantine route between Rome and Ravenna. The duchy grew into a large territory covering much of Umbria, the Marche and Abruzzo, largely independent of the kings in Pavia.
duchy-of-spoleto.r: The dukes of Spoleto acted like rulers in their own right, waging war on the Byzantines and sometimes defying the Lombard kings; Transamund II was deposed by Liutprand. After 774 it passed to Frankish dukes but kept its weight. Guy of Spoleto was crowned King of Italy in 889 and emperor in 891, and his son Lambert also became emperor. The town's Romanesque churches reflect its medieval wealth.
duchy-of-spoleto.e: In the 10th to 12th centuries the duchy was often held with Camerino or Tuscany by imperial appointees. Frederick Barbarossa sacked Spoleto in 1155. In 1198 Pope Innocent III took the duchy into the Papal States, where it remained until 1860.

duchy-of-milan.t: Northern Italy's richest state under the Visconti and Sforza, scene of Leonardo's Last Supper, and later a prize held by Spain and Austria.
duchy-of-milan.o: In 1395 Gian Galeazzo Visconti bought the title of duke from Emperor Wenceslas, turning the Lordship of Milan into an imperial duchy. Gian Galeazzo expanded it far into central Italy before his sudden death in 1402.
duchy-of-milan.r: After the last Visconti, Filippo Maria, died in 1447 and the Golden Ambrosian Republic failed, the condottiere Francesco Sforza became duke in 1450. Milan was a centre of arms making, silk and wool, with a strong bureaucracy. Ludovico Sforza employed Leonardo da Vinci, who painted the Last Supper. France invaded in 1499; after the last Sforza died in 1535 Habsburg Spain ruled through governors, followed by Austria from 1714, whose reforms suited thinkers such as Cesare Beccaria.
duchy-of-milan.e: Napoleon's army entered Milan in 1796, and the duchy was replaced by the Transpadane Republic and then in 1797 the Cisalpine Republic. Austria later ruled Lombardy as part of the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia.

duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg.t: The Ascanian duchy on the middle Elbe that won the Saxon electoral vote in 1356 and became the core of the Electorate of Saxony.
duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg.o: After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180, the Saxon ducal title passed to the Ascanian Bernhard of Anhalt, whose heirs held lands around Wittenberg on the Elbe and around Lauenburg in the north. In 1296 the inheritance was partitioned: Albert II kept Wittenberg, while his nephews received the Duchy of Saxe-Lauenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg.r: The duchy was small, but its Ascanian dukes claimed the full dignity of the old Duchy of Saxony, including the office of imperial arch-marshal and a vote in royal elections, which Lauenburg disputed. Rudolf I was a close ally of Emperor Charles IV. The territory was agrarian, with Wittenberg a modest residence town at an important Elbe crossing.
duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg.e: The Golden Bull of 1356 settled the dispute in Wittenberg's favour, recognising Rudolf I as prince-elector and creating the Electorate of Saxony. When the Ascanian line died out in 1422, the electorate passed to the Wettin margraves of Meissen.

duchy-of-pannonian-croatia.t: Slavic duchy between the Drava and Sava, centred on Sisak, whose duke Ljudevit led a great revolt against the Franks.
duchy-of-pannonian-croatia.o: After Charlemagne destroyed the Avar Khaganate in the 790s, the Slavs of the Sava valley came under Frankish overlordship as part of the march of Friuli. A duchy appears by about 810, with its seat at Sisak, the Roman Siscia.
duchy-of-pannonian-croatia.r: Its dukes governed a Slavic population as Frankish vassals. Between 819 and 823 Duke Ljudevit Posavski rebelled against harsh Frankish rule, drawing in the Timočani and others, and fought the Duchy of Croatia, before fleeing and being killed. Later, Duke Braslav held lands between the Drava and Sava and aided the East Frankish king Arnulf against Great Moravia in the 880s and 890s.
duchy-of-pannonian-croatia.e: Hungarian raids from the 890s weakened Frankish control. Around 925 the region was united with Dalmatian Croatia under Tomislav, forming the Kingdom of Croatia (925-1102); the area later became Slavonia.

deciates.t: Ligurian people near Antibes whose attacks on Greek colonies brought the first Roman army into southern Gaul in 154 BCE.
deciates.o: The Deciates were a Ligurian people living in the hills behind Antipolis (Antibes), a colony of Massalia. Polybius is the main source.
deciates.r: Like other Ligurian peoples of the coast they lived in fortified hilltop settlements and combined farming and herding with raids on the Greek coastal towns.
deciates.e: In 154 BCE the Deciates and the Oxybii besieged Antipolis and Nikaia, and Massalia appealed to the Roman Republic. The consul Quintus Opimius defeated them and handed part of their land to Massalia. Their territory later became part of the province of Alpes Maritimae.

denmark-norway.t: The Oldenburg kings' twin realm of Denmark and Norway, a Lutheran absolute monarchy with colonies from India to the Caribbean, lasting until 1814.
denmark-norway.o: After Sweden left the Kalmar Union in 1523, Denmark and Norway remained under one king, Frederick I. His son Christian III introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1536 and declared Norway a province of the Danish crown in 1537, though it kept its own laws. The realm also included Iceland, the Faroes, Greenland, and the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein.
denmark-norway.r: Copenhagen was the centre of government, funded by the Sound Toll on shipping into the Baltic. Christian IV built palaces and towns but lost wars with Sweden, and in 1658 Denmark ceded Scania. Frederick III introduced absolute monarchy in 1660, set down in the King's Law of 1665. Trading companies founded Danish India, the Danish Gold Coast and the Danish West Indies, and Norwegian timber and fish fed a growing merchant fleet.
denmark-norway.e: Allied with Napoleon after the British bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807, Denmark-Norway ended on the losing side. By the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden but kept Iceland, the Faroes and Greenland. Norway briefly declared independence as the Kingdom of Norway (1814) before entering Sweden-Norway.

duchy-of-bavaria-munich.t: The Wittelsbach duchy centred on Munich that outlasted its rival Bavarian branches and reunited the country under Albert IV in 1505.
duchy-of-bavaria-munich.o: The partition of 1392 gave John II the lands around Munich, the smallest share of the Wittelsbach inheritance in Upper Bavaria. His sons Ernest and William III ruled jointly after 1397, and in 1429 they received a share of the Duchy of Bavaria-Straubing.
duchy-of-bavaria-munich.r: The dukes ruled from the Alter Hof in Munich, a city grown rich on the salt trade. Duke Ernest had Agnes Bernauer, the commoner wife of his son Albert III, drowned at Straubing in 1435. Albert IV, duke from 1465, built a stronger, more centralised state, and Munich's Frauenkirche was completed under his rule in 1488.
duchy-of-bavaria-munich.e: Albert IV won the War of the Landshut Succession in 1505 and reunited most of Bavaria. His primogeniture decree of 1506 forbade further divisions, so the Duchy of Bavaria, with Munich as its capital, remained united from then on.

duchy-of-saxe-coburg-saalfeld.t: Ernestine duchy in Franconia and Thuringia whose ambitious family married into the royal houses of Europe.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-saalfeld.o: John Ernest, seventh son of Ernest the Pious, received Saalfeld in 1680. When the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg died out in 1699, he gained most of Coburg after a long dispute, forming Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-saalfeld.r: The duchy was Lutheran and small, with debts that led to an imperial debt commission in the 18th century. Duke Ernest Frederick and Duke Francis governed modestly; Francis was a collector whose prints formed the Coburg collections. Duke Ernest I was restored after French occupation in 1807. Francis's children married well: Leopold later became King of the Belgians and Victoria, Duchess of Kent, was mother of Queen Victoria.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-saalfeld.e: After Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg died out, Ernest I gave up Saalfeld and received Gotha in 1826, forming the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. Saalfeld went to Saxe-Meiningen, and the family's dynastic rise continued under the new name.

duchy-of-olesnica.t: A Silesian duchy that outlived its Piast founders by four centuries, passing to the Poděbrady, Württemberg and Brunswick families.
duchy-of-olesnica.o: In the division of the Duchy of Głogów among the sons of Henry III, Konrad I received Oleśnica (Oels), east of Wrocław, and ruled it as a separate duchy by 1320. In 1329 he did homage to King John of Bohemia, placing the duchy under the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-olesnica.r: The Piast dukes of Oleśnica at times also held other Silesian towns, including Koźle and part of Bytom. After their line died out in 1492, the duchy went to the Bohemian Poděbrady family, who introduced Lutheranism, and in 1647 by marriage to Sylvius Nimrod of Württemberg, whose line made Oleśnica a small centre of Baroque court culture and Lutheran printing.
duchy-of-olesnica.e: Silesia passed to Prussia in 1742. In 1792 the duchy went by marriage to the house of Brunswick, and when the last Brunswick duke died in 1884 it reverted to the Prussian crown, which granted it to the crown prince. Oleśnica became part of Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-saxe-romhild.t: Short-lived Ernestine duchy in southern Thuringia, one of the seven shares of Ernest the Pious's inheritance.
duchy-of-saxe-romhild.o: Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha died in 1675, and his sons ruled jointly until they divided the lands in 1680. Henry, the fourth son, received Römhild near the Franconian border, establishing the small Duchy of Saxe-Römhild.
duchy-of-saxe-romhild.r: Henry rebuilt Glücksburg Castle in Römhild and spent heavily on his court, leaving debts far greater than the tiny duchy's revenues. The territory was rural, Lutheran and administered by a handful of officials. Little else distinguishes its short history, which is known mainly from the disputes over its inheritance.
duchy-of-saxe-romhild.e: Henry died without children in 1710. His lands were divided among Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, Saxe-Meiningen and Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld after a long dispute, and Römhild later passed to Saxe-Meiningen.

despotate-of-serres.t: Realm of the despot Jovan Uglješa around Serres in eastern Macedonia, a successor of the Serbian Empire destroyed at the Maritsa in 1371.
despotate-of-serres.o: After Stefan Dušan's death in 1355, his widow, Empress Jelena, ruled Serres, the city he had taken from Byzantium in 1345. Around 1365 she handed power to the despot Jovan Uglješa, brother of Vukašin Mrnjavčević, who ruled eastern Macedonia from Serres.
despotate-of-serres.r: Uglješa governed a largely Greek population and was close to the monasteries of Mount Athos, to which he made many grants. In 1368 he reconciled his church with the Patriarch of Constantinople, ending the schism caused by Dušan's patriarchate. Alarmed by the Ottoman conquest of Thrace, he sought allies against them.
despotate-of-serres.e: In 1371 Uglješa and his brother Vukašin led a large army against the Ottomans and were killed at the Maritsa. Byzantium under Manuel II then retook Serres, which fell to the Ottomans in 1383.

duchy-of-bar.t: A Lorraine county raised to a duchy, divided between French and imperial allegiance, and united with the Duchy of Lorraine under René of Anjou's heirs.
duchy-of-bar.o: Bar-le-Duc's castle was built in the 10th century by Duke Frederick of Upper Lorraine. Around 1033 his heiress Sophie of Bar married Louis of Mousson, count of Montbéliard, and their descendants ruled the county of Bar as a separate principality between Champagne and Lorraine.
duchy-of-bar.r: The counts ruled a fertile land along the Meuse and Ornain. After a defeat by Philip IV, the Treaty of Bruges in 1301 made the western part, the Barrois mouvant, a fief of the French crown, while the rest stayed imperial. Robert I became the first duke in 1354. René of Anjou inherited Bar in 1430 after marrying Isabella of Lorraine.
duchy-of-bar.e: René's grandson René II united Bar and the Duchy of Lorraine in 1480, and the two shared rulers thereafter. Like Lorraine, Bar passed to Stanisław Leszczyński in 1737 and was annexed to the Kingdom of France on his death in 1766.

duchy-of-saxe-weissenfels.t: Albertine Saxon duchy on the Saale whose lavish court employed musicians and gave Bach an honorary title.
duchy-of-saxe-weissenfels.o: After Elector John George I of Saxony died in 1656, his son Augustus, already administrator of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg, received Weissenfels, Querfurt and other lands under his father's will, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Weissenfels. Augustus built the large Neu-Augustusburg palace at Weissenfels.
duchy-of-saxe-weissenfels.r: The duchy was Lutheran and depended on the Electorate of Saxony in foreign affairs. Its court was a centre of music and opera: Handel's father was surgeon to the duke, and Johann Sebastian Bach held the honorary title of Kapellmeister of Weissenfels from 1729. Lavish court spending left the state deeply in debt.
duchy-of-saxe-weissenfels.e: Johann Adolf II, the last duke and a Saxon field marshal, died in 1746, and the duchy reverted to the Electorate of Saxony. Weissenfels passed to Prussia in 1815 and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

duchy-of-bourbon.t: The central French duchy of a Capetian branch whose last great duke betrayed Francis I and whose cousins later became kings of France.
duchy-of-bourbon.o: The lords of Bourbon had held the Bourbonnais since the 10th century. In 1272 the heiress Beatrice of Bourbon married Robert of Clermont, son of Louis IX, and in 1327 Charles IV raised the barony to a duchy for their son Louis I, creating the Capetian house of Bourbon.
duchy-of-bourbon.r: The dukes ruled from Moulins and gathered Forez, Beaujolais, Auvergne and La Marche through marriage and inheritance, making their lands one of France's largest princely blocs. Louis II, called the Good Duke, was a model crusading prince. Anne of France and her husband Peter II governed the kingdom during the minority of Charles VIII.
duchy-of-bourbon.e: Charles III, constable of France, fell out with Francis I, who claimed his lands; he joined Charles V in 1523 and was killed leading the sack of Rome in 1527. His lands were confiscated and joined to the Kingdom of France, but a younger Bourbon line gave France Henry IV.

duchy-of-benevento.t: Southern Lombard duchy and later principality that outlived the Lombard Kingdom by three centuries, a centre of southern Italian culture.
duchy-of-benevento.o: Lombard warriors under Zotto established themselves at Beneventum in Campania around 571, perhaps first as soldiers in Byzantine pay. Under Arechis I the duchy expanded across most of southern Italy, apart from the Byzantine coastal cities, Calabria and Apulia's heel.
duchy-of-benevento.r: Benevento was effectively independent of Pavia; Duke Grimoald I even became King of the Lombards in 662. When Charlemagne took the north in 774, Arechis II took the title of prince and claimed the Lombard heritage, building the church of Santa Sofia. The duchy developed the Beneventan script and was a cultural centre linked to Monte Cassino. Civil war in 849 split it into Benevento and Salerno, and Capua later broke away.
duchy-of-benevento.e: Weakened by Arab raids, Byzantines and Normans, the principality shrank. In 1051 the city placed itself under Pope Leo IX, and when the last prince, Landulf VI, died in 1077, Benevento became a papal enclave, while its lands passed to the Normans.

deceangli.t: People of north-east Wales, the first target of Roman campaigns into Wales in 48, whose lead mines soon stamped their name on Roman ingots.
deceangli.o: The Deceangli lived in what is now Flintshire and Denbighshire, between the Dee estuary and the Clwyd valley, a region of hillforts such as Moel Hiraddug and Penycloddiau. They were probably a small Iron Age grouping of local communities and are first named by Tacitus.
deceangli.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society beyond the archaeology of their hillforts and farms. Their territory was rich in lead and silver ores on Halkyn Mountain, which the Romans quickly exploited; lead pigs found near Chester carry the inscription DECEANGL and a date of 74, showing that mining was organised under the name of the people.
deceangli.e: In 48 the governor Ostorius Scapula marched against the Deceangli, ravaging their land almost to the Irish Sea before trouble among the Brigantes recalled him. The area was secured by the fortress of Chester in the 70s, and the Deceangli are not known to have formed a civitas of Roman Britain.

duchy-of-raciborz.t: Upper Silesian duchy on the upper Oder, ruled first by Piasts and then by a Přemyslid branch from Opava until 1521.
duchy-of-raciborz.o: In the 1281 partition of the Duchy of Opole and Racibórz, Przemysław received Racibórz, the old capital of Upper Silesia. His son Leszek accepted Bohemian overlordship in 1327, and when Leszek died without heirs in 1336, the duchy passed to Nicholas II of Opava, a Přemyslid married to Przemysław's daughter.
duchy-of-raciborz.r: The Opava Přemyslids ruled Racibórz as part of a combined duchy of Opava and Racibórz, later separate. The duchy was a fertile land of grain and fish ponds, with a Polish-speaking population and German burghers. It was a Bohemian fief, and its dukes took part in the Hussite wars and the struggles between Bohemian and Hungarian kings.
duchy-of-raciborz.e: After the last Přemyslid duke died in 1521, Racibórz passed to John II the Good of Opole. When he died in 1532, it fell to the Bohemian crown, held by the Habsburgs and pledged to Brandenburg-Ansbach. It passed to Prussia in 1742 and to Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-bouillon.t: The Ardennes duchy whose castle Godfrey of Bouillon pawned for the First Crusade, later a small sovereign state of the La Marck and La Tour d'Auvergne families.
duchy-of-bouillon.o: Godfrey of Bouillon pledged his castle and lands to the bishop of Liège in 1096 to fund the First Crusade, and the bishops held Bouillon for centuries. From the mid-15th century the La Marck family gained control of it, and by the 1480s they ruled it in practice as an independent duchy.
duchy-of-bouillon.r: Bouillon was a forested, sparsely populated land around a great castle on the Semois. Robert II de la Marck and his heirs, also princes of Sedan, styled themselves dukes. Possession was contested between the La Marcks, their La Tour d'Auvergne heirs and Liège. In 1678 Louis XIV took Bouillon and gave it to Godefroy-Maurice de La Tour d'Auvergne under French protection.
duchy-of-bouillon.e: French troops annexed the duchy in 1795. After the Napoleonic Wars it went to the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in 1815 and to the Kingdom of Belgium in 1839.

dulkadirids.t: A Turkmen beylik around Elbistan and Marash that served as the buffer, and the battleground, between the Mamluks and the Ottomans.
dulkadirids.o: In 1337 the Mamluks recognised the Turkmen chief Zayn al-Din Karaja Bey as ruler of Elbistan and the surrounding uplands of the eastern Taurus, creating a vassal state on their northern frontier.
dulkadirids.r: The Dulkadirids led pastoral Turkmen tribes, raised horses and controlled the passes between Syria and Anatolia. Both Mamluks and Ottomans tried to control them through marriage and by backing rival claimants. Shah Suwar rebelled against the Mamluks with Ottoman encouragement and was executed in Cairo in 1472. Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt, a long-reigning ruler, built in Marash and resisted the rising Safavids.
dulkadirids.e: When Ala al-Dawla failed to support the Ottomans against the Safavids, Selim I's army defeated and killed him in 1515. His nephew Ali Bey ruled as an Ottoman vassal until he was executed in 1522 and the beylik was annexed.

duchy-of-pomerelia.t: The duchy of Gdansk Pomerania under the Samborides, whose end in 1294 led to centuries of conflict between Poland and the Teutonic Knights.
duchy-of-pomerelia.o: Eastern Pomerania, around Gdansk on the Vistula delta, was conquered by Boleslaw III of Poland in the early 12th century and governed for him by local nobles. In the mid 12th century these governors, the Samborides, began to rule on their own account, and Sambor I founded the Cistercian abbey of Oliwa in 1186.
duchy-of-pomerelia.r: Pomerelia controlled the mouth of the Vistula, and Gdansk grew into a busy port with German, Slavic and Danish merchants. Swietopelk II the Great, who ruled from the 1220s to 1266, threw off Polish overlordship, took the ducal title and fought long wars against the Teutonic Order.
duchy-of-pomerelia.e: His son Mestwin II, who died without sons, left the duchy to Przemysl II of Greater Poland under the Treaty of Kepno of 1282. After Mestwin's death in 1294, the land was contested, and in 1308 the Teutonic Knights seized Gdansk and held Pomerelia until it became part of Royal Prussia in 1466.

duchy-of-opole.t: Upper Silesian Piast duchy whose duke Władysław Opolczyk brought the Black Madonna to Częstochowa and whose last prince died in 1532.
duchy-of-opole.o: In 1281 the Duchy of Opole and Racibórz was divided among the sons of Władysław of Opole, and Bolko I received Opole on the Oder. He accepted Bohemian overlordship in 1327 along with other Upper Silesian dukes, while his descendants continued to rule.
duchy-of-opole.r: Władysław II of Opole served as palatine of Hungary and in 1382 founded the Pauline monastery of Jasna Góra at Częstochowa, bringing the Black Madonna icon. The Opole dukes later gathered much of Upper Silesia, and John II the Good issued a charter of privileges for the region and allowed the mining town of Tarnowskie Góry to develop. The population was largely Polish-speaking.
duchy-of-opole.e: With John II's death in 1532 the Upper Silesian Piasts died out, and Opole passed to the Bohemian crown under the Habsburgs, pledged at times to Brandenburg and the Polish Vasas. It went to Prussia in 1742 and to Poland in 1945.

dumnonii.t: Iron Age people of Devon and Cornwall, whose tin and remote farming settlements kept them apart from the coin-using kingdoms of the south-east.
dumnonii.o: The Dumnonii emerged from the Iron Age communities of the south-western peninsula, a land of hillforts, defended farmsteads known as rounds, and coastal promontory forts. Greek writers from Pytheas onwards describe the tin trade of the far south-west, and harbours such as Mount Batten on Plymouth Sound linked the region with Brittany and the wider Atlantic world.
dumnonii.r: No kings or coins of the Dumnonii are known, which suggests a looser society of local lineages rather than a single dynasty. Most people lived in small enclosed farms raising cattle and grain, while tin streaming in Cornwall and Dartmoor gave the region its main export. Courtyard houses and underground passages called fogous are distinctive of the far west.
dumnonii.e: Roman forces reached the south-west after 43, and around 55 the legio II Augusta built a fortress at Exeter. When the army moved on, the town became Isca Dumnoniorum, capital of a self-governing civitas, though the countryside stayed little Romanised. The name survived in the post-Roman Kingdom of Dumnonia and in the county name Devon.

duchy-of-rawa.t: A Masovian duchy in central Poland, one of the last Piast lands, incorporated into the Polish Crown in 1462.
duchy-of-rawa.o: After Boleslaw II of Masovia died in 1313, his lands were divided among his sons, and Siemowit II received the southern part around Rawa. Over the next 150 years Rawa was repeatedly joined to and separated from the other Masovian duchies as the family's branches divided their inheritance.
duchy-of-rawa.r: Rawa was a modest farming land with a brick castle built under Casimir III's influence in the 14th century. Its dukes were vassals of the Polish Crown from 1351. Siemowit III reunited most of Masovia in the 1370s and issued laws for it, but it was divided again among his heirs, and Rawa was ruled by the Siemowit and Wladyslaw lines of Plock.
duchy-of-rawa.e: When Siemowit VI and Wladyslaw II, the last dukes of the line, died in 1462, King Casimir IV took Rawa and Gostynin into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569). The land became the Rawa Voivodeship.

duchy-of-anhalt.t: Duchy that reunited the Anhalt lands in 1863 and became an industrial region on the Elbe and Saale.
duchy-of-anhalt.o: After the extinction of Anhalt-Köthen in 1847 and Anhalt-Bernburg in 1863, Duke Leopold IV Frederick of Anhalt-Dessau ruled all the Anhalt territories. In 1863 they were formally combined as the Duchy of Anhalt, with Dessau as capital.
duchy-of-anhalt.r: Anhalt was small but economically active, with sugar beet, lignite, potash and salt, and later chemical and engineering works. The Junkers aircraft factory at Dessau was founded in the 1890s by Hugo Junkers. A constitution of 1859, extended to the whole duchy, provided a diet. Anhalt joined the North German Confederation in 1867 and the German Empire in 1871.
duchy-of-anhalt.e: Duke Joachim Ernst, a minor, abdicated through his regent in November 1918, and the duchy became the Free State of Anhalt. After 1945 its territory was merged into Saxony-Anhalt, which still takes its name in part from the old duchy.

danishmendids.t: A Turkish dynasty of central and north-eastern Anatolia that rivalled the Seljuks of Rum and inspired the epic of Danishmend Gazi.
danishmendids.o: After the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071, a Turkmen leader known as Danishmend Gazi, whose origins are obscure, conquered Sivas, Tokat, Niksar, Amasya and later Malatya, founding one of the first Turkish principalities in Anatolia.
danishmendids.r: The Danishmendids ruled a largely Christian population of Greeks and Armenians through Turkmen warriors and a growing urban Muslim elite. In 1100 Danishmend Gazi captured Bohemond of Antioch, and his son Gazi Gumushtigin was for a time the strongest ruler in Anatolia, receiving the title malik from the caliph. They built mosques and madrasas in Tokat, Niksar and Kayseri. Their deeds were later celebrated in the Danishmendname, a Turkish epic of holy war.
danishmendids.e: After the death of Yagibasan in 1164 the family split and weakened. Kilij Arslan II of the Sultanate of Rum annexed Sivas around 1174 and the Malatya branch in 1178, ending the dynasty.

duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza.t: The Farnese duchy in Emilia, later held by Bourbons and by Napoleon's widow Marie Louise, which lasted until Italian unification.
duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza.o: In 1545 Pope Paul III detached Parma and Piacenza from the Papal States and gave them to his son Pier Luigi Farnese, already Duke of Castro. Pier Luigi was murdered in 1547 by nobles backed by the imperial governor of Milan.
duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza.r: The Farnese built a court at Parma, with the Pilotta palace and the wooden Teatro Farnese of 1618. Alessandro Farnese, Spain's general in the Netherlands, was its most famous duke. When the Farnese died out in 1731, Elisabeth Farnese, queen of Spain, passed the duchy to her son Charles of Bourbon. After Austrian rule from 1735, Philip of Bourbon founded the Bourbon-Parma line in 1748, with reforming minister Guillaume du Tillot.
duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza.e: France annexed the duchy in 1802. In 1814 it went to Marie Louise, Napoleon's widow, who ruled until 1847, then back to the Bourbons. In 1859 it joined the United Provinces of Central Italy and was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

duchy-of-bytom.t: Upper Silesian Piast duchy whose first duke became the first Silesian prince to pay homage to the King of Bohemia, in 1289.
duchy-of-bytom.o: When Władysław of Opole died in 1281, his lands were divided among his sons. Casimir received Bytom, an old market town in eastern Upper Silesia, together with lands around Gliwice and Koźle. In 1289 he paid homage to Wenceslaus II of Bohemia, the first Silesian duke to accept Bohemian overlordship.
duchy-of-bytom.r: The duchy was small, with farmland, forests and early silver and lead mining around Bytom. Casimir's son Władysław ruled it in the early 14th century, and later dukes divided it into smaller shares. The population was largely Polish-speaking, with German settlers in the towns.
duchy-of-bytom.e: After the Bytom line died out in 1355, the duchy was divided between the dukes of Oleśnica and Cieszyn and later fragmented further, with parts passing among Silesian princes until the end of the 15th century. It eventually came under the Bohemian crown, and Bytom is now in Poland.

duchy-of-styria.t: Alpine duchy of Graz and the Erzberg iron mountain, a Habsburg land for over six centuries and the shield of Inner Austria against the Ottomans.
duchy-of-styria.o: The March of Styria grew from a Carolingian border zone ruled from the 11th century by the Otakar counts of Steyr. In 1180 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised it to a duchy for Ottokar IV. By the Georgenberg Pact of 1186 it passed to the Babenbergs of the Duchy of Austria in 1192, and after Ottokar II of Bohemia it came to the Habsburgs in 1282.
duchy-of-styria.r: Styria was governed by its dukes with strong estates meeting in the Landhaus at Graz. Iron from the Erzberg made it an industrial heartland. From 1564 Graz was capital of Inner Austria under Archduke Charles II, who invited the Jesuits; his son Ferdinand II expelled Protestants. Repeated Ottoman raids made defence a constant concern. German was spoken in the north and Slovene in Lower Styria.
duchy-of-styria.e: Styria remained a crown land of the Habsburg Monarchy and Austria-Hungary until 1918. It was then divided: Lower Styria with Maribor went to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and is now in Slovenia, while the rest became the Austrian state of Styria.
