duchy-of-zagan.t: Silesian duchy that passed from the Piasts to the Wettins, Wallenstein and the Lobkowicz, and where Johannes Kepler worked for a time.
duchy-of-zagan.o: Żagań, in north-western Silesia, became the seat of a separate duchy in the division of the Głogów lands after 1274. It was ruled by branches of the Głogów Piasts, who accepted Bohemian overlordship in the 1320s and 1330s, and Żagań grew as a market town with a large Augustinian abbey.
duchy-of-zagan.r: The Piast dukes ruled until the turbulent Jan II the Mad sold Żagań to the Wettins of Saxony in 1472. It later returned to the Bohemian crown and in 1628 was granted to the general Albrecht von Wallenstein, who brought Johannes Kepler there. From 1646 the Lobkowicz family held it, building a baroque palace.
duchy-of-zagan.e: In 1742 Żagań passed to Prussia, and in 1786 the Lobkowicz sold it to Peter von Biron, Duke of Courland. His daughter Dorothea later held it as Duchess of Sagan. The town has been Polish since 1945.

duchy-of-urbino.t: The Montefeltro and della Rovere state in the Marche, whose ducal palace and court made Urbino a model of Renaissance civility.
duchy-of-urbino.o: The Montefeltro family, lords of a mountainous area on the borders of Romagna and the Marche, received Urbino as counts in the early 13th century; the register dates the county from 1213. They ruled as papal vicars and condottieri.
duchy-of-urbino.r: Federico da Montefeltro, a famous mercenary captain, was made duke in 1474 and built the Ducal Palace and a celebrated library. His son Guidobaldo's court inspired Baldassare Castiglione's Book of the Courtier, and Raphael was born in the city in 1483. In 1508 the duchy passed to Francesco Maria I della Rovere, nephew of Pope Julius II, and from 1523 Pesaro became the main residence. The duchy was also known for maiolica.
duchy-of-urbino.e: Francesco Maria II della Rovere died without a male heir in 1631, and the duchy, already promised by agreement, devolved to the Papal States, which ruled it until 1860.

duchy-of-friuli.t: The first Lombard duchy in Italy, a frontier march at Cividale guarding the north-eastern passes against Avars and Slavs.
duchy-of-friuli.o: When the Lombards entered Italy in 568, King Alboin left his nephew Gisulf at Forum Iulii (Cividale del Friuli) with chosen warrior families to hold the passes from the Julian Alps. It became the first Lombard duchy, and the name Friuli comes from Forum Iulii.
duchy-of-friuli.r: The dukes of Friuli were warrior frontier lords, often fighting the Avars and Slavs to the east. In 610 the Avars sacked Cividale and killed Duke Gisulf II. The historian Paul the Deacon came from a Friulian family. Duke Ratchis became king in 744; the altar he commissioned and the Tempietto Longobardo in Cividale are masterpieces of Lombard art. The patriarchs of Aquileia also resided at Cividale.
duchy-of-friuli.e: After Charlemagne conquered the Lombard Kingdom, Duke Hrodgaud of Friuli rebelled in 776 and was killed. Charlemagne replaced him with Frankish counts, and the territory became the March of Friuli.

danube-sich.t: The refuge of Zaporozhian Cossacks in the Ottoman Danube Delta after Catherine the Great destroyed their Sich.
danube-sich.o: When the Russian army abolished the Zaporozhian Sich in 1775, several thousand Cossacks fled to Ottoman territory. After moving between several sites, they settled in the Danube Delta, where the sultan allowed them to found a new Sich in return for military service. Its main centre from 1814 was at Dunavets, in modern Romania.
danube-sich.r: The Danube Sich kept the old Zaporozhian institutions of an elected kish otaman, a council and kurins. The Cossacks fished, farmed and fought in Ottoman campaigns, including against Serbian and Greek rebels. They clashed repeatedly with the Nekrasov Cossacks, Russian Old Believers settled nearby, over fishing grounds and Ottoman favour.
danube-sich.e: During the Russo-Turkish War of 1828, the kish otaman Osyp Hladky defected to Russia with part of the Host. In response the Ottomans destroyed the Sich. The defectors formed the Azov Cossack Host in Russia, while the others dispersed within Ottoman lands.

delphi.t: Sanctuary-state of Apollo on Mount Parnassus, whose oracle was consulted for centuries by Greek cities and foreign kings.
delphi.o: Delphi lies on the slopes of Mount Parnassus above the Pleistos valley. A cult of Apollo was established there by the 8th century BCE, and the oracle quickly gained renown, sanctioning colonies across the Mediterranean. The small town of Delphi grew up to serve the sanctuary.
delphi.r: The Delphians ran the shrine and the Pythia, Apollo's priestess, who gave the oracles. The Amphictyony, a council of neighbouring peoples, protected the sanctuary, and in the First Sacred War c. 595 BCE it destroyed Kirrha. The Pythian Games were reorganised in 586 BCE. Cities built treasuries along the Sacred Way, and the Alcmaeonids rebuilt the temple after 548 BCE.
delphi.e: The Phocian League seized Delphi in the Third Sacred War of 356 to 346 BCE, and the Aetolian League later dominated it. Rome freed Delphi in 191 BCE, and it lost independence by 146 BCE. The oracle declined under Roman rule and closed in the late 4th century CE.

duchy-of-guelders.t: A river principality on the Rhine, Maas and IJssel whose dukes resisted Burgundian and Habsburg rule until 1543.
duchy-of-guelders.o: Around 1096 Gerard of Wassenberg was first styled count of Guelders, after a castle near Geldern. His family added Zutphen through marriage around 1138 and moved their centre north to the Rhine and Veluwe. Nijmegen, Roermond, Arnhem and Zutphen became the four quarters of the territory.
duchy-of-guelders.r: The counts expanded steadily, though Reinald I lost the battle of Worringen in 1288. Emperor Louis IV made Reinald II a duke in 1339. Guelders was a land of river tolls, farming and Hanseatic towns. After the house of Egmond took power, Charles the Bold bought the duchy in 1473, but Charles of Egmond won it back and fought the Habsburgs for decades.
duchy-of-guelders.e: Duke William of Cleves lost the duchy to Charles V and ceded it by the Treaty of Venlo in 1543, joining it to the Habsburg Netherlands. In the Dutch Revolt it split: the northern quarters joined the Dutch Republic, while Upper Guelders around Roermond stayed Spanish.

duchy-of-schleswig.t: Duchy of southern Jutland on the Danish-German border, held by Danish royal princes and Holstein counts and fought over in the 19th-century Schleswig wars.
duchy-of-schleswig.o: Southern Jutland was the frontier of the Kingdom of Denmark, guarded by the Danevirke earthworks and home to the Viking Age trading town of Hedeby. From the 11th century it was governed as a jarldom or duchy by members of the royal family; Canute Lavard held it from 1115, and the dukes descended from King Abel made it a hereditary fief.
duchy-of-schleswig.r: The duchy straddled Danish and German worlds: Danish speech dominated in the north, German and Frisian in the south, and the town of Schleswig on the Schlei was its capital. From 1386 the counts of Holstein held it, and in 1460 the Treaty of Ribe made Christian I its duke, promising Schleswig and Holstein would stay forever undivided. Gottorp Castle became a seat of a ducal line.
duchy-of-schleswig.e: Rising Danish and German nationalism led to the First Schleswig War in 1848-1851 and the Second in 1864, after which Denmark ceded the duchy to Prussia and Austria. Prussia annexed it in 1866-1867. A 1920 plebiscite returned northern Schleswig to Denmark, while the south remains part of Germany.

duchy-of-opole-and-raciborz.t: Piast duchy of Upper Silesia that emerged from the division of Silesia and held off the Mongols in 1241 before splitting into four.
duchy-of-opole-and-raciborz.o: After the partition of the Polish realm, Silesia was held by the sons of Władysław II the Exile. In 1172 his son Mieszko IV Tanglefoot received a separate share around Racibórz, the core of Upper Silesia. In 1202 he added the Opole district, creating a duchy independent of the Lower Silesian Duchy of Silesia.
duchy-of-opole-and-raciborz.r: The Upper Silesian Piasts ruled a largely Polish-speaking land of forests, farmland and river towns on the upper Oder. Kazimierz I and his successors brought in German settlers and granted town charters under German law, founding or refounding places such as Opole and Racibórz. During the Mongol invasion of 1241, Mieszko II the Fat fought the raiders near Racibórz and Opole.
duchy-of-opole-and-raciborz.e: When Duke Władysław died in 1281, his four sons divided the duchy into the Duchies of Opole, Racibórz, Bytom and Cieszyn. These Upper Silesian duchies drifted towards the Kingdom of Bohemia and accepted Bohemian overlordship in 1327.

duchy-of-alsace.t: Frankish frontier duchy between the Vosges and the Rhine, ruled by the Etichonid family whose saint, Odile, is the patron of Alsace.
duchy-of-alsace.o: In the mid 7th century the Merovingian kings of Austrasia set up a duchy in Alsace to control the border with the Alemanni. The first known duke was Gundoin, and from around 662 power passed to Adalric, also called Eticho, founder of the Etichonid dynasty.
duchy-of-alsace.r: The dukes governed from their estates around Obernai and founded many monasteries. Adalric's daughter Odile founded the convent of Hohenburg on the mountain now called Mont Sainte-Odile, and his descendants endowed abbeys such as Honau and Murbach.
duchy-of-alsace.e: Around 740, after the death of Duke Liutfrid, the Carolingian mayors abolished the duchy, which had grown too independent, and divided Alsace into two counties, the Nordgau and the Sundgau. The Etichonid family remained powerful and gave rise to several later noble houses.

duchy-of-silesia.t: The Piast duchy of Silesia, created by the partition of Poland in 1138, which opened the region to German settlement and split into many small duchies.
duchy-of-silesia.o: By the testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138, Poland was divided among his sons, and Silesia, with its capital at Wrocław, went to the eldest, Władysław II the Exile. Expelled in 1146, he fled to the Empire; his sons returned in 1163 with the support of Frederick Barbarossa and ruled Silesia as a separate duchy.
duchy-of-silesia.r: Henry I the Bearded and his wife Saint Hedwig invited German settlers, founded towns under German law and monasteries such as Trzebnica. Henry I and Henry II the Pious tried to reunite Poland. Henry II was killed fighting the Mongols at the Battle of Legnica in 1241, a disaster for the duchy.
duchy-of-silesia.e: After Henry II's death his sons divided Silesia in 1248, the start of its fragmentation into numerous small Piast duchies. In the 14th century these accepted the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and Silesia passed later to the Habsburgs and, in 1742, to Prussia.

duchy-of-saxe-jena.t: Brief Ernestine duchy centred on the university town of Jena, carved out for a younger Weimar prince and gone within two decades.
duchy-of-saxe-jena.o: Duke William of Saxe-Weimar died in 1662 and his lands were divided among his sons. In 1672, after a further rearrangement following the extinction of Saxe-Altenburg, Bernhard received Jena and its surroundings as the Duchy of Saxe-Jena.
duchy-of-saxe-jena.r: Bernhard ruled from Jena, rebuilding the castle there and maintaining a modest Lutheran court. The University of Jena, founded in 1558, was shared among the Ernestine dukes and remained the town's main institution. The duchy was too small to pursue an independent policy and relied on its larger Ernestine relatives.
duchy-of-saxe-jena.e: Bernhard died in 1678 and his only son John William died as a child in 1690. The duchy was then divided between the Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach and Saxe-Weimar, with Jena itself eventually going to Weimar.

danish-west-indies.t: Denmark's Caribbean sugar colony of St Thomas, St John and St Croix, built on slave labour and sold to the United States in 1917.
danish-west-indies.o: The Danish West India Company settled St Thomas in 1672 and St John in 1718, and bought St Croix from France in 1733. Charlotte Amalie on St Thomas, with its excellent harbour, became the capital and a busy free port.
danish-west-indies.r: Sugar and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans made the islands profitable; at their peak most of the population was enslaved. An uprising on St John in 1733 was crushed with French help. In 1848, facing a revolt on St Croix, Governor-General Peter von Scholten declared emancipation. Charlotte Amalie thrived as a trading and coaling port where English and Dutch creole were widely spoken.
danish-west-indies.e: After sugar declined, Denmark sought to sell the islands. During the First World War the United States, worried about German naval bases, bought them for 25 million dollars, and they were transferred in 1917, becoming the United States Virgin Islands.

despotate-of-epirus.t: Byzantine Greek successor state in north-western Greece founded after 1204, a rival of Nicaea that passed through Greek, Italian and Serbian dynasties.
despotate-of-epirus.o: After the Fourth Crusade, Michael Komnenos Doukas, a relative of the Angelos emperors, took control of Epirus around 1205, ruling from Arta. His half-brother Theodore expanded the state, taking Thessalonica in 1224 and creating the Empire of Thessalonica, until his defeat by the Bulgarians at Klokotnitsa in 1230. The title despot was given to later rulers.
despotate-of-epirus.r: The rulers kept Byzantine administration and Orthodox church structures and claimed the imperial heritage against the Empire of Nicaea. Arta flourished, with churches such as the Panagia Parigoritissa. Michael II allied with the Latins against Nicaea but was defeated at Pelagonia in 1259. The Orsini of Cephalonia took over in 1318.
despotate-of-epirus.e: Serbia under Stefan Dushan annexed Epirus in 1348. Carlo I Tocco reunited Ioannina and Arta from 1411, but the Ottomans took Ioannina in 1430, Arta in 1449 and the last fortresses in 1479.

duchy-of-bavaria-landshut.t: The richest of the late medieval Bavarian duchies, ruled from Landshut by the 'Rich Dukes' and famed for the Landshut Wedding of 1475.
duchy-of-bavaria-landshut.o: In 1392 the three sons of Duke Stephen II divided Bavaria: Frederick took Bavaria-Landshut, John II the Duchy of Bavaria-Munich and Stephen III the Duchy of Bavaria-Ingolstadt. Landshut, seat of the Lower Bavarian dukes since the 13th century, became capital of the wealthiest share, which gained part of the Duchy of Bavaria-Straubing in 1429 and all of Ingolstadt in 1447.
duchy-of-bavaria-landshut.r: Three successive dukes, Henry XVI, Louis IX and George, were known as the Rich for the treasure they amassed from silver, salt tolls and strict financial administration, kept in Trausnitz castle and the fortress of Burghausen. Louis IX founded the University of Ingolstadt in 1472, and the wedding of George to Hedwig Jagiellon in 1475 was among the most lavish festivals of the age.
duchy-of-bavaria-landshut.e: George died in 1503 without sons, leaving his lands to his son-in-law Rupert of the Palatinate in breach of Wittelsbach house law. The War of the Landshut Succession of 1503 to 1505 gave most lands to Albert IV of Bavaria-Munich, while Palatinate-Neuburg was created for Rupert's sons.

danish-india.t: Denmark's trading posts in India, led by Tranquebar on the Coromandel Coast, where the first Protestant missionaries in India began work in 1706.
danish-india.o: A Danish expedition under Ove Gjedde reached south India, and in 1620 Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur granted the Danish East India Company the village of Tranquebar (Tharangambadi). The Danes built Fort Dansborg there, which became the centre of their Asian trade.
danish-india.r: Danish India was governed by the company and later the crown, trading in textiles, pepper and tea. In 1706 the German missionaries Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, sent by the Danish king, founded the Tranquebar Mission and translated the New Testament into Tamil. Serampore near Calcutta, acquired in 1755, became a centre of printing and of Serampore College, founded by English Baptists. Denmark also claimed the Nicobar Islands.
danish-india.e: Overshadowed by British India and loss-making, Denmark sold Tranquebar and Serampore to Britain in 1845 and gave up its claim to the Nicobar Islands in 1868-1869. Fort Dansborg and Tranquebar's churches still stand.

duchy-of-berg.t: A Rhineland duchy east of the Rhine with its capital at Düsseldorf, which became part of the Jülich lands and later a Napoleonic grand duchy.
duchy-of-berg.o: Count Adolf of Berg appears in 1101 with a castle on the Dhün river; the family later built Burg Castle on the Wupper. Engelbert I of Berg, Archbishop of Cologne, was murdered in 1225. In 1288 Count Adolf V helped defeat the archbishop at Worringen and granted Düsseldorf town rights.
duchy-of-berg.r: Berg was raised to a duchy in 1380. In 1423 it was united with the Duchy of Jülich and in 1521 with Cleves. Its industry developed early in the Wupper valley and around Solingen, known for blades. Elector Johann Wilhelm of the Palatinate ruled from Düsseldorf in the early 18th century, building it into a court city.
duchy-of-berg.e: After 1614 Berg and Jülich belonged to Palatinate-Neuburg and later Bavaria. In 1806 Napoleon made Berg a grand duchy for his brother-in-law Joachim Murat. In 1815 it passed to Prussia, and Düsseldorf is now capital of North Rhine-Westphalia.

duchy-of-camerino.t: An Apennine lordship of the Varano family in the Marche, raised to a duchy in 1515 before the popes reclaimed it.
duchy-of-camerino.o: The Varano family took control of Camerino, a hill town in the central Apennines, in the second half of the 13th century; Gentile da Varano is recorded as its leader from 1262. They ruled as papal vicars within the Papal States.
duchy-of-camerino.r: The Varano governed a hilly region of the Marche with income from wool, paper and the papal service of their condottieri. Giulio Cesare da Varano rebuilt the ducal palace in the 15th century. In 1502 Cesare Borgia seized Camerino and had Giulio Cesare and several sons killed. A surviving son, Giovanni Maria, regained the city, and Pope Leo X made him duke in 1515.
duchy-of-camerino.e: Giovanni Maria's heiress Giulia da Varano married Guidobaldo II della Rovere of Urbino, but Pope Paul III took Camerino in 1539, and in 1545 it returned to direct government of the Papal States.

duchy-of-cieszyn.t: Silesian duchy on the Olza ruled by Piasts until 1653 and then by the Habsburgs, whose divided land now lies in both Poland and the Czech Republic.
duchy-of-cieszyn.o: In the partition of Upper Silesia after 1281, Mieszko received Cieszyn, and by 1290 it was a separate duchy. He and his heirs accepted Bohemian overlordship in 1327. Cieszyn lay on the route from Bohemia and Moravia to Kraków and Hungary, through the Moravian Gate and the Jablunkov Pass.
duchy-of-cieszyn.r: The Cieszyn Piasts ruled for over three centuries. Duke Wenceslaus III Adam introduced Lutheranism in the 16th century, and the duchy kept a strong Protestant community even after the Counter-Reformation. Polish, Czech and German were spoken. The duchy prospered from farming, cloth and later coal and iron.
duchy-of-cieszyn.e: The last Piast, Elizabeth Lucretia, died in 1653, and the Habsburgs took the duchy; Albert of Saxe-Teschen later held the title. It remained part of Austrian Silesia until 1918. After a brief Polish-Czechoslovak war, it was divided along the Olza in 1920, splitting Cieszyn itself in two.

duchy-of-mecklenburg.t: The Baltic duchy of the Obotrite-descended Niklotings, raised to ducal rank in 1348, whose partitions shaped north-east Germany until 1701.
duchy-of-mecklenburg.o: The Niklotings, descendants of the Obotrite prince Niklot, had ruled the Lordship of Mecklenburg since the 12th century. In 1348 Emperor Charles IV raised Albert II and his brother John to dukes of the empire. Albert's son Albert became King of Sweden in 1364, and the duchy later absorbed the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Stargard and the County of Schwerin.
duchy-of-mecklenburg.r: The dukes shared power with strong estates of knights and towns, including the Hanseatic ports of Rostock and Wismar, and Rostock University was founded in 1419. The Reformation was formally adopted in 1549. The economy rested on grain grown on noble estates by increasingly bound peasants, and repeated partitions, notably the creation of the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow in 1621, weakened the dukes.
duchy-of-mecklenburg.e: During the Thirty Years' War Wallenstein held Mecklenburg from 1628 to 1631. When the Güstrow line died out in 1695, a succession dispute followed, settled by the Hamburg Compromise of 1701, which divided the land into the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

delian-league.t: Athenian-led alliance formed against Persia in 478 BCE that turned into an Athenian empire funding the Parthenon and Athens' war with Sparta.
delian-league.o: After the defeat of Xerxes, the Ionian and Aegean Greeks wanted to continue the war against Persia and resented the Spartan commander Pausanias. In 478-477 BCE they swore an alliance with Athens on the sacred island of Delos. The Athenian Aristides assessed each member's contribution of ships or money, set at 460 talents a year.
delian-league.r: Delegates first met on Delos, where the treasury was kept, but Athens controlled the fleet and the treasurers. Over time most members paid tribute rather than providing ships, and revolts by Naxos (c. 470 BCE), Thasos (465 BCE) and Samos (440 BCE) were crushed. The treasury moved to Athens in 454 BCE, and Pericles used its funds for the buildings of the Acropolis. Athens imposed its coinage, courts and settlers on allies.
delian-league.e: Cimon's victory at the Eurymedon (c. 466 BCE) secured the Aegean. Rivalry with Sparta led to the Peloponnesian War, in which many allies revolted after the Sicilian disaster of 413 BCE. Athens' surrender in 404 BCE dissolved the league.

decapolis.t: A defensive league of ten Alsatian imperial cities, founded in 1354, that guarded their freedoms until Louis XIV absorbed them into France.
decapolis.o: In 1354 Emperor Charles IV approved an alliance of ten imperial cities in Alsace: Haguenau, Colmar, Wissembourg, Sélestat, Obernai, Kaysersberg, Rosheim, Munster, Turckheim and Mulhouse. They promised one another aid against the nobility and the bishop of Strasbourg, under the protection of the imperial bailiff (Landvogt) at Haguenau.
decapolis.r: The league had no central government; delegates met in assemblies to settle disputes, share military costs and defend each member's rights. Membership changed: Mulhouse left in 1515 to ally with the Old Swiss Confederacy, and the Free Imperial City of Landau took its place in 1521. The members divided over the Reformation, with Colmar and Landau becoming Protestant while others stayed Catholic.
decapolis.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 transferred the imperial bailiwick to France, whose kings treated it as sovereignty. Louis XIV forced the cities to submit and had their walls razed in 1673, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed their annexation to the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-olomouc.t: The main Moravian appanage duchy of the Přemyslid dynasty, seat of a bishopric and base for princes who contested the Bohemian throne.
duchy-of-olomouc.o: After Bretislaus I died in 1055, Moravia was divided among his sons. Olomouc in central Moravia went to Vratislaus, then in 1061 to Otto I the Fair, whose line held it through the 12th century. The bishopric of Olomouc was restored in 1063, making the town Moravia's religious centre.
duchy-of-olomouc.r: Olomouc princes such as Svatopluk, who seized Prague in 1107, and Otto III were influential figures in the dynasty's power struggles. The town grew around the castle, which included a Romanesque bishop's palace built by Bishop Jindřich Zdík in the 1140s.
duchy-of-olomouc.e: Late in the 12th century the Moravian appanages lost their separate status. Moravia became a margraviate under imperial recognition, and around 1197 Vladislaus Henry united it. Olomouc remained Moravia's ecclesiastical capital; its bishopric became an archbishopric in 1777.

duchy-of-nassau.t: Rhineland duchy with spas at Wiesbaden and Bad Ems, the first German state to grant a constitution after Napoleon.
duchy-of-nassau.o: In 1806 the principalities of Nassau-Usingen and Nassau-Weilburg united as the Duchy of Nassau and joined the Confederation of the Rhine. After 1815, the Congress of Vienna added former Orange-Nassau lands, consolidating a state between the Rhine, Main and Lahn, with Wiesbaden as capital.
duchy-of-nassau.r: Nassau adopted a constitution in 1814, the first of the German states. The duchy was mixed Catholic and Protestant, and in 1817 it created one of the first united Lutheran-Reformed churches. Spa towns such as Wiesbaden, Bad Ems and Schlangenbad attracted international visitors, and the Rheingau's vineyards and the Lahn's iron mines supported the economy.
duchy-of-nassau.e: Duke Adolphe sided with Austria in 1866, and Prussia annexed Nassau into the Province of Hesse-Nassau. Adolphe later became Grand Duke of Luxembourg in 1890, where his descendants still reign.

delmatae.t: Illyrian people of the Dalmatian hinterland who fought Rome for two centuries and gave their name to the province of Dalmatia.
delmatae.o: The Delmatae lived in the karst uplands behind the Adriatic coast, around Delminium (near modern Tomislavgrad). Around 180 BCE they broke away from the Illyrian king Gentius and built their own league, extending their power over neighbouring peoples and the coastal towns.
delmatae.r: Their league joined communities of herders and farmers living in hillforts. They raided the Daorsi and the Greek cities of Issa's mainland colonies. Rome fought them in 156–155 BCE, when Scipio Nasica destroyed Delminium, and again in 119 and 78–76 BCE. In 48–44 BCE they defeated Roman forces under Aulus Gabinius.
delmatae.e: Octavian's campaign of 34–33 BCE took their strongholds such as Promona. They rose again in the Great Illyrian Revolt of 6–9 CE, and their last fortress, Andetrium, fell to Tiberius in 9 CE. Their name lived on in the Roman province of Dalmatia.

duchy-of-pomerania-stolp.t: The eastern Pomeranian duchy ruled from Stolp, whose prince Eric of Pomerania became king of the Kalmar Union.
duchy-of-pomerania-stolp.o: In 1368 a new partition of Pomerania-Wolgast gave the lands of Further Pomerania, east of the Świna and Oder, to Duke Bogislaw V, who ruled from Stolp (Słupsk). His dynasty kept close ties with Poland, and his daughter Elizabeth married Emperor Charles IV.
duchy-of-pomerania-stolp.r: The duchy covered Further Pomerania, a land of farms, forests and small towns such as Stolp and Rügenwalde. Its dukes balanced between the State of the Teutonic Order, Poland and Denmark. Eric of Pomerania, grandson of Bogislaw V, was elected king of the Kalmar Union in 1397.
duchy-of-pomerania-stolp.e: Deposed from his Scandinavian thrones, Eric retired first to Gotland and from 1449 to Rügenwalde (Darłowo), where he ruled part of the duchy until his death in 1459. Stolp then passed to Eric II of Pomerania-Wolgast, and all the Pomeranian lands were later reunited by Bogislaw X.

duchy-of-mirandola.t: The small Emilian state of the Pico family, birthplace of the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, which lasted four centuries.
duchy-of-mirandola.o: The Pico family held lands around Mirandola, north of Modena, and in 1311 Francesco Pico was named imperial vicar there by Henry VII. The family ruled as lords and imperial vassals, and the state was raised to a principality in 1596 and a duchy in 1617.
duchy-of-mirandola.r: The Pico governed a fortified town and the countryside of Mirandola and Concordia, often allied with France. The humanist Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, author of the Oration on the Dignity of Man, was a younger son of the family. In 1511 Pope Julius II personally led the siege of the fortress. Family quarrels and murders were frequent.
duchy-of-mirandola.e: Duke Francesco Maria Pico sided with France in the War of the Spanish Succession and was deposed by the emperor in 1708. In 1710 Mirandola was sold to Rinaldo d'Este, joining the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

drougoubitai.t: Slavic tribe west of Thessalonica that besieged the city in the 7th century and later gave its name to a Byzantine bishopric.
drougoubitai.o: The Drougoubitai settled in the plain west and north-west of Thessalonica, towards the Vardar and Pelagonia, in the early 7th century. They appear in the Miracles of Saint Demetrius among the tribes that attacked Thessalonica.
drougoubitai.r: Known only from Byzantine sources, they lived under their own chiefs and alternated between hostility and alliance with Thessalonica, at times supplying the city with grain. In the 680s they were involved in the affair of Kuver's Bulgars, who settled near them.
drougoubitai.e: By the 9th century the southern Drougoubitai were within Byzantine rule, with a bishopric of Drougoubiteia, while northern lands fell to the First Bulgarian Empire. The tribe then disappears as a distinct group.

dardanian-kingdom.t: Kingdom of the Dardani in Kosovo and the upper Vardar, a persistent threat to Macedon that allied with Rome before being absorbed into Moesia.
dardanian-kingdom.o: The Dardani lived in the plains of Kosovo and around Scupi (Skopje) from at least the 4th century BCE. A Dardanian monarchy appears by the mid-4th century, and some historians count Bardylis, the Illyrian king who fought Philip II, as Dardanian.
dardanian-kingdom.r: Dardanian kings led a mixed Illyrian and Thracian population of farmers and herders. They raided Macedonia repeatedly and took advantage of the Celtic invasions of 279 BCE. King Longarus allied with Rome against Philip V of Macedon around 200 BCE, and King Monunius minted coins at Dyrrhachium. Roman writers described the Dardani as rough but musical.
dardanian-kingdom.e: Rome fought the Dardani during the 1st century BCE, and Marcus Licinius Crassus brought them under control in 28 BCE. Their land became part of the province of Moesia and later the late Roman province of Dardania, birthplace of Constantine the Great and Justinian.

duchy-of-merania.t: A title duchy of the Andechs counts on the Adriatic coast, whose family married into the royal houses of France, Hungary and Poland before dying out in 1248.
duchy-of-merania.o: In 1152 Frederick Barbarossa gave Count Conrad of Dachau the title Duke of Merania, a coastal area on the Kvarner Gulf of Croatia and Istria. After the Dachau line died out, the Andechs counts of Bavaria took the title in 1180, holding lands in Bavaria, Franconia, Tyrol, Istria and Burgundy.
duchy-of-merania.r: The duchy was more a title than a territory, but the Andechs-Merania dukes were among the leading princes of the Empire. Berthold IV's daughters married widely: Agnes became Queen of France, Gertrude Queen of Hungary and mother of Saint Elizabeth, and Hedwig Duchess of Silesia, later Saint Hedwig.
duchy-of-merania.e: The family lost lands after allegedly being involved in the murder of King Philip of Swabia in 1208. The last duke, Otto II, died in 1248, and the lands were divided among the Wittelsbachs, the counts of Tyrol and others. Andechs became a monastery.

duchy-of-oswiecim.t: A Silesian Piast duchy on the Vistula, under Bohemian overlordship until the Polish king bought it in 1457.
duchy-of-oswiecim.o: Oswiecim, west of Krakow, belonged to the Silesian Duchy of Cieszyn. In 1315 it was split off for Wladyslaw, a son of the duke of Cieszyn, who became the first duke of Oswiecim. In 1327 his successor did homage to John of Bohemia, making the duchy a fief of the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-oswiecim.r: The duchy was a small land on the upper Vistula, with salt and trade routes between Krakow, Silesia and Moravia. Its Piast dukes were minor rulers balancing between Bohemia and Poland. In 1445 its lands were divided, and the Duchy of Zator was created for one branch of the family.
duchy-of-oswiecim.e: In 1457 Duke Jan IV sold Oswiecim to Casimir IV of Poland for 50,000 marks, and it was fully incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569) in 1564. The town's German name, Auschwitz, was later given to the Nazi concentration and extermination camp built nearby.

duchy-of-holstein.t: A German duchy ruled by the kings of Denmark for four centuries, whose bond with Schleswig sparked two 19th-century wars.
duchy-of-holstein.o: In 1460 the estates of the Duchy of Schleswig and the County of Holstein elected King Christian I of Denmark as their ruler, promising that the lands would remain 'forever undivided'. In 1474 Emperor Frederick III raised Holstein, a fief of the empire, to a duchy.
duchy-of-holstein.r: Holstein was governed together with Schleswig, but while Schleswig was a Danish fief, Holstein belonged to the Holy Roman Empire and later the German Confederation. From 1544 it was split between the royal line and the Duchy of Holstein-Gottorp, with their lands intermingled. Glückstadt, founded by Christian IV in 1617, became the seat of royal government. Lutheranism took hold in the 16th century.
duchy-of-holstein.e: Danish attempts to tie Schleswig more closely to the kingdom led to war in 1848 to 1851 and again in 1864, when Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark. Holstein came under Austrian administration in 1865 and was annexed by Prussia in 1866, becoming part of the province of Schleswig-Holstein.

duchy-of-gascony.t: Duchy between the Garonne and the Pyrenees, set up by the Franks to contain the Basques, which became the core of Gascon identity.
duchy-of-gascony.o: Around 602 the Frankish kings created a Duchy of Vasconia under a duke named Genial to control the Basques, who had pushed north of the Pyrenees into the old Roman Novempopulana. The region soon slipped from Frankish control and was often allied with the dukes of the Early Duchy of Aquitaine.
duchy-of-gascony.r: The Basques were notoriously hard to govern: in 778 they ambushed Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux. From the late 9th century a native dynasty descended from Sancho Mitarra ruled largely independently. Duke William Sánchez defeated Viking raiders and founded the abbey of Saint-Sever, and Bordeaux became the ducal seat.
duchy-of-gascony.e: The male line ended with Sancho VI William in 1032. After a succession struggle, Guy-Geoffrey, count of Poitou, secured Gascony in the 1050s and united it with the Duchy of Aquitaine. Gascony passed with Aquitaine to the English kings and kept its own Occitan dialect.

duchy-of-menumorut.t: Realm in the Crișana region around Biharea attributed by the Gesta Hungarorum to Menumorut, who resisted and then made peace with the Hungarians.
duchy-of-menumorut.o: Menumorut is known only from the Gesta Hungarorum, written around 1200. It places his duchy between the Tisza, the Someș and the Igfon forest, with its fortress at Bihar (Biharea), inhabited by Khazars and other peoples, around the time of the Hungarian conquest of the 890s.
duchy-of-menumorut.r: The Gesta says Menumorut refused to cede land to Árpád, claiming the Byzantine emperor as his lord. Hungarian forces besieged Bihar, and he agreed to marry his daughter to Árpád's son Zoltán. Excavations at Biharea show a fortified site of the period, but no contemporary written source confirms the ruler.
duchy-of-menumorut.e: According to the Gesta, Menumorut died around 904 and his lands passed to Zoltán, joining the Principality of Hungary. Romanian and Hungarian historians still debate whether the duchy existed as described.

duchy-of-pomerania-wolgast.t: The western of the two Pomeranian duchies created by the Griffin partition of 1295, ruled from the castle of Wolgast near the Baltic coast.
duchy-of-pomerania-wolgast.o: In 1295 the Griffin brothers Bogislaw IV and Otto I divided the Duchy of Pomerania. Bogislaw took the coastal lands north of the Peene and ruled from Wolgast. In 1325 his line gained the Principality of Rügen, and later partitions split off further branches, including the Duchy of Pomerania-Stolp in 1368.
duchy-of-pomerania-wolgast.r: The Griffins were a Slavic dynasty that had become thoroughly German in culture. Power was shared with the estates and with Hanseatic towns such as Stralsund, Greifswald and Anklam, which grew rich on Baltic trade, and Greifswald University was founded in 1456. Johannes Bugenhagen, a Pomeranian, helped bring the Lutheran Reformation, adopted at the Diet of Treptow in 1534.
duchy-of-pomerania-wolgast.e: The duchy was reunited with Stettin under Bogislaw X from 1478 and split off again in 1532. When Duke Philip Julius died childless in 1625, Bogislaw XIV of Pomerania-Stettin inherited it, uniting Pomerania for the last time shortly before Sweden occupied it in 1630; most of it later became Swedish Pomerania.

duchy-of-ferrara.t: The Este state on the Po whose court made Ferrara a capital of Renaissance poetry, painting and town planning.
duchy-of-ferrara.o: In 1264 the citizens of the Commune of Ferrara proclaimed Obizzo II d'Este their perpetual lord. The Este, a feudal family with lands near Padua, held Ferrara as papal vicars and added Modena and Reggio. Pope Paul II made Borso d'Este duke of Ferrara in 1471.
duchy-of-ferrara.r: The Este ran a brilliant court. Ercole I's planned extension of the city, the Addizione Erculea, was one of the first modern urban plans. Ferrara supported the poets Boiardo, Ariosto and Tasso and the painters of the Schifanoia frescoes. Alfonso I, husband of Lucrezia Borgia, was famous for his artillery. The duchy was a papal fief, while Modena was held from the emperor.
duchy-of-ferrara.e: Alfonso II died without a legitimate heir in 1597. Pope Clement VIII refused to recognise his cousin Cesare, and in 1598 Ferrara passed to the Papal States. The Este moved their court to the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

decantae.t: People of Easter Ross in northern Scotland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name resembles that of the Deceangli of Wales.
decantae.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Decantae on the east coast of the northern Highlands, usually located in Easter Ross and the Black Isle around the Cromarty and Dornoch Firths. Their name resembles that of the Deceangli of north-east Wales, possibly reflecting a shared Celtic element rather than any direct link.
decantae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or society. The fertile coastlands of Easter Ross supported farming communities, and the area has numerous hillforts, including vitrified forts such as Knockfarrel and Craig Phadrig, whose stone walls were fused by intense fire.
decantae.e: The Decantae do not appear after Ptolemy. Easter Ross later became an important district of the Kingdom of the Picts, with major monastic and sculptural sites such as Portmahomack, Nigg and Shandwick.

duchy-of-gaeta.t: Small coastal state between Rome and Naples that broke free of Byzantium in the 9th century and lasted until the Normans absorbed it in 1140.
duchy-of-gaeta.o: Gaeta, a fortified promontory on the Tyrrhenian coast, was part of Byzantine territory loosely tied to the Duchy of Naples. In the 9th century, amid Arab raids and Lombard pressure, it gained autonomy under local rulers styled hypatoi (consuls). Around 867 Docibilis I founded the dynasty that made it a hereditary state.
duchy-of-gaeta.r: The rulers of Gaeta, who later took the title of duke, controlled a small territory around the Gulf of Gaeta and grew rich from sea trade. They sometimes allied with Arab raiders settled at the Garigliano, then joined the Christian coalition that destroyed that base in 915. The duchy minted its own copper coins, and its charters, the Codex Caietanus, document its society.
duchy-of-gaeta.e: From 1032 Gaeta fell under the Lombard princes of Capua and then under Norman lords. In 1140 it submitted to Roger II and joined the Kingdom of Sicily, keeping a degree of municipal autonomy.

duchy-of-romagna.t: Cesare Borgia's brief state in Romagna, carved out with papal backing and studied by Machiavelli as a model of ruthless princely power.
duchy-of-romagna.o: Between 1499 and 1501 Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander VI, conquered the small lordships of Romagna and the Marche, including Imola, Forlì, Pesaro, Rimini and Faenza, with French and papal troops. In 1501 his father named him Duke of Romagna, with Cesena as the seat of government.
duchy-of-romagna.r: Cesare imposed order on a region torn by petty lords, setting up a central court of justice, the Rota, at Cesena. He sent his harsh governor Ramiro de Lorca to pacify the region, then had him executed in the square of Cesena in December 1502 to win popularity. At Senigallia that month he trapped and killed rebellious captains. Niccolò Machiavelli, a Florentine envoy, observed him closely and later praised his methods in The Prince.
duchy-of-romagna.e: Alexander VI died in August 1503 while Cesare was gravely ill. Pope Julius II, a Borgia enemy, reclaimed the towns for the Papal States, while Venice seized Rimini and Faenza.

danish-osel.t: Danish-ruled island of Saaremaa, bought in the Livonian War in 1559 and held by Denmark until it was lost to Sweden in 1645.
danish-osel.o: In 1559 Bishop Johann von Münchhausen sold the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek to Frederick II of Denmark, who gave it to his brother Magnus of Holstein. Magnus landed on Saaremaa in 1560, but his ambitions soon took him to the mainland as Ivan IV's vassal king of the Kingdom of Livonia.
danish-osel.r: After Magnus died in 1583, Denmark ruled Ösel directly through governors at Arensburg (Kuressaare). The island's German nobility kept their estates and privileges, and Estonian peasants remained serfs. Denmark valued the island as an outpost in the eastern Baltic and as a bargaining counter against Sweden.
danish-osel.e: Denmark lost the Torstenson War against Sweden, and by the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645 it ceded Ösel to Sweden, together with Gotland, Jämtland and Härjedalen. The island joined Swedish Livonia, and after 1721 it passed to Russia.

duchy-of-strzelce.t: A minor Upper Silesian appanage duchy around Strzelce, created in the Opole partition of 1313 and later reabsorbed by its parent duchy.
duchy-of-strzelce.o: When Bolko I of Opole died in 1313, his son Albert received Strzelce (Strehlitz), east of Opole, as his share of the Duchy of Opole. Albert did homage to King John of Bohemia in 1327, placing the small duchy under the Kingdom of Bohemia.
duchy-of-strzelce.r: The duchy comprised the castle town of Strzelce and its surrounding farmland. Its later history is poorly documented: after Albert's death it was held by members of the Opole dynasty, sometimes as a dower or appanage rather than as a fully separate state.
duchy-of-strzelce.e: By the mid-15th century Strzelce had been reabsorbed into the Duchy of Opole, which itself fell to the Bohemian crown in 1532. The town followed Silesia to Prussia in 1742 and to Poland in 1945, as Strzelce Opolskie.

duchy-of-carinthia.t: The oldest duchy of the Austrian lands, heir to Slavic Carantania, which kept its unique installation rite at the Prince's Stone until 1414.
duchy-of-carinthia.o: In 976 Emperor Otto II separated Carinthia from the Duchy of Bavaria to weaken the rebellious Duke Henry the Quarrelsome, creating the first new duchy of the Empire. It included Carantania and huge marches extending to Verona, Styria and Carniola, many of which later became separate.
duchy-of-carinthia.r: Dukes were installed at the Prince's Stone near Karnburg and the Duke's Chair on the Zollfeld, in a ceremony partly in Slovene. Ruling families included the Eppensteiners and the Sponheimers. The population was mixed German and Slovene. Mining of lead and iron, and the Habsburg rebuilding of Klagenfurt as capital from 1518, shaped later centuries.
duchy-of-carinthia.e: In 1335 the Habsburgs inherited Carinthia, which stayed in their hands as a crown land until 1918. The plebiscite of 1920 kept southern Carinthia in Austria, though some areas went to Yugoslavia and Italy. It is today an Austrian federal state.
